Autonomous systems must be justified with logic, testing, and repeatable performance. What evidence would you need? For a system claim, select the proof that shows how the logic or mechanism actually performed. Reveal Answer Best evidence: a labeled logic/system diagram plus mission test data, sensor readings, or repeated performance results connected to the claim. What should the engineer do next? Reveal Answer Engineering move: Record the failure point, identify the likely cause, revise the logic or mechanism, and retest with the same procedure. Evidence or opinion? Which statement is strongest: “It looks reliable,” “It completed 4 of 5 trials,” or “We changed the threshold because the sensor triggered early twice”? Reveal Answer Strongest: The threshold statement is evidence-based reasoning because it connects a revision to repeated observations. The 4-of-5 result is also useful performance evidence. Presentation and Course Hub Lesson Presentation Course Hub POE Unit 5 • Lesson 5.18 Capstone Design Review and Portfolio Reflection Focus question: How can you defend my capstone design using evidence and reflect on my growth as an aerospace engineering student. Download Presentation Back to Unit 5 POE Course Hub Capstone Evidence Connect requirements, subsystems, fabrication, testing, and documentation into a defensible aerospace engineering solution. DEFINE BUILD DEFEND Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning target I can defend my capstone design using evidence and reflect on my growth as an aerospace engineering student. Success looks like… You can explain how today’s capstone artifact supports a requirement, design decision, test result, or final defense. Deliverable Final design review and portfolio reflection Lesson Sequence From Capstone Question to Evidence Each step moves the final project from an idea toward a defensible engineering solution. Opening prompt: How does capstone design review and portfolio reflection move the capstone forward? Capstone connection: Identify the requirement, subsystem, evidence, or decision today’s work supports. Interactive vote: Choose the strongest capstone action and justify it. Guided work time: Build the deliverable using clear labels, notes, measurements, sketches, CAD, test plans, or data. Exit ticket: Identify what changed, what evidence supports it, and what needs to happen next. POE Connection Capstone Design Review and Portfolio Reflection in Context Capstone work should always connect a design decision to requirements and evidence. Mission requirement What must the system accomplish, and how will success be measured? Subsystem evidence What sketches, CAD, build notes, code, wiring, test data, or observations show how the system works? Design defense What decision can the team justify using the evidence collected today? Interactive Checks Questions to Use During the Lesson Use the reveal boxes after students vote, discuss, or write a quick response. Which action best supports a strong capstone decision? Options: choose the easiest idea; use requirements and evidence; focus only on appearance; or save documentation until the end. Reveal answer Best answer: use requirements and evidence. A capstone decision should be traceable to criteria, constraints, test results, observations, or documented trade-offs. What should the team do when the prototype works once but fails twice? The system succeeds in one trial, but repeated tests show inconsistent results. Reveal answer Record all trials, identify the failure mode, revise the weak subsystem or test setup, and retest before making a final claim. items.searchText: Centroids and Structural Cross-Sections POE Lesson 2.8: Centroids and Structural Cross-Sections | LockwoodSTEM A 45-minute Principles of Engineering lesson: Centroids and Structural Cross-Sections. You can describe how centroid location affects balance, loading, and structural behavior. 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like… How does centroid location affect balance, loading, and structural behavior? Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust What acts on it? What resists it? What proves it? Which Action Fits? Best answer: 2 Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Claim Evidence Reasoning What Evidence Would You Need? Best support: A + C What Should the Engineer Do Next? Best answer: B What You Submit Student Deliverables Before You Leave Lesson 2.8 Resources Lesson 2.8 Student Presentation POE Unit 2 • Lesson 2.8 Centroids and Structural Cross-Sections Focus Question: How does centroid location affect balance, loading, and structural behavior? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Objective You can describe how centroid location affects balance, loading, and structural behavior. Use structures, materials, loads, data, and evidence-based decisions to prepare for the payload support challenge. Analyze Test Justify Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets describe how centroid location affects balance, loading, and structural behavior. Connect today’s skill to aerospace structures and payload support systems. Identify evidence needed to support a structural design claim. Success Looks Like… You can make a structural decision using vocabulary, calculations, observations, or test data instead of “it seems strong.” Core habit: claim + evidence + reasoning. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Quick vote 7 min Structures link 8 min Core skill 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Scenario check 3 min Exit ticket Opening Prompt How does centroid location affect balance, loading, and structural behavior? Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection The centroid helps locate the balance point and understand how cross-section geometry affects structural behavior. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. The strongest next step turns a structural weakness into useful evidence. Mission Debrief What You Submit Use the required class format or Google Classroom instructions when assigned. items.searchText: Closed-Loop Control and Feedback POE Lesson 3.7: Closed-Loop Control and Feedback | LockwoodSTEM POE Unit 3 lesson page for Closed-Loop Control and Feedback You can explain how feedback can improve an autonomous aerospace system. Lesson Sequence What You Should Be Able To Do Closed-Loop Control and Feedback Key Idea Student Activity Aerospace Connection Question First, Reveal Second Which choice sounds most like engineering? What evidence would you need? What should the engineer do next? Evidence or opinion? Evidence for Lesson 3.7 Required evidence Quality check Exit ticket Lesson 3.7 Resources Lesson 3.7 Student Presentation Principles of Engineering POE Unit 3 • Lesson 3.7 Closed-Loop Control and Feedback Focus Question: How does feedback help an autonomous aerospace system adjust its behavior? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 3 Mission Objective You can explain how feedback can improve an autonomous aerospace system. Use mission logic, sensors, actuators, feedback, and test evidence to develop autonomous aerospace systems. Plan Test Iterate 45-Minute Flight Plan Lesson Sequence A focused class period that moves from mission logic to evidence-based system decisions. 5 min opening 6 min quick vote 7 min concept launch 8 min compare systems 10 min evidence challenge 6 min quick check 3 min debrief Learning Targets What You Should Be Able To Do Target You can explain how feedback can improve an autonomous aerospace system. Success Looks Like You can explain a control-system choice using logic, sensor data, testing, or system evidence rather than opinion. Evidence Output Feedback loop diagram Core Lesson Idea Closed-Loop Control and Feedback The presentation provides the full student-facing sequence; this page gives the key structure for the lesson. Key Idea Feedback loops compare what is happening to what should happen, then adjust the system to reduce error. Student Activity Diagram a feedback loop and explain how the system detects and corrects error. Aerospace Connection Connect the lesson to autonomous rovers, drones, sensors, ground-support systems, actuators, and mission-readiness testing. Interactive Checkpoints Question First, Reveal Second Use the prompts to create discussion before opening the answers. Which choice sounds most like engineering? Choose the option that compares system decisions against mission criteria and evidence. Reveal Answer Best answer: Compare options against criteria and evidence before deciding. Autonomous systems must be justified with logic, testing, and repeatable performance. What evidence would you need? For a system claim, select the proof that shows how the logic or mechanism actually performed. Reveal Answer Best evidence: a labeled logic/system diagram plus mission test data, sensor readings, or repeated performance results connected to the claim. What should the engineer do next? If a rover or ground-support system works once but fails on the next trial, what is the strongest next step? Reveal Answer Engineering move: Record the failure point, identify the likely cause, revise the logic or mechanism, and retest with the same procedure. Evidence or opinion? Which statement is strongest: “It looks reliable,” “It completed 4 of 5 trials,” or “We changed the threshold because the sensor triggered early twice”? Reveal Answer Strongest: The threshold statement is evidence-based reasoning because it connects a revision to repeated observations. The 4-of-5 result is also useful performance evidence. What You Submit Evidence for Lesson 3.7 Required evidence Feedback loop diagram Quality check Use clear labels and relevant vocabulary. Connect the evidence to the mission or system claim. Record test results, observations, or decisions clearly enough for another engineer to follow. Exit ticket One way this lesson connects to autonomous aerospace systems. One type of evidence that could support a system decision. One question you still have about control, sensors, actuators, feedback, or fluid power. items.searchText: Concept Generation and Decision Matrix IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.11 | Concept Generation and Decision Matrix | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 4 Lesson 4.11: Concept Generation and Decision Matrix. How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria? You can generate mechanism concepts and use a decision matrix to support a concept selection. 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria? What We Are Practicing Use These Moves Apply the Skill Which action best supports today’s engineering goal? What evidence would you need? What should the engineer do next? What You Submit Lesson Resources Lesson 4.11 PowerPoint Introduction to Engineering Design IED Unit 4 • Lesson 4.11 Concept Generation and Decision Matrix Focus question: How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria? Download Presentation Flight Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can generate mechanism concepts and use a decision matrix to support a concept selection. Generate Score Select Use system evidence to make the materials, mechanism, circuit, data, or prototype decision easier to inspect and defend. Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, prototype materials, and class data. Learning Targets Generate multiple possible concepts before choosing one. Use criteria to compare mechanism options fairly. Explain how decision matrix results support the selected concept. Success Looks Like You can generate mechanism concepts and use a decision matrix to support a concept selection. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria? Think first, then share one short response that connects today’s skill to materials, motion, circuit behavior, data quality, or prototype performance. Reveal: useful engineering move Start by naming the evidence you need before deciding the work is ready. In Unit 4, strong work is not just complete; it can be tested, explained, revised, and connected to system performance. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Concept generation prevents teams from locking into the first idea too soon. Key Idea 2 A decision matrix turns criteria into a more transparent comparison. Key Idea 3 Scores should be explained with evidence, not used as magic answers. Engineering Workflow Use These Moves Identify the system goal or design decision. Use today’s lesson to collect or create meaningful evidence. Apply the material, mechanism, circuit, data, CAD, or prototype skill carefully. Save the note, graph, sketch, photo, measurement, model, or test result that proves the work. Student Task Apply the Skill Create a short decision matrix comparing at least two prototype mechanism concepts. Checkpoint: be ready to show the evidence that proves your work is controlled, accurate, functional, tested, or ready to revise. Interactive Check Which action best supports today’s engineering goal? A Copy the first example without checking the system goal B Use today’s evidence to make a controlled design or system decision C Choose the easiest option because it is fastest D Make the prototype look complete before testing it Reveal Answer B — Use today’s evidence to make a controlled design or system decision. B — Compare multiple options against criteria before choosing a concept. Evidence Challenge What evidence would you need? Claim: “My concept generation and decision matrix work is accurate and ready to move forward.” A A photo, graph, sketch, or model view that shows the work B A statement that it looks good C Relevant measurements, test results, circuit checks, or observations D A file name that does not identify the lesson or prototype Reveal Answer A + C are the strongest evidence pair. A shows what was created or observed. C shows whether it meets the requirement or supports the design decision. Vague confidence is not enough. Scenario Response What should the engineer do next? A student working on this lesson notices the result does not match the expected system behavior. A Ignore it and keep going because the task is almost finished B Record the issue, identify the likely cause, revise, and check again C Delete the evidence and restart without notes D Choose the faster option even if it cannot be justified Reveal Answer B — Record the issue, identify the likely cause, revise, and check again. The strongest next step turns the problem into useful engineering evidence instead of hiding it or guessing. Student Deliverables What You Submit Engineering notebook entry for Lesson 4.11. Evidence connected to the lesson focus: sketch, material test, graph, photo, circuit check, prototype observation, CAD screenshot, or revision note. Short explanation connecting your evidence to a system decision. Exit response identifying what is ready, what changed, or what still needs revision. How can engineers generate creative solutions without choosing the first idea too quickly? You can generate multiple concepts and connect each idea to user needs and design criteria. 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like How can engineers generate creative solutions without choosing the first idea too quickly? What We Are Practicing Use These Moves Apply the Skill Which action best supports today’s engineering goal? What evidence would you need? What should the engineer do next? What You Submit Lesson Resources Lesson 5.5 PowerPoint Introduction to Engineering Design IED Unit 5 • Lesson 5.5 Concept Generation and Human-Centered Ideation Focus question: How can engineers generate creative solutions without choosing the first idea too quickly? Download Presentation Flight Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 5 Mission Focus You can generate multiple concepts and connect each idea to user needs and design criteria. Generate Diverge Connect Use user-centered evidence to make the capstone design decision easier to inspect, defend, and improve. Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, capstone planning tools, and prototype evidence. Learning Targets Generate multiple possible design concepts. Avoid selecting the first idea too early. Connect ideas to user needs, criteria, and constraints. Success Looks Like You can generate multiple concepts and connect each idea to user needs and design criteria. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How can engineers generate creative solutions without choosing the first idea too quickly? Think first, then share one short response that connects today’s skill to a user need, stakeholder, design criterion, prototype decision, or piece of evidence. Reveal: useful engineering move Start by naming the evidence you need before deciding the work is ready. In Unit 5, strong capstone work is not just complete; it is user-centered, responsible, tested, revised, and communicated clearly. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Early ideation should create options before narrowing. Key Idea 2 Creative ideas still need to connect to the user need. Key Idea 3 Sketches help teams compare features, tradeoffs, and assumptions. Engineering Workflow Use These Moves Identify the user need, stakeholder, or responsible design decision. Use today’s lesson to collect or create meaningful evidence. Apply the capstone skill carefully: research, define, plan, model, build, test, revise, or present. Save the note, sketch, CAD view, feedback, test result, photo, or reflection that proves the work. Student Task Apply the Skill Generate multiple concept sketches or descriptions and annotate how each concept supports the user need. Checkpoint: be ready to show evidence that connects the capstone work to the user need, criteria, feedback, testing, revision, responsibility, or final communication. Interactive Check Which action best supports today’s engineering goal? A Choose the first idea because it is easiest to build B Use today’s evidence to make a user-centered design decision C Make the prototype look complete before checking the user need D Ignore stakeholder feedback if it complicates the plan Reveal Answer B — Use today’s evidence to make a user-centered design decision. B — Generate several options and compare them against the user need. Evidence Challenge What evidence would you need? Claim: “My concept generation and human-centered ideation work is accurate and ready to move forward.” A A sketch, model, stakeholder note, plan, or prototype view that shows the work B A statement that the team likes the idea C Relevant criteria, feedback, test results, measurements, or observations D A polished page with no evidence or explanation Reveal Answer A + C are the strongest evidence pair. A shows what was created or observed. C shows whether it meets the user need, criterion, or responsible design claim. Vague confidence is not enough. Scenario Response What should the engineer do next? A team working on this lesson notices that its evidence does not fully support the capstone decision it wants to make. Learning Targets Describe the purpose of IED through an aerospace lens. Explain how engineering problems differ from typical assignments. Identify evidence engineers use to support design decisions. Success Looks Like… You can explain a design decision using more than “I think.” Core habit: Connect each design claim to evidence another person can inspect. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Engineer-actions vote 7 min IED + aerospace 8 min Mindset shift 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Quick check 3 min Exit debrief Opening Prompt What do engineers do? Think about actions, habits, and decisions—not job titles. Quick class share: Give one short answer using an action word such as design, build, test, fix, invent, solve, measure, or improve. Reveal the working definition Engineers use knowledge, tools, and creativity to solve problems under real constraints. 1 Define Clarify the need, user, criteria, and constraints. 2 Generate Create multiple possible solutions before choosing one. 3 Test Collect evidence from models, prototypes, data, and feedback. 4 Communicate Document decisions so others can understand and improve the work. Interactive Vote Engineer Actions: Which One Fits? Hold up fingers 1–4 or vote silently. Then justify your choice. Which action sounds most like engineering work? 1 Copying exact instructions to make the same model as everyone else 2 Choosing the first idea because it seems easiest to build 3 Testing two versions and comparing data before deciding 4 Making a design look impressive without checking if it works Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 3 Testing two versions and comparing data before deciding uses comparison, data, and a decision based on evidence. The other choices prioritize copying, ease, or appearance rather than proof. Carry-forward idea: In IED, an answer becomes stronger when it connects to evidence. Course Launch IED Through an Aerospace Lens Build transferable engineering habits through aerospace contexts and projects. Core Engineering Skills Sketching and visual communication Engineering notebook documentation CAD modeling and technical drawings Prototyping, testing, and data analysis Design reviews and evidence-based explanations Aerospace Connections Rocket launch pad design challenge Rocket models and assemblies Aircraft, drones, satellites, and rovers FabLab tools and manufacturing routines Human-centered aerospace capstone Turn + Talk Aerospace Connection Map Choose a rocket, drone, satellite, rover, or aircraft . Identify one design choice an engineer must make, then connect it to one kind of evidence. Sketch What features or shapes matter? Model What could be represented in CAD? Measure What dimensions or data matter? Test What would prove it works? Share-out target: one system + one design decision + one kind of evidence. Mindset Shift Assignment vs. Engineering Problem The goal is not just to finish; the goal is to make a design claim you can defend. Completion Mindset Typical Assignment Often has one expected answer Can be completed and put away Usually judged as correct or incorrect Mistakes are avoided Evidence Mindset Engineering Problem Has multiple possible solutions Must satisfy criteria and constraints Uses testing to compare designs Mistakes become evidence for improvement Key Idea Evidence-Based Engineering Engineers connect what they claim to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the design → 2 Evidence What proves or challenges the claim → 3 Decision What you do next because of the evidence Evidence can include: sketches; measurements; test data; observations; photos; prototypes; user feedback. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the two pieces of evidence that best support the claim. Claim: “Our launch pad design supports the rocket safely and is ready for testing.” A A labeled sketch showing where the rocket contacts the support B A photo that makes the prototype look finished C A stability test showing the pad does not tip with the rocket placed on it D A teammate saying the design is probably strong enough E A list of the materials used to build the base and support Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows design intent and the support locations. C provides direct performance evidence against a safety and stability criterion. Photos, material lists, and teammate opinions can support the story, but they do not prove the claim by themselves. Identify evidence needed to support a structural design claim. Success Looks Like… You can make a structural decision using vocabulary, calculations, observations, or test data instead of “it seems strong.” Core habit: claim + evidence + reasoning. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Quick vote 7 min Structures link 8 min Core skill 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Scenario check 3 min Exit ticket Opening Prompt Why do engineers test materials to failure and interpret stress-strain behavior? Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection Testing to failure reveals elastic behavior, yield, ultimate strength, fracture, and how materials respond under increasing load. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. The strongest next step turns a structural weakness into useful evidence. Mission Debrief What You Submit Use the required class format or Google Classroom instructions when assigned. Best answer: B Leave with a complete design-process artifact What You Submit Required notebook artifact Lesson 0.5 Lesson 0.4 Resources Lesson 0.4 Student Presentation Paper Airplane Design Process Worksheet STEMonstrations: Engineering Design Process Introduction to Engineering Design IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.4 Engineering Design Process Focus Question: How do engineers use testing and revision to improve a design? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Run a complete design cycle Use a paper-airplane challenge to define, build, test, compare, and revise a design with measurable evidence. Design Test Revise Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Complete a fast, measurable design cycle and create the first numbered notebook artifact. Learning Targets Describe the engineering design process as a flexible cycle. Apply the cycle to a paper-airplane distance challenge. Use test evidence to revise a design. Success Looks Like… You can explain what changed between Version 1 and Version 2 and support the change with test data. Core habit: A revision needs a reason, and the reason should come from evidence. 5 min Opening prompt 7 min Design cycle 6 min Challenge briefing 15 min Version 1 7 min Version 2 3 min Compare evidence 2 min Exit Opening Prompt Is the first design supposed to be the best? Engineers use early versions to create evidence—not to prove they were right immediately. Quick class share: Why might a first prototype be useful even when it does not perform well? Reveal the design-process idea The design process is a flexible cycle. Engineers define, generate, develop, construct, test, evaluate, revise, and communicate—often moving backward and forward as evidence changes. Design Cycle A flexible process—not a rigid checklist Different projects may repeat or combine stages. 1 Define Clarify the goal, criteria, and constraints. 2 Generate Create multiple possible solutions. 3 Develop Select and plan a promising approach. 4 Construct + Test Build a prototype and collect evidence. 5 Evaluate + Revise Compare results and improve the design. 6 Present Communicate the design and next steps. Design Sprint Paper Airplane Distance Challenge Complete one fast cycle with measurable evidence. Version 1 Create one individual concept sketch. Choose one team Version 1 concept. Build with one sheet of paper. Complete one official distance test. Record the distance to first ground contact. Version 2 Study Version 1 evidence. Choose one deliberate revision. Build with one new sheet of paper. Complete one official distance test. Compare the two results. Measurement: Record distance from the launch line to the first ground contact in feet and inches. Decision Challenge Which revision is evidence-based? Vote before revealing the answer. Version 1 curves sharply left and lands after 18 ft. Which Version 2 decision is strongest? A Change several folds at once because more change is better. B Adjust the uneven wing fold, keep other features the same, and retest. C Decorate the airplane so it looks faster. D Build a completely different airplane without recording Version 1. Reveal the evidence-based revision Best answer: B The observed left curve points to an asymmetry. Changing one likely cause makes the next test easier to interpret. Strong revision: observed problem → targeted change → new test. Evidence Check Leave with a complete design-process artifact Your worksheet becomes the first numbered notebook document. 1 Individual concept sketch is complete. 2 Version 1 and Version 2 distances are recorded. 3 The revision is described clearly. 4 The decision is supported by evidence. 5 The worksheet is numbered and added to the Table of Contents. Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Make thinking visible Improve notebook evidence so another person can trace what happened, why it changed, and what supports the decision. Label Record Explain Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Turn rough notes into clear, dated, labeled, evidence-based documentation. Learning Targets Explain what strong engineering documentation looks like. Improve the Lesson 0.4 paper-airplane worksheet. Connect documentation quality to engineering decisions and communication. Success Looks Like… Another person can understand your design, test, and revision without asking you to fill in missing details. Core habit: Document enough information for someone else to follow the work later. 5 min Opening prompt 8 min Weak vs. strong 8 min Documentation standard 15 min Revision workshop 5 min Peer check 2 min File work 2 min Exit Opening Prompt Could another person understand your work? Good documentation is written for the future reader—not only for the person who completed the activity. Quick class share: What information would be missing from the note “It worked”? Reveal the documentation standard Strong documentation makes engineering thinking visible. It is clear, dated, labeled, evidence-based, and detailed enough to support a review or repeat the work. Compare Weak vs. Strong Documentation More words do not automatically create better evidence. Weak Evidence Undated or unlabeled notes Missing sketches or measurements Vague claims such as “it worked” No explanation of changes Hard for another person to follow Strong Evidence Dated, labeled, and organized Sketches show important features Data and observations are specific Decisions are explained with evidence Another person can understand the work Documentation Standard Use five checks throughout the course These checks apply to notebook pages, photos, screenshots, data tables, and design-review evidence. Clear Another person can understand what happened. Dated The work can be traced over time. Labeled Sketches, tables, and images have meaning. Evidence-Based Claims connect to data or observations. Review-Ready There is enough detail to explain a decision. Revision Workshop Improve the Lesson 0.4 artifact Use the documentation standard to strengthen the paper-airplane worksheet. Review the evidence Check the date and page number. Verify that sketches and versions are labeled. Confirm that both distances are recorded. Replace vague statements with specific observations. Explain why the revision was chosen. Upgrade a weak note Weak: “We fixed the wing and it worked better.” Stronger: “Version 1 curved left. We corrected the uneven left-wing fold. Version 2 traveled 12 ft farther and followed a straighter path.” Quick Check Which note is review-ready? Vote before opening the answer. 1 “Changed it because it was bad.” 2 “After Version 1 curved left, we leveled the wing tips. Version 2 traveled straighter.” Reveal the stronger note Best answer: 2 It identifies the observation, the change, and the result. The reader can follow the reasoning. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Concept vote 7 min Aerospace link 8 min Compare options 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Quick check 3 min Exit ticket Lesson Targets What Students Should Be Able To Do Learning Target I can present a mechanism design and justify it using sketches, calculations, prototype evidence, and test data. Evidence Final design review presentation and reflection Success Looks Like Students can explain a mechanism decision using vocabulary, measurements, calculations, test observations, or design evidence. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves The page highlights only the student-facing elements that make sense outside the full slide deck. 1. Start with the mission problem Students identify what engineering task this topic helps solve: lift, move, rotate, transfer, measure, support, power, or control. 2. Connect to aerospace systems Students map the topic to a rover, aircraft, rocket, drone, or satellite mechanism and name the evidence that would prove it worked. 3. Use evidence to decide Students compare mechanism choices and practice choosing evidence that supports a claim rather than relying on appearance or preference. Interactive Checks Questions Before Answers Use the prompts first. Expand the answer only after students vote or respond. Prompt 1: Which choice sounds most like engineering? Students choose among easy, copied, impressive-looking, or evidence-based decision-making. Reveal answer Best answer: Compare options against criteria and evidence before deciding. This keeps the decision connected to the problem, measurable expectations, and proof another person can inspect. Prompt 2: What evidence would you need? Students select the strongest evidence for a mechanism decision that is ready to use in the Unit 1 challenge. Reveal answer Best evidence: a labeled sketch/diagram plus measurement, calculation, or repeated test data. Photos and preferences can support the story, but they do not prove performance by themselves. Prompt 3: What should the engineer do next? Mechanical advantage is evidence. It compares input and output force or distance so a design claim can be tested. 45-Minute Flight Plan What Students Should Be Able To Do How the Lesson Moves 1. Download Presentation Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Mechanical advantage is evidence. It compares input and output force or distance so a design claim can be tested. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Concept vote 7 min Aerospace link 8 min Compare options 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Quick check 3 min Exit ticket Lesson Targets What Students Should Be Able To Do Learning Target I can calculate work and mechanical advantage using measured force and distance data from a mechanism. Evidence Work and mechanical advantage calculation set Success Looks Like Students can explain a mechanism decision using vocabulary, measurements, calculations, test observations, or design evidence. Activity Flow How the Lesson Moves The page highlights only the student-facing elements that make sense outside the full slide deck. 1. Start with the mission problem Students identify what engineering task this topic helps solve: lift, move, rotate, transfer, measure, support, power, or control. 2. Connect to aerospace systems Students map the topic to a rover, aircraft, rocket, drone, or satellite mechanism and name the evidence that would prove it worked. 3. Use evidence to decide Students compare mechanism choices and practice choosing evidence that supports a claim rather than relying on appearance or preference. Interactive Checks Questions Before Answers Use the prompts first. Expand the answer only after students vote or respond. Prompt 1: Which choice sounds most like engineering? Students choose among easy, copied, impressive-looking, or evidence-based decision-making. Reveal answer Best answer: Compare options against criteria and evidence before deciding. This keeps the decision connected to the problem, measurable expectations, and proof another person can inspect. Prompt 2: What evidence would you need? Students select the strongest evidence for a mechanism decision that is ready to use in the Unit 1 challenge. Reveal answer Best evidence: a labeled sketch/diagram plus measurement, calculation, or repeated test data. Photos and preferences can support the story, but they do not prove performance by themselves. Prompt 3: What should the engineer do next? A mechanism works once but produces inconsistent output on the next trial. Reveal answer Best next step: record the issue, identify the likely cause, revise one thing, and retest. The engineering move is to use the problem as data rather than hiding or restarting without learning. Today’s Student Work Main Deliverable Work and mechanical advantage calculation set Use force and distance data to calculate work and mechanical advantage for a mechanism. Label the mechanism, input, output, motion, and evidence clearly. Use data, calculations, or observations when available. Connect the work to the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Objective You can identify tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads in aerospace structures. Analyze Test Justify Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets identify tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads in aerospace structures. Connect today’s skill to aerospace structures and payload support systems. Identify evidence needed to support a structural design claim. Success Looks Like… You can make a structural decision using vocabulary, calculations, observations, or test data instead of “it seems strong.” Core habit: claim + evidence + reasoning. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Quick vote 7 min Structures link 8 min Core skill 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Scenario check 3 min Exit ticket Opening Prompt How do different force and load types affect aerospace structures? Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection Loads such as tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed forces create different failure risks. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. The strongest next step turns a structural weakness into useful evidence. Mission Debrief What You Submit Use the required class format or Google Classroom instructions when assigned. Think about systems, tools, safety habits, models, and evidence—not just finishing a task. Quick class share: What evidence, tool, or system behavior would help answer today’s focus question? C shows whether it meets the requirement or supports the design decision. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? A Ignore it and keep going because the task is almost finished B Record the issue, identify the likely cause, revise, and check again C Delete the evidence and restart without notes D Choose the faster option even if it cannot be justified Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the issue, identify the likely cause, revise, and check again. A test should answer a specific question connected to a design requirement. Quick class share: What is the difference between “try it” and “test it”? Reveal the testing standard A useful test has a criterion, a repeatable action, and evidence to record. The result should guide a clear next decision. Aerospace Context Testing happens before commitment Real launch systems are checked as integrated structures, not only as separate parts. Before launch, integrated systems are checked against specific operating requirements. Classroom tests should also connect directly to criteria. Image: NASA/Aubrey Gemignani, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Test Criteria Match each test to a requirement Record what actually happens—not what the team hoped would happen. Stability Test Does the pad stand without tipping? Record: pass/fail, wobble, tipping direction, photo. Rocket Fit Test Does the provided rocket sit securely? Record: contact points, slipping, movement, alignment. Support Test Does the structure hold without bending or collapsing? Record: weak joints, bending, sliding, deformation. Feature Check Can the team explain the function of realistic launch-pad features? Record: labels and functional explanation. Test Cycle Test → record → revise The improvement must connect to an observed weakness. 1 Test Run the criteria checks consistently. → 2 Record Identify strengths, weaknesses, and failure points. → 3 Revise Make one evidence-based improvement and retest. Improvement Options Choose changes that address test results Do not add parts without a reason. Widen the base to improve stability. Reinforce weak joints or support columns. Adjust rocket-support spacing or angle. Add bracing to reduce bending or twisting. Improve alignment so the rocket sits securely. Remove parts that add weight without function. Scenario Response The pad holds the rocket but wobbles Choose the strongest next step before opening the answer. A Keep it because it did not fall. B Add realistic-looking details. C Record the wobble, locate the weak area, revise the base or supports, and retest. D Repeat the same test without recording anything. Reveal the evidence-based next step Best answer: C The wobble is a specific weakness. The team should record it, target the likely cause, and collect new evidence after revision. Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection Repeatable procedures make test data trustworthy enough to compare materials, structures, and design changes. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. Analyze Test Justify Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets perform non-destructive tests and use observations to infer useful material properties. Connect today’s skill to aerospace structures and payload support systems. Identify evidence needed to support a structural design claim. Success Looks Like… You can make a structural decision using vocabulary, calculations, observations, or test data instead of “it seems strong.” Core habit: claim + evidence + reasoning. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Quick vote 7 min Structures link 8 min Core skill 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Scenario check 3 min Exit ticket Opening Prompt How can non-destructive tests reveal useful material properties without damaging a part? Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection Non-destructive tests provide observations about stiffness, flexibility, surface condition, or defects without destroying the sample. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. The strongest next step turns a structural weakness into useful evidence. Mission Debrief What You Submit Use the required class format or Google Classroom instructions when assigned. A Move quickly without checking evidence B Use today’s evidence to make a controlled design or documentation decision C Choose the easiest option and hope it works D Make the work look complete without verifying it Reveal Answer B — Use today’s evidence to make a controlled design or documentation decision. Evidence Output Fluid power calculation set Core Lesson Idea Pressure, Force, and Pascal’s Law The presentation provides the full student-facing sequence; this page gives the key structure for the lesson. Key Idea Pascal’s Law explains how pressure applied through a confined fluid can create force at another location based on area. Student Activity Complete pressure-force-area calculations and interpret what changes force output. Aerospace Connection Connect the lesson to autonomous rovers, drones, sensors, ground-support systems, actuators, and mission-readiness testing. Interactive Checkpoints Question First, Reveal Second Use the prompts to create discussion before opening the answers. Which choice sounds most like engineering? For a system claim, select the proof that shows how the logic or mechanism actually performed. Reveal Answer Best evidence: a labeled logic/system diagram plus mission test data, sensor readings, or repeated performance results connected to the claim. What should the engineer do next? Which statement is strongest: “It looks reliable,” “It completed 4 of 5 trials,” or “We changed the threshold because the sensor triggered early twice”? items.searchText: Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints IED Lesson 0.6: Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints | LockwoodSTEM A 45-minute Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on problem definition, criteria & constraints. Define before designing 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like… What happens when a team chooses a solution too early? Launch systems solve multiple connected needs Problem vs. Solution “We are going to build a rocket stand.” “We need a way to support the rocket safely during setup.” Criteria, constraints, success, and evidence Criteria Constraints Success Criteria Evidence Criterion or constraint? Criteria Constraints Define before brainstorming What You Submit Required worksheet Lesson 0.7 Lesson 0.6 Resources Lesson 0.6 Student Presentation Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.6 Problem Definition, Criteria & Constraints Focus Question: How do engineers define the problem before designing a solution? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Define before designing Separate the need from a preferred solution, then identify the goals and limits that guide design decisions. Need Goals Limits Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Practice writing a problem statement that leaves room for multiple possible solutions. Learning Targets Separate a problem statement from a solution idea. Write a clear problem statement. Identify criteria and constraints for a design challenge. Success Looks Like… Your problem statement identifies the need without choosing the final product too early. Core habit: Define the user, need, criteria, and constraints before generating solutions. 5 min Opening prompt 8 min Problem vs. solution 8 min Criteria + constraints 10 min Classification challenge 10 min Worksheet 2 min Check 2 min Exit Opening Prompt What happens when a team chooses a solution too early? A preferred product can hide the real need and reduce the number of possible solutions. Quick class share: What is the difference between “build a rocket stand” and “support a rocket safely during setup”? Reveal the distinction The problem describes the need. The solution is one possible response. Good problem definition leaves room for multiple designs that can be compared against criteria and constraints. Aerospace Context Launch systems solve multiple connected needs Observe the number of structures and interfaces surrounding the rocket. A launch system is more than a rocket. Ground structures must satisfy needs for support, access, stability, safety, and operations. Image: NASA/Aubrey Gemignani, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Mindset Shift Problem vs. Solution Define the need before naming the final product. Solution Too Early “We are going to build a rocket stand.” Names a product immediately Can lock the team into one idea Makes alternatives harder to compare Problem Definition “We need a way to support the rocket safely during setup.” Explains the user and need Leaves room for multiple solutions Guides criteria and constraints Core Vocabulary Criteria, constraints, success, and evidence Use these terms throughout the design challenge. Criteria Goals the design should meet. Example: supports the rocket securely. Constraints Limits the design must follow. Example: approved classroom materials only. Success Criteria How the team knows the design worked. Example: does not tip during the stability test. Evidence Proof used to justify decisions. Example: sketches, photos, data, and observations. Classification Challenge Criterion or constraint? Classify each statement before opening the answer. A. The launch pad must fit the provided rocket. B. The design should include a realistic access feature. C. Teams may use only approved classroom materials. D. The prototype should stand without tipping. Reveal the classification Criteria B and D describe performance goals. Constraints A and C establish required limits or conditions. A statement may function differently in another project. Classification depends on how the challenge is written. Activity Define before brainstorming Complete the worksheet without selecting a final solution too early. Read the scenario carefully. Identify the user, need, and reason. Write the problem in one or two clear sentences. List criteria the design should meet. List constraints that limit the design. Check that the statement does not assume one final solution. Mission Debrief What You Submit Create the definition that will guide later concept work. You can build a structural prototype safely and test it using a repeatable procedure. 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like… How can prototype load testing show whether a structure meets the design criteria? Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust What acts on it? What resists it? What proves it? Which Action Fits? Best answer: 2 Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Claim Evidence Reasoning What Evidence Would You Need? Best support: A + C What Should the Engineer Do Next? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Objective You can build a structural prototype safely and test it using a repeatable procedure. Use structures, materials, loads, data, and evidence-based decisions to prepare for the payload support challenge. Analyze Test Justify Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets build a structural prototype safely and test it using a repeatable procedure. Connect today’s skill to aerospace structures and payload support systems. Identify evidence needed to support a structural design claim. Success Looks Like… You can make a structural decision using vocabulary, calculations, observations, or test data instead of “it seems strong.” Core habit: claim + evidence + reasoning. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Quick vote 7 min Structures link 8 min Core skill 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Scenario check 3 min Exit ticket Opening Prompt How can prototype load testing show whether a structure meets the design criteria? Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection Load testing must be controlled, documented, and repeatable so performance claims can be defended. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. The strongest next step turns a structural weakness into useful evidence. Mission Debrief What You Submit Use the required class format or Google Classroom instructions when assigned. Success Looks Like You can run prototype tests, collect user feedback, and record evidence without changing the results. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt What evidence shows whether a prototype is successful for the user? Think first, then share one short response that connects today’s skill to a user need, stakeholder, design criterion, prototype decision, or piece of evidence. Reveal: useful engineering move Start by naming the evidence you need before deciding the work is ready. In Unit 5, strong capstone work is not just complete; it is user-centered, responsible, tested, revised, and communicated clearly. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Testing should reveal the truth, not prove the team was right. Key Idea 2 User feedback can show needs that performance data may miss. Key Idea 3 Honest evidence makes revision stronger. Engineering Workflow Use These Moves Identify the user need, stakeholder, or responsible design decision. Use today’s lesson to collect or create meaningful evidence. Apply the capstone skill carefully: research, define, plan, model, build, test, revise, or present. Save the note, sketch, CAD view, feedback, test result, photo, or reflection that proves the work. Student Task Apply the Skill Run prototype tests or feedback activities and record results, observations, and limitations. A Choose the first idea because it is easiest to build B Use today’s evidence to make a user-centered design decision C Make the prototype look complete before checking the user need D Ignore stakeholder feedback if it complicates the plan Reveal Answer B — Use today’s evidence to make a user-centered design decision. B — Record what actually happened, including problems and limitations. Evidence Challenge What evidence would you need? A 2D side profile can rotate around a centerline to form the full 3D part. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 Revolve creates circular parts from a profile and axis. Learning Targets Understand the Rocket Launch Pad Design Challenge brief. Identify the problem, criteria, and constraints before brainstorming. Create an individual concept before combining ideas into one team concept. Success Looks Like… The team concept combines useful features from multiple individual ideas and addresses the challenge requirements. Core habit: Generate individually first, then combine features rather than simply choosing one person’s idea. 5 min Opening prompt 8 min Challenge brief 7 min Launch-pad examples 7 min Define requirements 8 min Individual sketch 7 min Combine concepts 3 min Exit Opening Prompt What does a launch pad need to do? Look past appearance and identify functions: support, stability, access, alignment, protection, and organization. Quick class share: Name one launch-pad feature and explain the need it serves. Reveal the challenge mindset Research is useful when you connect a feature to its function. Do not copy a real launch pad at full complexity. Adapt useful ideas to the classroom challenge. Challenge Brief Design and build a launch pad The first complete Unit 0 challenge begins here. Design Challenge Your team will create a launch pad that: Fits and supports the provided 3D-printed rocket Stands on its own Includes research-informed launch-pad features Uses only approved classroom materials Is justified through sketches, documentation, testing, and presentation Visual Research Observe structure and function Use the image to identify support, access, stability, and ground-system features. Use real systems for inspiration—not for direct copying. Identify the function of each feature before adapting an idea. Image: NASA/Aubrey Gemignani, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Requirements Keep the design target visible Every concept should be checked against the same requirements. Fit + Support The provided rocket must sit securely. Stability The pad must stand without tipping or collapsing. Realistic Features Include features connected to launch-pad functions. Materials Use approved classroom materials; no custom 3D-printed parts. Documentation Use sketches, notes, tests, and explanations. For a system claim, select the proof that shows how the logic or mechanism actually performed. Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Protect people and the workspace Recognize the behaviors, PPE, and permission systems required before using tools, machines, and materials. Notice Protect Report Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Connect safe behavior to engineering quality, shared responsibility, and permission to use equipment. Learning Targets Identify major safety expectations for the engineering classroom and FabLab. Explain PPE and safe behavior expectations around tools and materials. Understand the signed acknowledgment requirement before tool use. Success Looks Like… You can recognize an unsafe condition, stop, and explain the correct next action. Core habit: When something seems unsafe, stop immediately and ask before continuing. 5 min Opening prompt 7 min Why safety matters 8 min PPE + behavior 10 min FabLab orientation 6 min Scenario vote 6 min Acknowledgment 3 min Debrief Opening Prompt What can go wrong before a tool is even turned on? Safety begins with awareness, preparation, and behavior—not only with emergency response. Quick class share: Identify one unsafe condition that could affect a person, a tool, a material, or the quality of a project. Reveal the engineering connection Safety is an engineering requirement. Unsafe behavior can injure people, damage equipment, waste materials, and make test results unreliable. Professional Workspace Safety protects more than people Technical spaces use controlled procedures because quality and safety are connected. Professional technical spaces depend on controlled behavior, clear procedures, and attention to the work area. Image: NASA Glenn Research Center, public domain via Wikimedia Commons Non-Negotiables Know the baseline expectations These expectations apply before activity-specific tool rules are introduced. PPE Prepare yourself Wear safety glasses when directed or required. Wear closed-toe shoes for fabrication activities. Tie back long hair. Secure loose clothing and dangling jewelry. Use gloves only when appropriate and directed. Behavior Protect the workspace No horseplay, rushing, or distracting others. Use tools and materials only with permission. Keep work areas and walkways clear. Respect active build zones. Report damage, injuries, and unsafe conditions immediately. Scenario Vote What should happen first? Vote before opening the answer. A student notices that a cutting tool has a loose handle, but the class is already behind schedule. A Use it carefully and tell the teacher later. B Ask a teammate to test it first. C Stop, keep others from using it, and report it immediately. D Put it back without saying anything. Reveal the safest response Best answer: C Stop, prevent use, and report the condition. Schedule pressure never overrides safety. Stop Do not continue with unsafe equipment. Protect Keep others away from the hazard. Report Tell the teacher immediately. Access Requirement Signed acknowledgment comes before tool use Orientation does not replace individual equipment certifications. 1 Review Student and parent/guardian review classroom and FabLab expectations. 2 Return Submit the signed paper acknowledgment as a graded completion item. 3 Certify Complete separate tool certifications before operating specific equipment. Until the acknowledgment is returned: you may participate in class, but you may not use FabLab tools or machines.
