Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection Static equilibrium means forces and moments are balanced, which helps engineers predict support reactions and stability. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. The strongest next step turns a structural weakness into useful evidence. Mission Debrief What You Submit Use the required class format or Google Classroom instructions when assigned. How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works? You can write a testing protocol that identifies variables, criteria, procedures, and data to collect. 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works? What We Are Practicing Use These Moves Apply the Skill Which action best supports today’s engineering goal? What evidence would you need? What should the engineer do next? What You Submit Lesson Resources Lesson 4.17 PowerPoint Introduction to Engineering Design IED Unit 4 • Lesson 4.17 Testing Protocol Development Focus question: How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works? Download Presentation Flight Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 4 Mission Focus You can write a testing protocol that identifies variables, criteria, procedures, and data to collect. Define Control Plan Use system evidence to make the materials, mechanism, circuit, data, or prototype decision easier to inspect and defend. Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation, your engineering notebook, prototype materials, and class data. Learning Targets Identify the test goal and success criteria. Define variables, constants, and repeated trials. Plan how results will be recorded and compared. Success Looks Like You can write a testing protocol that identifies variables, criteria, procedures, and data to collect. Launch Learn Apply Check Submit Opening Prompt How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works? Think first, then share one short response that connects today’s skill to materials, motion, circuit behavior, data quality, or prototype performance. Reveal: useful engineering move Start by naming the evidence you need before deciding the work is ready. In Unit 4, strong work is not just complete; it can be tested, explained, revised, and connected to system performance. Core Skill What We Are Practicing Key Idea 1 A fair test is planned before data collection begins. Key Idea 2 Test protocols help teams avoid changing too many variables at once. Key Idea 3 The data table should match the decision the team needs to make. Engineering Workflow Use These Moves Identify the system goal or design decision. Use today’s lesson to collect or create meaningful evidence. Apply the material, mechanism, circuit, data, CAD, or prototype skill carefully. Save the note, graph, sketch, photo, measurement, model, or test result that proves the work. Student Task Apply the Skill Write a prototype testing protocol with criteria, variables, repeated trials, and a data table plan. Checkpoint: be ready to show the evidence that proves your work is controlled, accurate, functional, tested, or ready to revise. Interactive Check Which action best supports today’s engineering goal? A Copy the first example without checking the system goal B Use today’s evidence to make a controlled design or system decision C Choose the easiest option because it is fastest D Make the prototype look complete before testing it Reveal Answer B — Use today’s evidence to make a controlled design or system decision. B — Define the test variables and data plan before running the test. Evidence Challenge What evidence would you need? Claim: “My testing protocol development work is accurate and ready to move forward.” A A photo, graph, sketch, or model view that shows the work B A statement that it looks good C Relevant measurements, test results, circuit checks, or observations D A file name that does not identify the lesson or prototype Reveal Answer A + C are the strongest evidence pair. A shows what was created or observed. C shows whether it meets the requirement or supports the design decision. Vague confidence is not enough. Scenario Response What should the engineer do next? A student working on this lesson notices the result does not match the expected system behavior. A Ignore it and keep going because the task is almost finished B Record the issue, identify the likely cause, revise, and check again C Delete the evidence and restart without notes D Choose the faster option even if it cannot be justified Reveal Answer B — Record the issue, identify the likely cause, revise, and check again. The strongest next step turns the problem into useful engineering evidence instead of hiding it or guessing. Student Deliverables What You Submit Engineering notebook entry for Lesson 4.17. Evidence connected to the lesson focus: sketch, material test, graph, photo, circuit check, prototype observation, CAD screenshot, or revision note. Short explanation connecting your evidence to a system decision. Exit response identifying what is ready, what changed, or what still needs revision. items.title: Trusses and Member Forces
items.description: A 45-minute Principles of Engineering lesson: Trusses and Member Forces.
items.searchText: Trusses and Member Forces POE Lesson 2.7: Trusses and Member Forces | LockwoodSTEM A 45-minute Principles of Engineering lesson: Trusses and Member Forces. You can explain how trusses distribute loads and identify members likely to be in tension or compression. 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like… How do trusses distribute loads through members in tension and compression? Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust What acts on it? What resists it? What proves it? Which Action Fits? Best answer: 2 Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Claim Evidence Reasoning What Evidence Would You Need? Best support: A + C What Should the Engineer Do Next? Best answer: B What You Submit Student Deliverables Before You Leave Lesson 2.7 Resources Lesson 2.7 Student Presentation POE Unit 2 • Lesson 2.7 Trusses and Member Forces Focus Question: How do trusses distribute loads through members in tension and compression? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 2 Mission Objective You can explain how trusses distribute loads and identify members likely to be in tension or compression. Use structures, materials, loads, data, and evidence-based decisions to prepare for the payload support challenge. Analyze Test Justify Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Use this page with the lesson presentation and your engineering notebook. Learning Targets explain how trusses distribute loads and identify members likely to be in tension or compression. Connect today’s skill to aerospace structures and payload support systems. Identify evidence needed to support a structural design claim. Success Looks Like… You can make a structural decision using vocabulary, calculations, observations, or test data instead of “it seems strong.” Core habit: claim + evidence + reasoning. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Quick vote 7 min Structures link 8 min Core skill 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Scenario check 3 min Exit ticket Opening Prompt How do trusses distribute loads through members in tension and compression? Think about loads, materials, geometry, safety factors, testing, and evidence—not just whether the structure looks finished. Quick class share: What evidence would help an engineer answer today’s focus question? Reveal the working connection Trusses use geometry to spread loads; individual members often carry tension or compression rather than bending. Loads Geometry Materials Test Data POE Connection Aerospace Structures Must Earn Trust Unit 2 connects structural analysis, material selection, and testing to a payload support structure that must be defended with evidence. Loads What acts on it? Tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion, and distributed loads affect how a structure behaves. Materials + Shape What resists it? Material properties and cross-section geometry affect strength, stiffness, mass, and failure behavior. Evidence What proves it? Calculations, observations, repeated tests, and load data help justify structural decisions. Interactive Vote Which Action Fits? Vote before opening the answer reveal. Which action best supports today’s structural engineering work? 1 Assume the structure works because it looks strong 2 Compare the design to criteria using evidence, calculations, or test results 3 Choose the lightest material without checking load performance 4 Skip documentation until the final prototype is complete Reveal the strongest engineering choice Best answer: 2 Structural choices need criteria and evidence. A design may look strong but still fail because of load path, material choice, geometry, or weak connections. Carry-forward idea: In POE, strong structural decisions are testable and defensible. Key Idea Claim → Evidence → Reasoning Engineers connect what they believe to proof that others can inspect. 1 Claim What you believe about the structure, material, load path, or design decision. → 2 Evidence Measurements, calculations, observations, photos, repeated trials, or comparison data. → 3 Reasoning Why the evidence supports the claim and what the team should do next. Evidence can include: force diagrams; dimensions; load data; mass; photos; calculations; material observations; revision notes. Mini Challenge What Evidence Would You Need? Select the strongest evidence before opening the reveal. Claim: “Our payload support structure is strong enough and efficient enough for the challenge.” A A labeled sketch showing supports, load path, and likely high-stress areas B A statement that the team likes the design C Load test data, mass data, or calculations connected to the criteria D A photo that makes the prototype look complete E A short explanation connecting the evidence to the next design decision Reveal the best evidence pair Best support: A + C A shows the structural intent and load path. C shows measured or calculated performance. E is also useful because it explains what the evidence means for the next decision. Scenario Response What Should the Engineer Do Next? Choose the strongest next step and explain your reasoning. A prototype holds the load once, but the second test shows bending near one connection. A Ignore it because the structure held once B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, reinforce or revise the connection, and retest C Decorate the structure so it looks more finished D Start over without documenting what happened Reveal the strongest next step Best answer: B Record the bending, identify the likely cause, revise the connection, and retest. The strongest next step turns a structural weakness into useful evidence. Mission Debrief What You Submit Use the required class format or Google Classroom instructions when assigned. Student Deliverables Engineering notebook entry for Lesson 2.7. Truss force path diagram Evi POE Unit 2 Lesson

items.searchText: Unit 0 Portfolio Check & Design Reflection IED Lesson 0.12: Unit 0 Portfolio Check & Design Reflection | LockwoodSTEM A 45-minute Introduction to Engineering Design lesson on unit 0 portfolio check & design reflection. Audit the evidence and reflect 45-Minute Flight Plan Learning Targets Success Looks Like… How can a portfolio show growth? Check the full evidence trail Use specific evidence—not generic praise Explain Support with Which reflection is stronger? B is stronger. What Unit 0 established Define Document Test Improve Communicate What You Submit Final Unit 0 evidence Unit 1 Lesson 0.12 Resources Lesson 0.12 Student Presentation Project Reflection Template Introduction to Engineering Design IED Unit 0 • Lesson 0.12 Unit 0 Portfolio Check & Design Reflection Focus Question: How does reflection help engineers prepare for the next design challenge? Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 0 Mission Objective Audit the evidence and reflect Verify that the Unit 0 portfolio shows a complete design process and use specific evidence to explain growth. Audit Reflect Transfer Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan Close the unit by checking evidence quality and identifying habits to carry into technical sketching. Learning Targets Organize the complete Unit 0 notebook portfolio. Verify that launch-pad documentation is complete. Reflect on teamwork, testing, improvement, and design-process growth. Success Looks Like… Your portfolio shows the path from problem definition to tested prototype, and your reflection cites specific evidence. Core habit: Reflection is strongest when it names a specific decision, result, challenge, or improvement. 5 min Opening prompt 10 min Portfolio audit 15 min Complete evidence 8 min Reflection 4 min Self-check 2 min Carry forward 1 min Close Opening Prompt How can a portfolio show growth? A portfolio is not a pile of finished pages; it is an evidence trail across the design process. Quick class share: Which piece of Unit 0 evidence best shows a change in your thinking or design? Reveal the portfolio purpose A strong portfolio shows the path from idea to evidence-based improvement. Reflection helps identify which habits should carry into the next challenge. Portfolio Audit Check the full evidence trail Use the list to find missing, incomplete, or unclear work before writing the reflection. 1 Notebook and course-resource routines are established. 2 Paper-airplane worksheet is complete, numbered, and revised. 3 Problem definition, criteria, and constraints work is complete. 4 Individual and team launch-pad concepts are present. 5 Build plan is labeled and build-ready. 6 Prototype build notes and change evidence are complete. 7 Testing and improvement evidence is complete. 8 Final design review and reflection are included. Reflection Use specific evidence—not generic praise A reflection should explain decisions, challenges, improvements, and future actions. Explain How the team used the design process Your strongest contribution The biggest challenge The improvement with the biggest impact What you would change with more time Support with Specific examples Test results or observations Clear connection to notebook evidence Honest discussion of problems Recognition of teamwork Quick Check Which reflection is stronger? Vote before opening the answer. A. “The project went well and our team worked hard.” B. “Our first base tipped during the stability test. I suggested widening it by 2 in, and the revised prototype remained upright in the retest.” Reveal the stronger reflection B is stronger. It names the problem, contribution, change, and result. A may be true, but it does not provide evidence of learning or improvement. Carry Forward What Unit 0 established These habits become the foundation for technical sketching, CAD, prototyping, and later design reviews. Define Start with the need, criteria, and constraints. Document Make thinking and decisions visible. Test Use repeatable checks to create evidence. Improve Revise based on specific results. Communicate Defend the final design clearly. Download Lesson Presentation View Lesson Plan What You Submit Back to Unit 3 Mission Objective You can explain how aerospace control systems use logic, feedback, sensors, and actuators to complete mission tasks. Use mission logic, sensors, actuators, feedback, and test evidence to develop autonomous aerospace systems. Plan Test Iterate 45-Minute Flight Plan Lesson Sequence A focused class period that moves from mission logic to evidence-based system decisions. 5 min opening 6 min quick vote 7 min concept launch 8 min compare systems 10 min evidence challenge 6 min quick check 3 min debrief Learning Targets What You Should Be Able To Do Target You can explain how aerospace control systems use logic, feedback, sensors, and actuators to complete mission tasks. Success Looks Like You can explain a control-system choice using logic, sensor data, testing, or system evidence rather than opinion. Evidence Output Aerospace control system map Core Lesson Idea Unit Launch: Autonomous Aerospace Systems The presentation provides the full student-facing sequence; this page gives the key structure for the lesson. Key Idea Autonomous aerospace systems combine mission goals, sensing, logic, actuation, and feedback to complete tasks with less direct human control. Student Activity Create a control-system map showing mission goal, sensors, logic, actuators, feedback, and evidence. Aerospace Connection Connect the lesson to autonomous rovers, drones, sensors, ground-support systems, actuators, and mission-readiness testing. Download Presentation Unit 1 Overview POE Hub Mechanisms Mission Efficiency compares useful output work to input work; losses reveal friction, flex, slipping, or poor alignment. Define Test Defend Use this lesson to connect mechanism behavior to measurable evidence. Mission Briefing 45-Minute Flight Plan A focused lesson sequence that builds toward the VEX Rover Mechanisms Challenge. 5 min Opening prompt 6 min Concept vote 7 min Aerospace link 8 min Compare options 10 min Evidence challenge 6 min Quick check 3 min Exit ticket Lesson Targets What Students Should Be Able To Do Learning Target I can calculate work, power, and efficiency using measured input and output data from a mechanical system. items.searchText: 3D Print Failure Detective IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.5 3D Print Failure Detective Inspect failed prints, identify likely causes, and recommend a controlled correction for each failure. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A print farm has produced several failed parts. Before changing settings, the team needs evidence-based diagnoses. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common print defects Use physical evidence to diagnose causes Separate printer, material, model, and setup issues Plan controlled troubleshooting tests Materials What You Need Set of failed prints or failure photographs Magnifier Ruler or calipers Failure inspection sheet Slicer access Procedure Student Instructions Number each failed sample and photograph it from two angles. Describe only visible evidence before naming a cause. Classify the failure as adhesion, extrusion, temperature, support, geometry, layer shift, stringing, or another category. Identify the most likely cause and one alternative cause. Locate the slicer or printer setting connected to the likely cause. Recommend one controlled change; do not change multiple variables at once. Rank the samples from easiest to hardest to correct. Choose one sample and outline a three-print troubleshooting sequence. Requirements Engineering Requirements Analyze at least four samples Include visible evidence for every diagnosis Provide one likely and one alternative cause Recommend only one primary change per test Use correct printing vocabulary Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not operate or service a printer unless authorized Do not touch hot components Do not claim certainty when evidence is incomplete Deliverables What You Submit Failure inspection sheets Annotated photographs or sketches Cause/evidence/correction table Ranked correction list Three-print troubleshooting plan Reflection Reflection Questions Which failure had the clearest evidence? Which diagnosis was most uncertain? Why should only one variable change at a time? What information from the original print job would improve your diagnosis? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Describe the defect before diagnosing it. “The first layer detached at one corner” is stronger evidence than “bad adhesion.” Common Mistake Changing temperature, speed, bed level, and material at once may fix the print but prevents you from learning the cause. Stretch Goal Slice a small test coupon that isolates the suspected problem and predict the result. Career Connection Additive manufacturing technicians and quality engineers diagnose defects using visual evidence, process data, and controlled testing. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → IED Unit 2 Page

items.searchText: Accessible Aerospace Packaging Design ADM 4.3 Accessible Aerospace Packaging Design | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Skyline Aircraft Support Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.3 Accessible Aerospace Packaging Design Design protective packaging that can be opened by a user with limited hand strength. Intermediate 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Skyline Aircraft Support Department: Packaging Engineering Goal: Protect a sensor while improving accessibility. Background Engineering Context A maintenance kit for aircraft technicians contains a fragile sensor. Current packaging protects the part but is difficult to open while wearing gloves or for users with limited grip strength. Your team must redesign the package without reducing protection. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify user and product requirements Prototype accessible packaging features Balance protection, material use, and usability Conduct a repeatable user test Equipment What You Need Sample component or dimensional model Cardboard/paperboard/foam and approved materials Cutting and measuring tools Scale User test rubric Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Measure the component and document fragile surfaces. Interview or use the provided user profile to identify opening challenges. Define measurable requirements for protection, opening force, material, and size. Sketch three concepts with different opening methods. Use a decision matrix to select one concept. Build a full-size prototype. Conduct a protection test and an opening test with at least three users or simulated conditions. Record time, errors, and user feedback. Revise one feature and retest. Requirements Engineering Requirements Protect the component during the approved drop/handling test Open in under 20 seconds without tools Use clear opening cues Use no more than the approved material allowance Allow the package to close securely for transport Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved safe materials and cutting tools Do not expose users to sharp staples or edges Do not reveal the component during the protection test Collect anonymous usability feedback Deliverables What You Submit User-needs summary Three concept sketches Decision matrix Prototype Protection and usability data Revision evidence Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which accessibility feature helped most? What tradeoff occurred between security and ease of opening? How did user data change the design? How could packaging be made more sustainable? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use large tabs, clear grip zones, and obvious opening direction rather than relying only on text instructions. Common Mistake Designing for the average user can exclude technicians wearing gloves or users with limited dexterity. Stretch Goal Redesign the package for one-handed opening or reusable return shipping. Career Connection Packaging engineers combine material science, logistics, accessibility, branding, and product protection. Background Engineering Context A product can meet its immediate performance goal while creating hidden environmental or social impacts during material extraction, manufacturing, use, maintenance, or disposal. Objectives What You Will Practice Use life-cycle thinking Identify impacts across product stages Distinguish evidence from assumptions Recommend feasible design changes Materials What You Need Research access Life-cycle map template Engineering notebook At least three credible sources Procedure Student Instructions Choose an approved product such as a drone battery, aircraft seat component, composite panel, satellite enclosure, or rocket packaging. Define the product function and expected service life. Map raw materials, processing, manufacturing, transportation, use, maintenance, and end-of-life. For each stage, identify energy, material, waste, emissions, safety, or labor considerations. Mark the three stages with the greatest likely impact and support the choice with evidence. Generate four improvement ideas. Evaluate ideas for impact reduction, technical feasibility, cost, and possible unintended consequences. Recommend two improvements and identify how success would be measured. Requirements Engineering Requirements Include every major life-cycle stage Use at least three credible sources Identify at least three impact categories Recommend two feasible improvements Include one unintended consequence or tradeoff Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not claim precise environmental numbers without a valid source Keep the scope clear and manageable Use respectful language when discussing labor or community impacts Deliverables What You Submit Life-cycle map Source list Impact hotspot analysis Four improvement ideas Two recommendations with metrics Tradeoff statement Reflection Reflection Questions Which life-cycle stage was easiest to overlook? Which recommendation had the best impact-to-feasibility balance? What assumption most affected your analysis? How could product life be extended? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define the system boundary. State what is included and excluded from the analysis. Common Mistake “Recyclable” does not guarantee recycling will occur. Consider collection, separation, contamination, and market demand. Stretch Goal Compare a reusable and single-use version of the same product. Career Connection Sustainability, materials, supply-chain, and systems engineers evaluate product impacts beyond initial manufacture. items.searchText: Automated Circuit Assembly Cell ADM 3.5 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Satellite Electronics Systems Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.5 Automated Circuit Assembly Cell Design a virtual workcell that transports, positions, and verifies components for circuit assembly. Advanced 3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Satellite Electronics Systems Department: Automation Integration Goal: Simulate a complete component assembly and inspection cell. Background Engineering Context A satellite electronics supplier wants to automate a simplified circuit-board assembly process. The cell must deliver parts in order, avoid collisions, and include a quality-verification step before the product exits. Objectives What You Will Practice Integrate robot, conveyor, and sensor behavior Sequence a multi-step automated assembly Use simulation for system verification Document interfaces and production logic Equipment What You Need Digital twin environment Virtual robot and conveyors Virtual sensors/inspection point Component models Python or simulation logic Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define a three-component assembly sequence. Create a layout showing incoming parts, assembly position, inspection point, and exit. Develop a state or flow diagram for the complete cycle. Program the robot to retrieve and place components in the required order. Add conveyor logic that prevents a new board from entering while assembly is active. Add a simulated inspection decision with pass and reject routes. Run ten simulated boards and record failures and cycle times. Revise the layout or logic until ten consecutive boards pass the system test. Prepare an interface diagram showing signals between devices. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete ten consecutive simulated assemblies Place all components in the correct order Prevent simultaneous use of an occupied zone Route failed inspection results to reject Provide a documented reset procedure Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the provided virtual equipment set No overlapping robot/conveyor motion in unsafe zones All device interactions require a defined signal or condition Final program must include comments Deliverables What You Submit Workcell layout State/flow diagram Simulation program Ten-board test log Device interface diagram Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which interface was hardest to coordinate? Where was a buffer needed? What physical tolerance would matter most? How would a real camera inspect the assembly? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define device ownership of each zone so two machines never command the same space at once. Common Mistake Programming each device separately without a shared state model often creates deadlocks or collisions. Stretch Goal Add a rework loop that returns one failed board for a second assembly attempt. Career Connection Systems integrators combine robots, conveyors, sensors, and inspection equipment into complete production cells. AeroPack Systems Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Automated Packaging Cell Coordinate conveyors, sensors, and pneumatic gates to move twenty products without a jam. Advanced 2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroPack Systems Department: Packaging Automation Goal: Move twenty parts through packaging without a jam. Background Engineering Context AeroPack Systems packages flight-control components. Parts occasionally arrive too close together, causing collisions at pneumatic routing gates. Your team must redesign the sequence so parts remain spaced and every route completes safely. Objectives What You Will Practice Coordinate conveyor and pneumatic actions Use sensors instead of fixed delays where appropriate Create a state-based production sequence Test and document reliability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Entry, transport, and exit conveyors Object or distance sensor Pneumatic cylinders Twenty disks/cubes Python project Procedure Student Instructions Draw a flowchart from part entry through final destination. Mark every point where a sensor confirmation is needed. Run the existing sequence and record where waiting or collisions occur. Program one-part operation using sensor confirmation before each routing action. Add logic that prevents a second part from entering an occupied zone. Run ten parts, identify failures, and revise. Run a final twenty-part reliability trial. Create a timing diagram showing conveyor and cylinder states for one cycle. Requirements Engineering Requirements Transfer twenty consecutive parts with zero jams Preserve order of arrival Stop conveyors when a routing gate changes position Complete the final trial in under five minutes Constraints Constraints & Safety Conveyor speed may not exceed 70% No manual repositioning during a run Use only approved sensors and cylinders Pneumatic actions must complete before the next part enters the zone Deliverables What You Submit System flowchart Final Python program Timing/state diagram Twenty-part reliability log Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which sensor replaced the most unreliable timer? How did you prevent two parts from occupying one zone? Where could a jam still occur? What should the system do after a detected fault? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Treat each conveyor zone as occupied or clear and do not release a new part until the next zone is confirmed available. Common Mistake Adding long waits may hide a timing problem but reduces throughput and does not guarantee safety. Stretch Goal Add an automatic jam timeout that stops the system and flashes the signal tower. Career Connection Packaging automation engineers integrate conveyors, gates, sensors, and safety logic in high-volume facilities. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.4 Autonomous Sample Retrieval Mission Program a rover to navigate to a sample, collect it, and return to a defined home zone. Advanced 3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A planetary science rover has detected a high-priority sample. Communication delay prevents direct teleoperation, so the rover must complete a short autonomous sequence. Objectives What You Will Practice Integrate motion, sensing, and manipulation Plan a mission sequence Use checkpoints and fault stops Validate a multi-step autonomous system Materials What You Need Rover platform Approved sensors Simple gripper or collection device Sample object Marked mission course Programming environment Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Map the mission course and identify navigation checkpoints. Create a flowchart for travel, detection, collection, return, and safe stop. Program and test each stage independently. Add a timeout or fault response for each critical stage. Integrate the full sequence at low speed. Run three official autonomous missions without code changes between trials. Record mission time, success at each checkpoint, and failure mode. Revise the system based on evidence. Requirements Engineering Requirements No manual control after mission start Collect and retain the sample Return to the home zone Include at least two sensor-based decisions Use fault handling for missed sample or blocked path Complete two of three official missions Constraints Constraints & Safety Maintain an emergency stop Use a clear enclosed course No high-speed impacts Test mechanisms separately before full integration Deliverables What You Submit Mission map Flowchart or state diagram Commented code Checkpoint test evidence Official mission log Post-mission review Reflection Reflection Questions Which subsystem caused the most mission risk? How did you isolate faults during development? Which checkpoint should be verified twice? What would change with a communication delay? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Integrate one tested subsystem at a time rather than debugging navigation, sensing, and collection simultaneously. Common Mistake A full program that fails gives little diagnostic information if each mission stage was never tested separately. Stretch Goal Add an alternate return route when the primary path is blocked. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Beam Failure Prediction Predict where a beam will fail, test it, and explain the difference between prediction and evidence. Intermediate 1 class period Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover instrument bracket uses a cantilevered support. Before destructive testing, engineers must predict the critical region and expected failure mode. Objectives What You Will Practice Draw free-body diagrams Identify bending moment trends Distinguish stress from deflection Compare prediction with test evidence Materials What You Need Uniform beam samples Clamp or support fixture Incremental masses Ruler Marker Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Measure the beam geometry and mark several observation stations. Draw the beam, support, applied load, and reactions. Predict the region of maximum bending moment and likely failure location. Predict whether the beam will bend elastically, permanently deform, buckle, or fracture. Load the beam in approved increments and record deflection at one location. Stop at the instructor limit or after failure. Compare the observed behavior with the prediction. Write one reason for any mismatch. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete prediction before testing Use consistent load position Record load and deflection for every increment Identify observed failure mode with evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Wear eye protection Use a shield for brittle samples if directed Keep body parts away from the failure zone Do not exceed approved loads Deliverables What You Submit Free-body diagram Prediction statement Load-deflection table Failure photo or sketch Prediction-versus-result analysis Reflection Reflection Questions Why was the support region critical? When did behavior stop appearing elastic? What measurement uncertainty affected the graph? How would doubling thickness change stiffness? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark the beam before testing so you can connect deformation to a specific location. Common Mistake Predicting failure only from where the load is applied ignores the internal bending moment distribution. Stretch Goal Compare two beams with equal mass but different cross-section shapes. Career Connection Structural test engineers compare analytical predictions with physical tests before certifying flight hardware. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Black-Box System Investigation Analyze an unknown input-output system and develop a functional model without opening it. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Mission engineers frequently work with subsystems supplied by another team. They may know the inputs and outputs but not every internal detail. Your team must characterize an unknown classroom system. Objectives What You Will Practice Define system boundaries Identify inputs, processes, outputs, and feedback Plan controlled tests Create and revise a functional model Materials What You Need Instructor-provided black-box device or simulation Approved test inputs Stopwatch or measurement tools Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Observe the system without operating it and define the system boundary. List possible inputs, outputs, energy transfers, and internal processes. Plan at least four controlled tests that change one input at a time. Run the tests and record quantitative and qualitative outputs. Create an initial block diagram. Use evidence to revise the model and predict a new result. Run one confirmation test and evaluate the prediction. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least four controlled tests At least one quantitative output Functional model must show input, process, output, and feedback if present Final prediction must be tested Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not open, alter, overload, or bypass safety limits on the system Use only approved inputs Stop testing if behavior becomes unsafe or inconsistent Deliverables What You Submit Test plan Data table Initial and revised system diagrams Prediction and confirmation result Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which test provided the most useful information? What part of the internal process remains uncertain? How did your model change after testing? What additional sensor would improve the investigation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Choose tests that isolate one variable rather than changing several conditions at once. Common Mistake Assuming the first explanation is correct can lead to confirmation bias. Actively look for evidence that could disprove it. Stretch Goal Create a fault scenario and explain how the outputs would change. Career Connection Systems engineers use functional models to integrate propulsion, avionics, structures, and controls developed by different teams. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.5 Build a Simple Electromechanical Device Design and build a simple electromechanical device such as an alarm, fan, indicator, mini conveyor, or launcher with a safe, defined function. Advanced 2-3 class periods Creative Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace support task needs a device that senses or receives an input and produces a mechanical or visual output. Objectives What You Will Practice Create a system block diagram Build a basic electrical circuit Integrate electrical and mechanical components Test and revise a device Materials What You Need Low-voltage power source Switch or approved sensor Motor, buzzer, LED, or actuator Wires and breadboard as appropriate Approved mechanical materials Multimeter Procedure Student Instructions Choose an approved task and write a one-sentence function statement. Create an input-process-output block diagram. Draw a circuit diagram and label voltage, components, and polarity. Create a mechanical sketch showing how the output does useful work. Build and inspect the electrical circuit before connecting the mechanical load. Test one subsystem at a time. Run at least five full-system trials and record success, current, speed, or another performance measure. Revise one feature and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use only instructor-approved low-voltage components Include a user-controlled stop or power-disconnect method Show both circuit and mechanical diagrams Complete five repeated trials Document one revision Constraints Constraints & Safety No connection to wall power No projectiles, exposed blades, or unsafe pinch points Keep current within component ratings Power must be disconnected before rewiring Deliverables What You Submit Function statement System block diagram Circuit diagram Mechanical sketch Working device or demonstration Five-trial test table Revision reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which subsystem caused the most problems? How did electrical limits affect mechanical performance? What safety feature was most important? How would you make the device more reliable? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Test the electrical output before attaching a mechanical load. This isolates faults. Common Mistake Randomly changing wiring and mechanics at the same time makes troubleshooting much harder. Stretch Goal Add an automatic sensor input or a second operating mode. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.5 Capstone Mission Defense Prepare and defend the rover design using traceable requirements, test evidence, and risk-based recommendations. Advanced 2-3 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A client review board must decide whether the rover is ready for mission demonstration. Teams will present concise evidence and respond to technical questions. Objectives What You Will Practice Synthesize design and test evidence Communicate technical tradeoffs Respond to review questions Make a defensible readiness recommendation Materials What You Need Rover or capstone system Requirements and verification evidence Presentation software Engineering notebook Design review checklist Procedure Student Instructions Select the five mission requirements most important to readiness. Create one slide or visual for each requirement showing design response and verification evidence. Include system architecture, key tradeoffs, major revision, and unresolved risk. Prepare a five-minute presentation with assigned team roles. Conduct a rehearsal and remove unsupported claims. Present to the review board. Answer questions using data, drawings, code, or test evidence. Submit a final readiness recommendation and action list. Requirements Engineering Requirements Presentation is no longer than five minutes before questions Every major claim links to evidence Include at least one failed test or revision State unresolved risks honestly All team members contribute Final recommendation is Ready, Conditionally Ready, or Not Ready Constraints Constraints & Safety Use professional and respectful review behavior Do not conceal failed tests Follow safe demonstration boundaries No last-minute unverified hardware changes Deliverables What You Submit Final presentation Requirement-to-evidence summary Risk register Board question log Readiness recommendation Individual reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which evidence was most persuasive? What question exposed the weakest part of the design? How did the team communicate uncertainty? What action should happen before another mission attempt? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Lead with mission requirements and evidence, not a chronological story of everything the team did. Common Mistake Using confident language without test support can reduce reviewer trust. Stretch Goal Complete a second defense after addressing the review board’s top three action items. Background Engineering Context Engineering projects often begin with incomplete client statements such as “make this easier” or “we need a better holder.” Objectives What You Will Practice Ask effective stakeholder questions Separate needs from proposed solutions Write measurable requirements Present and justify a concept Materials What You Need Client interview form Engineering notebook Sketching tools Decision matrix template Presentation materials Procedure Student Instructions Pair with a classmate and assign client and designer roles. Requirements Engineering Requirements Ask at least eight interview questions Include measurable criteria and clear constraints Generate three distinct concepts Use a decision matrix Show how the final recommendation responds to client needs Constraints Constraints & Safety Problem must be safe and classroom appropriate No personal or sensitive information Designer may not simply build the client’s first suggested solution Complete within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Interview notes Confirmed problem statement Criteria and constraints Three concept sketches Decision matrix Two-minute recommendation Client feedback Reflection Reflection Questions Which question produced the most useful information? Intermediate 1-2 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Precision Cell Engineering Department: Robot Safety Goal: Restore safe operation after a fixture change. Background Engineering Context A fixture was added to an existing workcell, creating a collision risk along the original direct path. Engineers need a new path that preserves production speed and maintains a documented safety margin. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify collision zones in a digital model Create safe intermediate waypoints Compare path length and cycle time Verify clearance in simulation and physical operation Equipment What You Need Digital twin Physical workcell if approved Virtual obstacle/fixture Python program Measurement tool Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Run the original path in simulation and capture the collision location. Define a required clearance margin around the obstacle. Create three alternative waypoint paths. Measure or estimate path length for each. Simulate each path and record cycle time and minimum clearance. Select the shortest path that meets the clearance requirement. Verify the selected path at reduced speed on the physical cell. Document final coordinates and the reason each waypoint exists. Requirements Engineering Requirements Zero collisions in ten simulated cycles Maintain the required clearance margin Add no more than 20% to original cycle time Verify one reduced-speed physical cycle Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not remove the obstacle Do not exceed the approved work envelope All waypoint coordinates must be documented Physical verification requires instructor approval Deliverables What You Submit Collision screenshot Three path concepts Clearance/cycle-time comparison Final code Physical verification notes Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why was the shortest geometric path not necessarily the safest? Precision Robotics Inc. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Compare Absolute and Relative Motion Program the same geometric production path using absolute and relative motion, then recommend the better method. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Precision Robotics Inc. Department: Controls Engineering Goal: Select a reusable motion strategy for multiple workcells. Background Engineering Context Precision Robotics is creating reusable code for several similar workcells. Engineers disagree about whether the path should be programmed with absolute coordinates or relative increments. You must test both approaches using the same task. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish absolute and relative robot movement Create equivalent programs using two motion strategies Compare readability, editability, and execution Support a programming recommendation with evidence Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm with drawing tool or simulated points Python project Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Choose a rectangular or stepped path with at least eight movements. Sketch the path and label the starting coordinate and all dimensions. Program Version A using absolute move_to() coordinates. Program Version B using move_inc() for repeated or dimension-based moves. Run each version three times and record execution time and positioning success. Change the path width by 20 mm in both programs. Record how many lines or values had to change. Compare code length, readability, reuse, and risk of accumulated error. Write a recommendation for a factory that may move the fixture later. Requirements Engineering Requirements Both programs must complete the same path Use at least eight motion commands Complete three successful trials per version Include comments that identify the coordinate strategy Constraints Constraints & Safety Use identical speed settings for both versions Do not alter the physical workcell between trials Begin from the same Home position Keep the tool above the approved surface Deliverables What You Submit Absolute-motion program Relative-motion program Timing and editability comparison table Annotated path sketch Written recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Which method was easier to understand? Which method was easier to resize? Where could relative error accumulate? When would a hybrid approach be best? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Absolute positions are useful for known fixtures; relative moves are useful for repeated patterns and reusable geometry. Common Mistake A relative program depends on the current position. Starting from the wrong point shifts every later move. Stretch Goal Create a hybrid program that uses absolute coordinates for setup and relative movement for the repeated pattern. Career Connection Robot programmers select coordinate strategies based on fixture stability, product variation, and maintainability. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 1 Page

Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.3 Create Picture-Only Assembly Instructions Disassemble an approved object and create picture-only instructions that another student can use to reassemble it. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An international customer needs assembly instructions that can be understood without translating text. Objectives What You Will Practice Create exploded and sequential technical visuals Identify assembly order Communicate safety and orientation visually Test instructions with a user Materials What You Need Approved object with 5-15 components Phone or camera Sketching tools Page-layout software or paper Parts tray Procedure Student Instructions Select and photograph the assembled object. Disassemble it carefully while recording the order and orientation of every part. Create a numbered parts layout photograph or exploded sketch. Plan 6-12 assembly steps. Create one image for each step using arrows, highlights, and orientation symbols; do not use explanatory sentences. Add visual warnings where a user could reverse, force, or damage a part. Give the instructions and mixed parts to another student. Observe without speaking, record confusion points, and revise at least two images. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use no explanatory sentences in the assembly steps Include all parts exactly once Show orientation and movement clearly Include at least one visual safety or caution symbol Allow a test user to complete assembly without verbal coaching Constraints Constraints & Safety Object must be instructor-approved No powered or spring-loaded device may be opened without permission Keep all parts contained and return the object to working condition Deliverables What You Submit Parts layout or exploded view 6-12 picture-only steps User-test observation notes Two documented revisions Final instruction sheet Reflection Reflection Questions Where did the test user hesitate? Which visual symbol worked best? How did you show depth or orientation? What would you change for a younger user? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep the camera angle consistent unless a new view is necessary to reveal a hidden feature. Common Mistake A beautiful image may still be unclear. Every image must answer: what moves, where, and in which orientation? Stretch Goal Redesign the instructions to fit on one double-sided sheet while remaining usable. Your mechanical team must create a compact reduction system using available gears. Objectives What You Will Practice Calculate gear ratio Relate speed and torque Compare multiple gear-train layouts Document a mechanical recommendation Materials What You Need Available classroom gears or VEX gear inventory Axles and supports or CAD layout tools Calculator Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Inventory available gear tooth counts. Create three possible gear-train combinations near a 4:1 reduction. Calculate theoretical ratio and output speed for each. Sketch or model each layout and identify required shafts and supports. Compare size, number of parts, direction of rotation, and likely friction. Select one design and build or mock up the gear train. Measure input and output rotations to verify the actual ratio. Requirements Engineering Requirements Target reduction between 3.8:1 and 4.2:1 Output shaft must rotate continuously without gear interference All calculations must show driver and driven gears Recommendation must compare at least three concepts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only available gears and approved structural parts Do not apply motor power until alignment is checked by hand Keep hair and fingers clear of moving gears Deliverables What You Submit Three concept layouts Gear-ratio calculations Built or CAD-modeled final design Measured ratio data Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Questions Why might actual performance differ from the theoretical ratio? Which layout used the fewest parts? How did the reduction affect output torque and speed? What support would prevent gear skipping? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip For compound gear trains, multiply the ratio of each stage rather than adding ratios. Common Mistake Using pitch diameter or tooth count inconsistently will produce an incorrect ratio. Stretch Goal Redesign the gearbox to provide two selectable ratios. Identify at least three printability problems. Create two redesign sketches and select one. Modify overhangs, holes, wall thickness, orientation surfaces, or part segmentation. Slice the redesign using the same printer and comparable settings. Compare estimates and check that all functional dimensions remain correct. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce support material by at least 50% or eliminate supports Reduce print time or material use by at least 15% Preserve specified functional dimensions Maintain minimum printable wall thickness Document all slicer settings used for comparison Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the same printer profile and layer height for baseline and redesign Do not remove functional features No print is required unless approved Use classroom-safe geometry and scale Deliverables What You Submit Baseline slicer screenshot and estimates Three identified printability problems Two redesign sketches Revised CAD file Final slicer screenshot Before/after comparison table Design explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which geometry caused the most support? What change produced the largest improvement? Did reducing print time create a new tradeoff? How would injection molding change the design rules? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Before changing the part, rotate it in the slicer. Sometimes orientation solves more than redesign. Common Mistake Comparisons are invalid if the baseline and redesign use different layer heights or infill settings without explanation. Stretch Goal Create a two-part version that prints even faster and compare assembly complexity. Career Connection Additive manufacturing engineers adjust geometry, orientation, supports, and process settings to improve quality and cost. items.title: Digital Twin Validation Study
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Digital Twin Validation Study ADM 3.1 Digital Twin Validation Study | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. AeroSim Manufacturing Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Digital Twin Validation Study Compare simulated and physical robot motion and quantify the model error. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroSim Manufacturing Department: Virtual Commissioning Goal: Verify that the digital twin predicts physical performance. Background Engineering Context A new robotic process was developed in a digital twin before the physical cell was available. Before production begins, engineers must verify that simulated positions, paths, and cycle times accurately represent the real workcell. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan a simulation-to-physical validation test Collect comparable position and timing data Calculate error and explain discrepancies Recommend model updates Equipment What You Need Digital twin or simulation environment Physical VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Measurement tools Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Select five robot target positions distributed through the work envelope. Record each simulated coordinate and predicted travel time. Run the simulated path three times and record cycle time. Transfer the same program to the physical cell after safety review. Measure actual endpoint position or reference alignment at each target. Run three physical trials and record cycle time. Calculate position error and percent timing difference. Identify at least three causes of mismatch and update one model setting. Repeat one test to evaluate the improvement. Requirements Engineering Requirements Validate at least five positions Use three simulation and three physical timing trials Calculate error using a consistent method Document one model correction Constraints Constraints & Safety Use approved speeds during initial physical testing Verify clearance before automatic operation Do not adjust physical hardware during comparison Use the same command sequence in both systems Deliverables What You Submit Validation test plan Simulation and physical data table Error calculations and graph Updated model screenshot Validation conclusion Reflection Reflection Questions Which variable produced the largest mismatch? Why might physical acceleration differ from simulation? What tolerance is acceptable for this process? What additional sensor would improve validation? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Validate the highest-risk positions first: low clearance, long reach, or near workcell boundaries. Common Mistake A simulation that looks correct is not validated until physical measurements are compared. Stretch Goal Create an acceptance limit and automatically flag positions that exceed it. Career Connection Digital manufacturing engineers validate digital twins before deploying high-cost robotic processes. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 3 Page

items.title: Emergency Communications Tower
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Emergency Communications Tower IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.3 Emergency Communications Tower Build the tallest free-standing paper tower that supports a 200 g payload for 30 seconds. Intermediate 45 minutes Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context After a hurricane, a temporary communications antenna must be raised above nearby debris. The emergency team has limited materials and needs a structure that is tall, stable, and quick to deploy. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply structural design principles Plan within strict material limits Test and improve a prototype Use measurements to compare performance Materials What You Need 20 index cards 30 cm masking tape Scissors Ruler or tape measure 200 g test mass Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Study the materials without building for two minutes. Sketch one tower concept and label the base, vertical supports, and payload platform. Predict the tower height and identify the most likely failure point. Build for 15 minutes using only the issued materials. Measure the height before adding the payload. Place the 200 g mass on the top platform for 30 seconds. If the tower fails, document the failure location and make one repair using remaining material. Retest and calculate a performance score: successful height in centimeters divided by grams of material used. Requirements Engineering Requirements Stand without being attached to the table or floor Support 200 g for 30 seconds Use no more than 20 cards and 30 cm of tape Include a platform that prevents the payload from sliding Provide a measured final height Constraints Constraints & Safety 15-minute initial build time No glue, staples, string, or added materials Payload must be placed by hand without holding the tower Height is measured from table surface to top of payload Deliverables What You Submit Initial sketch and height prediction Photo before testing Measured height and material use Failure observation or success evidence Performance score calculation Three-sentence redesign recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions How did the base width affect stability? Where did compression or bending appear? Which material use produced the most strength? What would you change with five additional cards? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Folded card sections resist bending better than flat cards. Test triangular, tubular, and layered shapes. Common Mistake A very tall narrow tower may score well before testing but fail under the payload. Stability is part of performance. Stretch Goal Rebuild with only 12 cards and attempt to achieve at least 80% of your original height. Career Connection Structural and civil engineers design temporary towers, supports, and deployable structures for emergencies and field operations. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → IED Unit 0 Page

items.title: Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit POE 0.1 Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.1 Emergency Tool-Use Safety Audit Inspect a simulated engineering workspace, identify hazards, and produce a corrected setup plan. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace prototyping team is preparing for a rapid repair task. Before work begins, the team needs an independent safety review of tools, PPE, cords, materials, and traffic flow. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common FabLab and shop hazards Match PPE to the task Communicate corrective actions clearly Apply stop-work authority responsibly Materials What You Need Instructor-provided workstation or safety photo Safety checklist Engineering notebook PPE examples Procedure Student Instructions Review the assigned workstation without touching anything. Record at least eight observations: safe practices, hazards, or missing controls. Classify each hazard by severity: low, medium, or high. For every hazard, write one corrective action and who should complete it. Create a revised workstation sketch showing safe tool placement, material flow, and walking space. Perform a second inspection after corrections are made. Write a brief go/no-go recommendation for starting work. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least five legitimate hazards or risk controls Include PPE, housekeeping, electrical, cutting/tool, and movement considerations Every hazard must have a specific corrective action Final recommendation must be supported by evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not operate tools during the audit Do not stage unsafe conditions for a photograph Follow instructor directions for handling PPE and equipment Deliverables What You Submit Completed safety audit Annotated workstation sketch Corrective-action table Final go/no-go recommendation Notebook reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which hazard had the highest potential consequence? Which correction was easiest to implement? How can a safe workspace also improve efficiency? When should a student stop work and ask for help? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Separate the probability of an incident from the severity of its outcome when ranking risk. Common Mistake Listing “be careful” is not a corrective action. State what must physically or procedurally change. Stretch Goal Create a 60-second safety briefing that a team leader could deliver before the task begins. Career Connection Aerospace technicians, test engineers, and manufacturing engineers complete pre-task hazard reviews before high-risk work. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → POE Unit 0 Page
