items.title: Engineering Drawing Makeover
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Engineering Drawing Makeover IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Engineering Drawing Makeover Revise a weak engineering drawing so it communicates the part clearly and can be used for fabrication or inspection. Intermediate 60 minutes Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A manufacturing technician returned a drawing because it was incomplete, cluttered, and difficult to inspect. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize missing drawing information Apply dimensioning standards Improve layout and readability Add appropriate notes and tolerances Materials What You Need Instructor-provided weak drawing or prior student drawing Drafting tools or CAD drawing workspace Drawing checklist Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Audit the drawing for missing views, dimensions, units, scale, title block information, notes, and tolerances. Mark at least eight issues directly on a copy. Choose the minimum set of views needed to define the part. Rearrange the views for alignment and readable spacing. Add or correct dimensions, avoiding duplication. Add centerlines, hidden lines, hole notes, and detail views where needed. Complete the title block and add general tolerances. Use the checklist to perform a final self-inspection. Requirements Engineering Requirements Correct at least eight identified issues Use consistent units and dimension style Include a complete title block Include enough views to define the part Use tolerances only where they support function or inspection Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change the part geometry unless the drawing reveals an impossible feature Keep the final drawing on one sheet Follow the class drawing standard Deliverables What You Submit Annotated original drawing Revised drawing Completed drawing checklist Short explanation of the three most important corrections Reflection Reflection Questions Which missing item created the greatest manufacturing risk? How did you decide which views to keep? Where did you use a tolerance and why? How could an inspector use your revised drawing? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every dimension should have a purpose: location, size, or relationship. Common Mistake Adding more dimensions can create conflicts. Avoid dimensioning the same feature in multiple places. Stretch Goal Exchange drawings with a partner and perform a blind completeness audit. Career Connection Mechanical designers and documentation specialists maintain drawings throughout a product’s life cycle. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → IED Unit 1 Page

items.title: Engineering Failure Investigation
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Engineering Failure Investigation IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.5 Engineering Failure Investigation Investigate a major engineering failure and identify how design-process improvements could have reduced the risk. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering failures are rarely caused by a single bad decision. They often involve technical limits, communication problems, testing gaps, and pressure from schedules or cost. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish immediate causes from root causes Connect evidence to design-process decisions Identify ethical and communication factors Develop prevention recommendations Materials What You Need Internet research access Engineering notebook Presentation or document software At least two credible sources Procedure Student Instructions Choose an approved case such as Challenger, Columbia, Mars Climate Orbiter, Tacoma Narrows Bridge, Hyatt Regency walkway, or another instructor-approved failure. Create a short timeline of at least five events before the failure. Identify the system or component that failed first. Use a five-whys analysis to identify at least one technical root cause and one organizational root cause. Find evidence of a warning, test result, or concern that was missed or misunderstood. Map the failure to stages of the engineering design process. Develop three specific prevention actions involving design, testing, communication, or decision-making. Present the investigation in a one-page visual brief or three-minute presentation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use at least two credible sources Separate facts from your own conclusions Include both technical and human/organizational factors Provide three actionable prevention recommendations Cite sources in a consistent format Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not use graphic images Do not copy a prewritten case summary Keep the final product to one page or three minutes Use respectful language when discussing injuries or loss of life Deliverables What You Submit Timeline Five-whys root cause analysis Engineering design process map Three prevention actions Source list One-page brief or short presentation Reflection Reflection Questions Which warning sign was most important? Where could better testing have changed the outcome? How did communication influence the failure? What responsibility does an engineer have when a safety concern is ignored? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Ask “What allowed this condition to exist?” instead of stopping at “Which part broke?” Common Mistake A root cause is not simply the last event before failure. Look for deeper design, process, and communication conditions. Stretch Goal Compare two failures and identify one recurring pattern in engineering decision-making. Career Connection Safety, reliability, systems, and quality engineers study failures to prevent recurrence and improve standards. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → IED Unit 0 Page

items.title: Engineering Notebook Excellence Audit
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Engineering Notebook Excellence Audit IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.4 Engineering Notebook Excellence Audit Upgrade one incomplete or weak notebook entry into a professional engineering record. Beginner 30-45 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering notebooks are legal and technical records of design work. A clear notebook allows another person to understand what happened, reproduce a test, and trace why decisions were made. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize the features of strong engineering documentation Improve clarity and organization Add missing technical evidence Reflect on design decisions Materials What You Need Engineering notebook One previous notebook entry Ruler Pen or pencil Colored pencil or highlighter Procedure Student Instructions Choose a previous entry that is incomplete, difficult to follow, or missing evidence. Use a checklist to identify missing date, title, purpose, sketches, measurements, labels, results, and reflection. Create a revised version on a new page without erasing the original record. Add at least one labeled sketch or diagram. Add a table, measurement, calculation, or test result that supports the work. Write a short reflection describing what happened, what changed, and what should happen next. Ask a classmate to read the revised page for 60 seconds and explain the work back to you. Make one final improvement based on that feedback. Requirements Engineering Requirements Keep the original entry unchanged Include a date and descriptive title Use complete labels and units Include at least one visual and one quantitative piece of evidence End with a next-step statement Constraints Constraints & Safety No copied text from another student Revised page must fit on one notebook spread Use permanent notebook practices established in class Deliverables What You Submit Completed notebook audit checklist Original page reference Revised notebook entry Peer feedback note Three improvement rules you will use in future entries Reflection Reflection Questions What information was missing from the original entry? Could another student reproduce the work from your revised page? Which change improved clarity the most? How will better documentation help during a design review? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use headings and white space to guide the reader. More writing is not always clearer writing. Common Mistake Decorating a page is not the same as documenting evidence. Prioritize technical content over appearance. Stretch Goal Create a one-page “excellent notebook entry” guide for a new IED student. Career Connection Engineers use notebooks, test logs, and change records to communicate across teams and support patents, safety reviews, and manufacturing decisions. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → IED Unit 0 Page

items.title: Engineering Portfolio Showcase
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Engineering Portfolio Showcase IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.5 Engineering Portfolio Showcase Transform your strongest project into a concise portfolio case study that demonstrates process, evidence, revision, and communication. Advanced 2-3 class periods Creative Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An engineering portfolio should show how you think, not only display a final object. Objectives What You Will Practice Curate technical evidence Explain a design process clearly Improve visual and written communication Reflect on growth and tradeoffs Materials What You Need One completed IED project Original notebook and files CAD/screenshots/photos Presentation or page-layout software Portfolio checklist Procedure Student Instructions Select a project with enough evidence to show at least one meaningful revision. Write a 40-60 word project overview including the problem, user or client, and final outcome. Choose 6-10 artifacts that show problem definition, concepts, CAD, build, test, and revision. Improve one weak artifact, such as a sketch, drawing, photograph, graph, or CAD view. Create a before/after or problem/revision comparison. Write three short captions that explain decisions rather than merely name images. Create a one-page case study or 3-5 slide presentation. Deliver a two-minute presentation and use feedback to make one final revision. Requirements Engineering Requirements Show the problem, process, evidence, revision, and result Use only your own work or clearly identify team contributions Include at least one quantitative result Include one honest limitation or unresolved issue Use consistent visual hierarchy and readable text Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not include private student information Do not claim sole credit for team work Keep the final case study to one page or five slides Use high-quality, appropriately cropped images Deliverables What You Submit Project overview 6-10 curated artifacts One improved artifact Before/after comparison Final case study or slides Two-minute presentation Final reflection Reflection Reflection Questions What does the portfolio reveal about your engineering process? Which artifact provides the strongest evidence? What did you remove and why? How would you describe your growth this year? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every image needs a job. Include it only if it supports a decision, test, revision, or result. Common Mistake A portfolio made only of polished final images hides the engineering process that employers and programs want to see. Stretch Goal Create a second version tailored to an internship, college program, or competition audience. Career Connection Engineers use portfolios and technical presentations to communicate capability, design thinking, and project impact. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → IED Unit 5 Page

items.title: Factory Throughput Simulation
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Factory Throughput Simulation ADM 3.4 Factory Throughput Simulation | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Nova Factory Systems Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.4 Factory Throughput Simulation Use a digital twin to balance robot, conveyor, and buffer capacity before changing the physical line. Advanced 2-3 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Nova Factory Systems Department: Industrial Simulation Goal: Select the best production-line configuration virtually. Background Engineering Context Nova Factory Systems is considering three production-line configurations. Building each physically would be costly, so your team must simulate the alternatives and recommend the best design for throughput and reliability. Objectives What You Will Practice Build and compare production scenarios Identify bottlenecks and buffer effects Analyze throughput and utilization data Complete an evidence-based trade study Equipment What You Need Digital twin or factory simulation Three provided layout scenarios Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define the production sequence and output target. Build or load Scenario A with the baseline robot and conveyor settings. Run a simulated production period and record output, idle time, and blocked time. Create Scenario B by changing conveyor speed or buffer capacity. Create Scenario C by changing robot path or station assignment. Run each scenario for the same simulated duration. Calculate throughput, robot utilization, and average work-in-process. Create a weighted decision matrix using output, reliability, complexity, and cost. Recommend one scenario and identify one risk before physical implementation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Compare exactly three scenarios Use identical simulated production duration Report throughput and at least two additional metrics Support recommendation with a decision matrix Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved changes for each scenario Do not change multiple unrecorded variables Simulation assumptions must be listed The recommended scenario must preserve safety Deliverables What You Submit Three simulation configurations Scenario data table Graphs of key metrics Decision matrix Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which scenario had the highest throughput? Did highest throughput also produce the least work-in-process? What assumption could change the recommendation? Which result should be verified physically first? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Record every simulation assumption; a precise answer from an unrealistic assumption is still unreliable. Common Mistake Comparing scenarios with different run durations or starting inventory produces misleading results. Stretch Goal Perform a sensitivity analysis by changing demand or failure rate. Career Connection Manufacturing simulation engineers test factory layouts and schedules before companies commit capital. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 3 Page

items.title: Fit and Tolerance Investigation
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Fit and Tolerance Investigation IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.3 Fit and Tolerance Investigation Design and test a tolerance coupon that identifies useful clearance, transition, and press-fit dimensions for the classroom printer. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Two CAD parts may share the same nominal dimension but still fit differently after printing because of machine and material variation. Objectives What You Will Practice Connect nominal dimensions to physical fit Design a controlled experiment Collect repeated measurements Recommend tolerances from evidence Materials What You Need Fusion 360 3D printer and approved filament Calipers Tolerance data sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Choose a nominal peg or hole size approved by the instructor. Create a parametric coupon with at least six fit offsets spanning loose to tight. Label each test position in the model. Predict which offsets will produce clearance, transition, and press fits. Slice and print using recorded settings and orientation. Measure printed pegs and holes before fit testing. Test each fit using the same procedure and rate insertion force and retention. Recommend one offset for each target fit and explain uncertainty. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use one nominal size and at least six controlled offsets Keep all non-offset geometry identical Record printer, material, orientation, layer height, and scale Measure at least three printed features Define a repeatable fit-rating method Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not force parts in a way that creates sharp fragments Use only approved print settings Results apply only to the tested machine, material, and orientation unless additional evidence is collected Deliverables What You Submit Parametric coupon file Prediction table Printed coupon Measurement and fit data Recommended clearance/transition/press-fit offsets Short limitations statement Reflection Reflection Questions How did actual dimensions compare with CAD? Which fit category had the widest acceptable range? How did print orientation affect the result? Why should tolerances be based on process capability? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Change only the fit offset. Keep every other feature and test condition constant. Common Mistake One successful fit is not enough evidence. Manufacturing variation requires repeated or carefully controlled testing. Stretch Goal Repeat the best three fits in a second orientation or material and compare. Career Connection Design and manufacturing engineers specify tolerances based on function and process capability, not guesswork. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → IED Unit 3 Page

items.title: Friction Surface Investigation
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Friction Surface Investigation IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Friction Surface Investigation Compare friction for three surface materials and recommend the best tray liner. Beginner 60-90 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A payload tray slides during rover motion. The team needs evidence about which surface pairing provides the most resistance to sliding. Objectives What You Will Practice Design a controlled friction test Measure force or critical angle Collect repeated data Use averages to make a recommendation Materials What You Need Small test block Wood, plastic, foam, or other approved surfaces Spring scale or adjustable ramp Protractor Ruler Data sheet Procedure Student Instructions Choose either a pull-force method or incline-angle method. Define the independent, dependent, and controlled variables. Prepare three surfaces with equal test area. Run at least five trials per surface using the same block and load. Record force or critical angle for every trial. Calculate mean and range for each surface. Create a graph and identify any outlier. Recommend a liner and explain one limitation of the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Test at least three surfaces Complete five trials per surface Keep block mass and contact area constant Calculate mean and range Create one labeled graph Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved surfaces Do not exceed spring-scale capacity Keep hands clear of a moving block Recommendation is based on dry classroom conditions Deliverables What You Submit Test plan and variables Raw data table Mean/range calculations Graph Material recommendation Test limitation Reflection Reflection Questions Which surface had the most consistent data? What variable was hardest to control? How could dust or moisture affect the result? Would the best high-friction material always be best for a moving mechanism? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark a consistent starting position and pull direction for every trial. Common Mistake Do not base a conclusion on the single highest measurement; use repeated data. Stretch Goal Repeat the chosen surface with two different loads and compare the effect. Career Connection Tribology and mechanical engineers study friction, wear, and lubrication in vehicles, machines, and aerospace mechanisms. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson → IED Unit 4 Page

Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small sensor package must survive a hard landing. Your team will design a structure that manages impact energy without simply surrounding the payload with excessive material. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply energy absorption concepts Design controlled deformation Use iterative drop testing Evaluate protection versus mass Materials What You Need Small payload or raw egg substitute Paper, straws, foam, cardboard, tape, or approved materials Mass scale Drop test area Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Record payload dimensions, mass, and failure risks. Sketch two concepts using crumple zones, suspension, landing legs, or protective frames. Select one concept and define a maximum structure mass. Build the first prototype and photograph it before testing. Conduct a low-height drop, inspect, and revise. Increase to the official height only after passing the lower test. Record damage, orientation, and structural deformation. Calculate total system mass and summarize protection performance. Requirements Engineering Requirements Payload must remain contained Structure must fit within the assigned envelope Mass must remain below the unit limit No loose material may scatter during testing Complete at least two test-and-revision cycles Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the designated drop zone No throwing or launching Wear eye protection if required Retrieve the device only after the area is clear Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Prototype photos Test log Mass record Damage assessment Final redesign explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which feature absorbed the most energy? Did the structure protect by staying rigid or deforming? How did landing orientation affect results? What would change for a higher drop speed? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Plan where the structure should deform; accidental deformation may transfer load directly to the payload. Common Mistake Adding soft material everywhere can increase mass without controlling the load path. Stretch Goal Improve survival height by 25% without increasing mass. Advanced 2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Background Engineering Context Before final demonstration, the project manager needs a coordinated plan showing how each rover requirement will be inspected, analyzed, demonstrated, or tested. Objectives What You Will Practice Map requirements to verification Sequence tests safely Define objective pass/fail criteria Plan data collection Materials What You Need Final requirement list Rover design information Verification matrix template Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Number every mission requirement. Choose inspection, analysis, demonstration, or test for each. Write an objective pass/fail statement. Identify equipment, setup, data, and responsible team role. Arrange verification activities from low risk to high risk. Identify requirements that can be verified in one combined test. Create a retest rule for failed or inconclusive results. Conduct a tabletop review with another team. Requirements Engineering Requirements Every requirement has one or more verification methods Every method has a measurable pass/fail criterion Plan includes setup, equipment, and data to record Safety checks precede powered testing Retest criteria are defined Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not schedule destructive tests before non-destructive evidence is collected Avoid using demonstration when quantitative data are required Identify assumptions and unavailable equipment Deliverables What You Submit Verification matrix Test sequence Data-recording plan Peer-review corrections Final readiness statement Reflection Reflection Questions Which requirement was most difficult to verify? What tests could be combined without confusing results? How will you handle an inconclusive result? What requirement creates the greatest test risk? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Test one requirement under one clearly controlled condition unless a combined test is deliberately planned. Common Mistake “It worked” is not a pass/fail criterion. State the measured threshold and condition. Stretch Goal Create a verification dashboard that automatically marks requirements complete. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Landing-Zone Probability Model Use repeated test data to estimate the probability that a payload lands inside a target zone. Advanced 2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A relief drone drops small emergency packages. The team must determine whether the current deployment method is reliable enough for a defined landing zone. Objectives What You Will Practice Use descriptive statistics Model target success probability Visualize two-dimensional test data Communicate risk and limitations Materials What You Need Approved drop or launch simulation Target grid At least 20 trial coordinates Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define the target-zone boundaries and coordinate origin. Collect or analyze at least 20 landing coordinates. Plot every point on a scaled scatter plot. Calculate mean x and y position and spread in each direction. Count successful landings and calculate observed success rate. Identify directional bias and possible environmental causes. Recommend an aim-point adjustment or process change. Predict the expected number of successes in 50 future drops. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 20 trials Target success defined before data collection All points shown, including misses Include observed probability and directional bias Recommendation must acknowledge sample-size limits Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a safe simulation or approved low-energy system Maintain a clear test zone Do not alter data after seeing target results Deliverables What You Submit Coordinate data Scatter plot Success-rate calculation Bias analysis Aim-point recommendation Future-performance prediction Reflection Reflection Questions Did the mean landing point fall inside the target? Can a high average accuracy still produce poor reliability? How would wind change the distribution? What sample size would increase confidence? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep both coordinate directions; reducing the result to distance alone can hide a directional bias. Common Mistake Assuming the observed percentage is an exact future probability ignores limited sample size. Stretch Goal Create an elliptical landing zone that contains approximately 80% of the observed points. Career Connection Guidance, navigation, and test engineers quantify dispersion and probability for payload delivery, landing, and release systems. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson → POE Unit 4 Page

Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.5 Lean Manufacturing Improvement Project Identify and remove motion, waiting, transportation, and over-processing waste from a workcell. Advanced 2-3 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Lean Operations Goal: Reduce waste and improve verified cycle time by 15%. Background Engineering Context Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing meets quality requirements but uses more time and motion than necessary. Your team will complete a Lean observation, collect baseline data, and implement a software improvement supported by evidence. Objectives What You Will Practice Recognize common forms of manufacturing waste Create current-state and future-state process maps Measure cycle time and value-added time Implement and verify an improvement Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Current production program Stopwatch Process-map template or paper Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Observe five cycles without changing the program. List examples of motion, waiting, transportation, defects, and over-processing. Create a current-state process map with times for each step. Mark which steps directly add value for the customer. Select one software change that removes or reduces waste. Predict the expected time savings. Implement the change and run ten verification cycles. Create a future-state map and calculate percent improvement. Prepare a two-minute improvement presentation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least four examples of waste Implement at least one software improvement Improve average cycle time by at least 15% Maintain product quality and safety Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not remove required inspection or safety actions Change one major variable at a time Use measured data rather than opinion No hardware purchases Deliverables What You Submit Waste observation sheet Current/future process maps Updated code Before/after data and graph Improvement presentation Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which step added the least customer value? Did removing a wait create a new risk? How did the future-state map change? What improvement would require hardware? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Lean improvement removes non-value-added work while protecting quality, safety, and customer requirements. Common Mistake Treating every wait as waste can remove a wait that is actually required for sensor stability or safe motion. Stretch Goal Calculate estimated annual hours saved if the improvement runs 1,000 cycles per week. Career Connection Lean specialists and industrial engineers lead kaizen events that reduce waste and improve flow. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Lightweight Bracket Redesign Redesign an instructor-provided bracket to reduce modeled mass by at least 20% while preserving interfaces and basic load capability. Advanced 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An aerospace bracket meets the required shape but is heavier than necessary. Every gram matters in flight hardware. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply design-for-lightweighting strategies Use CAD mass properties Preserve functional interfaces Document design tradeoffs Materials What You Need Starter bracket file or drawing Fusion 360 Material property assignment Engineering notebook Optional 3D printer Procedure Student Instructions Open the baseline bracket and record material, mass, envelope dimensions, and interface locations. Highlight no-change zones such as mounting holes and contact surfaces. Sketch two lightweighting concepts using ribs, pockets, tapered walls, or pattern changes. Select one concept and predict the mass reduction. Create the redesigned model using parameters. Assign the same material and measure final mass. Inspect minimum wall thickness, sharp internal corners, and print orientation. Create a before/after comparison and explain how load could travel through the redesigned part. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce modeled mass by at least 20% Preserve all mounting hole locations and interface dimensions Maintain minimum 2 mm wall thickness unless approved Avoid unsupported features that make printing impractical Use at least one rib or load-path feature Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the same assigned material for both mass calculations Do not simply scale the entire part Part must remain printable on classroom equipment No formal claim of structural safety without testing or analysis Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Baseline and final mass-property screenshots Fusion file Before/after visual comparison Manufacturability check Design justification Reflection Reflection Questions Where did you remove the most material? How did you preserve the load path? What new failure risk did the redesign create? What physical test would you perform next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Keep material along likely load paths and remove it from large low-stress areas. Common Mistake Cutting random holes may reduce mass but can create stress concentrations and weak connections. Stretch Goal Print both versions and compare mass, print time, and a simple non-destructive stiffness test. Career Connection Aerospace mechanical engineers use topology, ribs, pockets, and material selection to reduce mass while maintaining function. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → IED Unit 2 Page

Your team will create a small truss structure and compare strength-to-mass performance. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify tension and compression members Use triangulation effectively Measure structural performance Calculate strength-to-mass ratio Materials What You Need Craft sticks, paper strips, or approved structural material Adhesive Mass scale Test weights Ruler Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define the required chassis span and payload location. Sketch two truss patterns and label expected tension/compression members. Estimate material quantity and mass for each concept. Select and build one chassis using consistent joints. Measure final mass and inspect alignment. Load the chassis in approved increments while observing deformation. Record maximum successful load and failure location. Calculate load-to-mass ratio and recommend one redesign. Requirements Engineering Requirements Span the required distance without intermediate support Support the assigned base payload for 30 seconds Use a clearly identifiable truss pattern Record mass before testing No repair during an official load trial Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved adhesives and cutting tools Wear eye protection during destructive testing if required Keep hands and faces away from the load path Do not exceed instructor load limits Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Member-force predictions Structure mass Load-test table Failure analysis Redesign recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Which members appeared to be in compression? Where did the first visible deformation occur? How did joint quality affect performance? What change would improve strength without adding much mass? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Compression members often fail by buckling before the material itself crushes. Common Mistake Adding material everywhere increases mass but may not strengthen the critical load path. Stretch Goal Rebuild one member or joint and demonstrate a 15% improvement in load-to-mass ratio. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Line-Following Recovery Logic Program a rover to follow a path and recover when the line is temporarily lost. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A warehouse-style rover transports equipment through a marked route. Dust or damaged floor markings may interrupt the path, so the rover needs recovery behavior. Objectives What You Will Practice Use feedback control Create state-based logic Test fault recovery Measure path performance Materials What You Need Rover with optical or line sensors Marked course with one intentional gap Programming environment Stopwatch Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Create baseline line-following logic and test it on a continuous path. Define the conditions that indicate the line has been lost. Design a recovery sequence such as stop, search left, search right, and timeout. Add a safe stop if the line cannot be found. Run five trials through a path containing a gap. Record recovery success, completion time, and any departures from the lane. Tune the logic and repeat five official trials. Requirements Engineering Requirements Follow the normal path without manual control Recover from the designated gap Stop safely after the search timeout Complete at least four of five official trials Code must include meaningful comments Constraints Constraints & Safety Use low operating speed during development Maintain a clear test area Provide immediate stop control Do not allow uncontrolled searching outside the boundary Deliverables What You Submit State diagram Commented code Baseline and final results Recovery success rate Tuning explanation Reflection Reflection Questions What event caused the rover to enter recovery mode? Which search pattern worked best? How did timeout length affect safety? What additional sensor could improve recovery? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Draw the control states before writing code: Follow, Lost, Search Left, Search Right, Stop. Common Mistake Adding more nested conditionals without a state plan can make recovery behavior unpredictable. Stretch Goal Add a second fault such as an obstacle that interrupts the path. Career Connection Autonomy engineers design fault-handling states so robotic vehicles remain safe when sensors or navigation references are lost. Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Machine Vision Quality Inspection Use an optical sensor to classify parts and reject items that do not meet the color specification. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Quality Assurance Goal: Automatically identify and route production batches. Background Engineering Context An aerospace connector supplier uses color to identify production batches. Parts from the wrong batch must not reach assembly. Your workcell must measure hue, classify each incoming disk, and route it to an accepted or rejected location. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect and interpret optical-sensor data Select threshold values from repeated measurements Use conditional logic for automated decisions Calculate inspection accuracy Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Optical sensor 6-Axis Arm Red and green disks plus one unknown/test disk Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Turn on the optical sensor light at a consistent power. Collect at least ten hue readings for each known color and record the range. Choose threshold values that separate the two groups. Create an inspection function that returns the detected class. Program the robot to inspect and route each disk. Test a randomized sequence of twenty disks without changing thresholds. Record true color, detected color, and destination. Calculate accuracy and revise thresholds only if the data supports a change. Requirements Engineering Requirements Inspect twenty randomized parts Achieve at least 95% correct classification Send uncertain readings to a reject location Return to a safe position between parts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use one optical sensor Keep lighting and inspection distance consistent Do not identify colors manually during the final run Hardware locations remain fixed Deliverables What You Submit Hue calibration table Python inspection and routing program Twenty-part confusion/accuracy table Threshold justification Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why were repeated readings necessary? Which color had the widest range? How should the system handle an uncertain value? How could ambient light affect production? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the midpoint between non-overlapping data ranges as a starting threshold, then verify it with randomized tests. Common Mistake Choosing a threshold from one reading often fails when lighting or part position changes. Stretch Goal Add a third color or a confidence band that automatically rejects borderline readings. Career Connection Machine-vision and quality engineers build inspection systems that prevent defective or incorrect parts from reaching customers. Aegis Aerospace Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.1 Manufacturing Cybersecurity Risk Assessment Identify cyber risks in a connected manufacturing cell and recommend layered safeguards. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Aegis Aerospace Department: Operational Technology Security Goal: Reduce cyber risk in a connected manufacturing workcell. Background Engineering Context A connected aerospace factory experienced unusual robot commands after a maintenance laptop was attached to the network. Production was stopped before damage occurred. Your team must assess the workcell using confidentiality, integrity, and availability principles. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply the CIA triad to manufacturing systems Identify technical and human vulnerabilities Prioritize risk using likelihood and impact Recommend layered controls Equipment What You Need Workcell/network diagram Risk matrix template Scenario cards Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the provided workcell diagram and identify all devices, connections, and users. List at least ten assets or data types that require protection. Identify at least eight vulnerabilities, including one human-factor risk. For each risk, score likelihood and impact from 1 to 5. Plot risks on a matrix and select the four highest priorities. Recommend preventive, detective, and recovery controls for each priority. Create an incident response sequence for an unexpected robot command. Present the top risks and explain how each relates to confidentiality, integrity, or availability. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least eight distinct vulnerabilities Include risks to safety and production availability Recommend at least two controls for each top risk Include an isolation and recovery procedure Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not test real malware or bypass security controls Use only provided diagrams and scenarios Recommendations must preserve authorized maintenance access Distinguish safety stop from cybersecurity response Deliverables What You Submit Annotated system diagram Risk register and matrix Top-four mitigation plan Incident response flowchart Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which risk had the highest safety impact? How can data integrity affect physical quality? Why are backups not sufficient prevention? What training would reduce human risk? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use layered defense: one control may fail, so combine access control, monitoring, segmentation, and recovery. Common Mistake Cybersecurity is not only confidentiality; altered coordinates can create a physical hazard. Stretch Goal Design a network-segmentation diagram separating office, maintenance, and production systems. Career Connection Operational technology cybersecurity specialists protect robots, PLCs, sensors, and industrial networks. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.4 Manufacturing Readiness Review Perform a manufacturing readiness review of another student’s rocket assembly and identify issues before production. Intermediate 60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A prototype is ready for printing, but releasing unreviewed files can waste machine time and material. Objectives What You Will Practice Evaluate CAD and drawing completeness Check manufacturability and assembly readiness Prioritize production risks Communicate corrective actions Materials What You Need Peer CAD assembly and drawings Readiness checklist Slicer software Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Confirm the correct file revision and project requirements. Inspect component names, missing files, joints, and assembly interference. Check each part for print orientation, unsupported geometry, thin walls, and excessive size. Review drawings for dimensions, tolerances, notes, and BOM consistency. Open STL files in the slicer and check scale, units, manifold errors, and estimated print time. Record every issue as observation, consequence, and recommended correction. Classify issues as release blocker, important correction, or optional improvement. Meet with the designer and verify the top three actions. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use the complete readiness checklist Identify at least five evidence-based observations Classify each issue by priority Check both CAD and slicer readiness Provide actionable corrections Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not edit another student’s files directly Keep feedback professional and confidential within the class Do not approve a design with unresolved release blockers Deliverables What You Submit Completed readiness checklist Issue-priority table Slicer evidence Top-three correction summary Final release recommendation: ready, ready with corrections, or not ready Reflection Reflection Questions Which issue posed the greatest waste risk? Which check was easiest to overlook? How did the slicer reveal problems not obvious in CAD? What would be on your personal preflight checklist? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write findings as “Observed condition - possible consequence - recommended action.” Common Mistake A readiness review is not a style critique. Focus on issues that affect function, fabrication, inspection, or assembly. Stretch Goal Review the corrected package and document whether each release blocker was closed. Career Connection Manufacturing, configuration, and quality engineers review files before production to prevent defects and wasted resources. items.title: Manufacturing Throughput Investigation
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Manufacturing Throughput Investigation ADM 1.5 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Orion Manufacturing Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Manufacturing Throughput Investigation Use production data to increase the number of parts processed per hour without reducing quality. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orion Manufacturing Department: Continuous Improvement Goal: Increase hourly production using verified software improvements. Background Engineering Context Orion Manufacturing expects a surge in demand. The workcell is reliable, but engineers suspect waiting, excessive clearance, and repeated setup motions are limiting output. Teams will compete for the best verified throughput improvement. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure throughput and identify bottlenecks Apply continuous-improvement methods Calculate production-rate improvement Present evidence-based recommendations Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Cubes or disks Python project Stopwatch Spreadsheet or graph paper Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define one production cycle and the required quality criteria. Run ten baseline cycles and record total time, errors, and idle periods. Create a process map showing robot motion, pickup, transport, placement, and waits. Classify at least three examples of motion, waiting, or over-processing waste. Propose three changes and predict their effect. Implement one change at a time and collect new ten-cycle data. Select the best reliable program and calculate parts per hour. Prepare a short presentation with before/after data and remaining bottlenecks. Requirements Engineering Requirements Improve verified throughput by at least 20% Maintain 100% successful transfers during the final ten-cycle run Use at least two different data displays Document each program change Constraints Constraints & Safety No hardware relocation Robot speed may not exceed approved limits A controlled stop must remain functional Only one variable should be changed between diagnostic trials Deliverables What You Submit Baseline and final Python programs Process map Ten-cycle data tables Before/after graph Parts-per-hour calculation Three-minute presentation Reflection Reflection Questions Which bottleneck limited the original system? Did the fastest trial also have the best reliability? Why should engineers change one variable at a time? What hardware investment would produce the next improvement? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Throughput depends on the slowest repeated step, not simply the maximum robot speed. Common Mistake A single successful fast run is not proof of a reliable production improvement. Stretch Goal Run fifty final cycles and calculate reliability, mean cycle time, and range. Career Connection Continuous improvement and industrial engineers use cycle studies to increase output without buying new equipment. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 1 Page

items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Measurement Accuracy Competition IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Measurement Accuracy Competition Measure a set of mystery parts as accurately and consistently as possible. Beginner 45 minutes Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Quality inspectors must make fast, repeatable measurements and report them with the correct precision. Objectives What You Will Practice Select appropriate measuring tools Read scales and calipers correctly Record units and precision Analyze measurement variation Materials What You Need 10-15 mystery objects Ruler Dial or digital calipers Measurement data sheet Calculator Procedure Student Instructions Create a data table with object ID, feature, tool, measurement, and units. Measure each assigned feature once without seeing the reference value. Repeat three selected measurements after a five-minute delay. Calculate the difference between repeated measurements. Compare your results with instructor reference values after all data are submitted. Calculate absolute error for each reference measurement. Identify the tool and feature associated with your largest error. Write a two-step plan for improving measurement reliability. Requirements Engineering Requirements Measure at least ten features Use the most appropriate available tool Record all values with units and realistic precision Repeat at least three measurements Calculate error or variation correctly Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not alter or mark the objects Do not share measurements before the class reveal Use safe caliper pressure on fragile parts Deliverables What You Submit Completed measurement table Repeated-measurement comparison Absolute error calculations Accuracy ranking or score Improvement plan Reflection Reflection Questions When was a ruler sufficient? When were calipers necessary? Did your repeated measurements agree? What caused your largest error? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Close calipers gently. Excess force can compress a part or tilt the jaws. Common Mistake Extra decimal places do not make a measurement accurate. Report only the precision supported by the tool. Stretch Goal Calculate the class mean and range for three measurements and identify possible outliers. Career Connection Quality technicians, machinists, and manufacturing engineers rely on repeatable inspection data to approve parts. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → IED Unit 1 Page

items.title: Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift POE 1.2 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.2 Mechanical Advantage Rescue Lift Build a compact lifting mechanism that raises a simulated payload with limited input force. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A lunar crew must raise a damaged equipment package onto a rover platform. The crew has limited force available and needs a lightweight mechanical aid. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply mechanical advantage Measure input and output force Compare ideal and actual performance Identify friction losses Materials What You Need String Pulleys or lever materials Spring scale Mass set Meter stick Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Select either a pulley or lever concept. Calculate the ideal mechanical advantage before building. Build the mechanism with secure supports. Measure the input force required to raise the assigned payload at constant speed. Calculate actual mechanical advantage and efficiency. Identify two locations where energy is lost. Modify one feature to improve performance. Repeat the force measurement and compare results. Requirements Engineering Requirements Lift the assigned payload at least 20 cm Input force must be below the instructor-set limit Payload must remain controlled and not swing freely Include ideal MA, actual MA, and efficiency calculations Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved masses Never place hands below a suspended load Inspect supports before every test Do not lift the payload above the approved height Deliverables What You Submit Concept sketch Calculations Force data table Before/after efficiency comparison Final recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Where did friction reduce performance? Did increasing mechanical advantage change the distance pulled? What design feature improved control? How would lunar gravity affect the force requirement? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Move the load slowly and steadily; acceleration will distort force readings. Common Mistake Ignoring the input distance can make a high mechanical advantage system seem “free.” Work must still be transferred. Stretch Goal Add a self-locking or braking feature that holds the load without continuous input. Career Connection Mechanical systems engineers design hoists, deployment mechanisms, and cargo-handling equipment for spacecraft and ground operations. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → POE Unit 1 Page

items.searchText: Mechanism Efficiency Showdown POE 1.5 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.5 Mechanism Efficiency Showdown Compete to transfer a fixed payload through a required path using the least input energy or force. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A ground-support team needs a mechanism to move a delicate payload between two stations. Multiple teams will propose machines and compare efficiency, reliability, and complexity. Objectives What You Will Practice Combine simple machines Measure input force and distance Calculate work and efficiency Defend a design using performance evidence Materials What You Need Approved pulleys, gears, levers, wheels, axles, or linkages Spring scale Meter tape Fixed payload Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the payload path and boundaries. Sketch two mechanism concepts that use at least two simple-machine elements. Estimate mechanical advantage and input travel. Build one design and complete a low-load functional test. Measure average input force and input distance for three official trials. Calculate input work and compare it with useful output work. Record success rate and completion time. Prepare a one-minute defense of the design. Requirements Engineering Requirements Move the payload from start to finish without direct hand contact Use at least two mechanical elements Complete three official trials Provide work and efficiency calculations Scoring includes efficiency, reliability, and simplicity Constraints Constraints & Safety No launching or free-falling payloads Use only approved stored energy Inspect supports and connections before testing Stop immediately if parts bind or fail Deliverables What You Submit Two concept sketches Calculations Official trial table Efficiency result Design defense Reflection Reflection Questions What feature improved efficiency most? Did the most efficient design also finish fastest? How did part count affect reliability? What would you change for a more fragile payload? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Measure force while the system moves at steady speed; peak starting force may not represent the full trial. Common Mistake Comparing only completion time ignores input effort and reliability. Stretch Goal Redesign to complete the same task with 25% fewer parts. Career Connection Mechanical design and operations engineers evaluate cargo-handling systems using efficiency, reliability, maintainability, and safety. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → POE Unit 1 Page

Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.5 Mission Data Dashboard Create the clearest and most useful dashboard for a rover test data set. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A mission manager needs to make a quick go/no-go decision using data from speed, temperature, battery voltage, sensor faults, and task completion. Objectives What You Will Practice Select meaningful data displays Avoid misleading graphs Create performance thresholds Communicate an engineering decision Materials What You Need Instructor-provided rover test data Spreadsheet or visualization software Mission requirements Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the data dictionary and mission success criteria. Identify the five most decision-relevant measures. Choose an appropriate chart, table, or status indicator for each. Create threshold colors or flags based on stated requirements. Build a one-page dashboard. Write a go/no-go recommendation using evidence from the dashboard. Exchange dashboards and have another team answer three mission questions. Revise any display that caused confusion. Requirements Engineering Requirements One-page dashboard At least three different visualization types Every visual must include labels and units Thresholds must come from mission criteria No decorative chart may obscure data Recommendation must be traceable to the dashboard Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not alter source data Clearly identify missing data Avoid color-only communication when possible Deliverables What You Submit Dashboard Data-selection rationale Go/no-go recommendation Peer usability results Revised final version Reflection Reflection Questions Which visual supported the fastest decision? What information was unnecessary? How did you display uncertainty or missing data? What graph choice could mislead a viewer? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Design the dashboard around decisions the user must make, not around every variable available. Common Mistake Using a visually impressive but inappropriate graph can hide patterns or exaggerate differences. Stretch Goal Create a live version that automatically updates when new rows are added. Career Connection Flight-test, systems, and mission-operations teams use dashboards to monitor vehicle health and test readiness. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson → POE Unit 4 Page

items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Mission Team Communication Protocol POE 0.4 Mission Team Communication Protocol | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.4 Mission Team Communication Protocol Design and test a concise communication protocol for a multi-station engineering task. Intermediate 1 class period Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover test team must coordinate a driver, sensor observer, data recorder, and safety lead. Miscommunication could damage hardware or invalidate test data. Objectives What You Will Practice Define clear team roles Create standardized callouts Use closed-loop communication Evaluate communication performance Materials What You Need Role cards Simple timed team task Communication log Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Assign four team roles and define each role’s authority. Write standard callouts for ready, start, stop, fault, data confirmed, and reset. Create a rule requiring the receiver to repeat critical commands. Run a baseline task using normal conversation and record errors or delays. Run the task again using the protocol. Compare completion time, errors, and missed information. Revise two parts of the protocol. Requirements Engineering Requirements Every critical command must receive confirmation One person must have stop-work authority Protocol must distinguish normal completion from emergency stop Testing must include before/after evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a low-risk instructor-approved task No running or unsafe movement The safety lead may stop the task at any time Deliverables What You Submit Role chart Communication protocol Baseline and final performance table Revision notes Team reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which callout prevented the most confusion? Did the protocol slow the team down or make it faster overall? What information should never be assumed? How could the protocol work in a noisy environment? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use short, unique phrases that cannot be confused with casual conversation. Common Mistake Adding too many callouts can make the system harder to use. Standardize only critical information. Stretch Goal Add a hand-signal or visual backup for two critical commands. Career Connection Flight-test and launch teams use disciplined communication because ambiguous instructions can create serious risk. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → POE Unit 0 Page

items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Offline Programming Deployment ADM 3.2 Offline Programming Deployment | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Orbital Components Group Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Offline Programming Deployment Develop and debug a complete robot task in simulation before its first physical run. Advanced 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orbital Components Group Department: Virtual Commissioning Goal: Deploy a new robot task with minimal physical downtime. Background Engineering Context A spacecraft-component line cannot pause while engineers experiment with new code. Your team must program a replacement handling task offline, verify it virtually, and deploy it with minimal physical-cell downtime. Objectives What You Will Practice Develop robot logic in an offline environment Use virtual testing to identify collisions and errors Create a controlled deployment checklist Compare predicted and actual commissioning time Equipment What You Need Simulation/digital twin environment VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm Parts and fixtures Python project Deployment checklist Procedure Student Instructions Receive the required pickup, inspection, and placement sequence. Measure or verify all fixture coordinates in the virtual model. Write the full program without operating the physical robot. Run at least ten simulated cycles and resolve every collision or fault. Record predicted cycle time and create a risk checklist. Perform a line-by-line safety review before physical deployment. Run the physical system first at reduced speed. Correct only differences that could not be predicted virtually. Record total physical commissioning time and compare it with the predicted plan. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete ten fault-free simulated cycles before deployment Complete the first physical cycle at reduced speed Achieve five consecutive physical cycles Document every change made after deployment Constraints Constraints & Safety No physical trial-and-error before simulation approval Hardware coordinates must be verified Safety stop must be tested before deployment Use approved reduced speed for first run Deliverables What You Submit Offline Python program Simulation test log Collision/risk checklist Deployment checklist Physical commissioning record Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which issue was discovered only in the physical cell? How much physical downtime did offline programming save? Which model detail was most important? How should future fixtures be documented? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Treat the first physical run as verification, not as the first debugging session. Common Mistake Assuming fixture coordinates are identical between virtual and physical cells can cause immediate collisions. Stretch Goal Deploy a second product variation using only parameter changes. Career Connection Offline robot programmers prepare and validate production code without interrupting active factory lines. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell ADM 1.1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Optimize the Pick-and-Place Workcell Reduce robot cycle time while maintaining 100% successful part transfers. Intermediate 1 class period Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Automated Assembly Goal: Increase output without purchasing a second robot. Background Engineering Context A small aerospace supplier uses a 6-axis robot to move components from an incoming fixture to a pallet. The program works, but the robot travels through several unnecessary positions and pauses longer than needed. Management wants a software-only improvement before purchasing additional equipment. Objectives What You Will Practice Analyze robot motion and identify non-value-added travel Measure and calculate average cycle time Revise movement commands while preserving safety Use test evidence to justify an improvement Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell 6-Axis Arm with magnet end effector Cubes or disks Stopwatch or elapsed-time display Python project Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Load the current pick-and-place program and verify that it completes one full cycle correctly. Run five cycles and record each cycle time. Calculate the average. Sketch the robot path and label every pickup, clearance, travel, and drop-off point. Identify at least three moves, waits, or height changes that may be reduced or combined. Create a copy of the program and make one change at a time. After each change, run five cycles and record accuracy and average time. Select the fastest version that completes ten consecutive transfers without an error. Calculate the percent improvement and summarize the changes that mattered most. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce average cycle time by at least 15% Complete ten consecutive transfers with no drops or collisions Begin and end at the approved Home position Keep all movement within the approved work envelope Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change hardware locations Robot speed may not exceed 100% The magnet must remain the end effector A safety stop must remain available Deliverables What You Submit Original and revised Python programs Robot-path sketch with identified waste Five-trial before/after timing table Percent-improvement calculation Notebook reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which change produced the greatest time savings? What tradeoff did you observe between speed and reliability? Which motion would you redesign if the workcell layout could change? How would one second saved per cycle affect a factory running 8 hours per day? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Optimize path length and unnecessary waits before increasing motor speed. Common Mistake Removing every clearance point may create a collision even when the start and end coordinates are correct. Stretch Goal Achieve a 25% improvement and verify the program for 25 consecutive parts. Career Connection Manufacturing and automation engineers optimize robot motion because small cycle-time savings compound across thousands of parts. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 1 Page
