items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Peer Design Review of the Rocket IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.4 Peer Design Review of the Rocket Conduct a professional, evidence-based review of another team’s rocket design and recommend prioritized improvements. Intermediate 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineering teams use formal reviews to identify risk before spending time and money on fabrication. Objectives What You Will Practice Use criteria to evaluate a design Separate observations from opinions Identify design risk Give actionable technical feedback Materials What You Need Another team’s rocket sketches or model Design review form Engineering notebook Ruler or calipers if permitted Procedure Student Instructions Review the project criteria and constraints before seeing the design. Inspect the design silently for three minutes and record only observations. Ask the design team three clarifying questions. Evaluate fit, stability, manufacturability, assembly, documentation, and safety. Identify two strengths supported by evidence. Identify three risks and rate each as low, medium, or high. Write one specific recommendation for each risk. Meet with the team for five minutes and explain the highest-priority recommendation. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use respectful, technical language Support every rating with observed evidence Identify at least two strengths and three risks Make recommendations specific enough to act on Prioritize the recommendations Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not redesign the project for the team Do not change or handle a model without permission Keep feedback focused on criteria and constraints Deliverables What You Submit Completed design review form Risk-priority table Three recommendations Brief feedback summary signed by both teams Reflection Reflection Questions Which risk was most likely to affect performance? How did the team’s explanation change your evaluation? Which recommendation could be completed fastest? What feedback would help your own design? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the pattern “I observed..., which may cause..., so I recommend...” for clear feedback. Common Mistake “I do not like it” is not engineering feedback. Tie comments to requirements, evidence, or risk. Stretch Goal Review the revised design later and document whether each high-priority risk was reduced. Career Connection Design review engineers and project teams use preliminary and critical design reviews to find issues before production or flight. items.searchText: Pneumatic Sample-Lift Mechanism POE 3.3 Pneumatic Sample-Lift Mechanism | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.3 Pneumatic Sample-Lift Mechanism Use a pneumatic actuator to lift or position a sample while controlling motion and air use. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover must transfer a soil sample from the ground to an onboard analysis tray. Your team will prototype the actuator portion of the mechanism. Objectives What You Will Practice Describe pneumatic energy conversion Select cylinder motion and linkage Control extend/retract sequence Identify pinch and pressure hazards Materials What You Need Low-pressure classroom pneumatic kit Cylinder Tubing and fittings Control valve or programmed solenoid Lightweight sample object Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define the start and end positions of the sample. Sketch two mechanisms using the cylinder directly or through a linkage. Select one concept and identify pinch points. Assemble the circuit with pressure off. Check tubing and fittings before enabling air. Run manual low-pressure extension and retraction. Add control logic or a repeatable operating procedure. Complete ten transfer cycles and record faults or air leaks. Requirements Engineering Requirements Move the sample through the required height or angle No uncontrolled dropping Complete ten cycles without a tubing disconnect Include a safe default state Document the pneumatic diagram Constraints Constraints & Safety Depressurize before changing tubing Keep fingers clear of pinch points Use only instructor-set pressure Wear eye protection if required Deliverables What You Submit Concept sketches Pneumatic diagram Final mechanism photo Cycle test log Safety analysis Reflection Reflection Questions Why was the cylinder bore or stroke appropriate? Where could the mechanism jam? What happened when air flow changed? How could a sensor confirm motion? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Arrange the mechanism so a loss of pressure moves the system toward a safe state whenever possible. Common Mistake Changing tubing while the system is pressurized can cause sudden motion or hose release. Stretch Goal Add a sensor interlock that prevents the next step until the cylinder reaches position. Career Connection Fluid-power and mechatronics engineers use pneumatic systems for clamps, deployment devices, and factory support equipment. items.searchText: Portfolio-Quality Exploded View IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.2 Portfolio-Quality Exploded View Create a professional exploded view, BOM, and assembly-order visual suitable for a portfolio or design review. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A technical presentation needs one image that clearly explains how the rocket assembly fits together. Objectives What You Will Practice Create an exploded assembly view Use balloons and a BOM consistently Communicate assembly sequence Improve technical drawing layout Materials What You Need Completed rocket assembly CAD Fusion 360 drawing workspace Drawing checklist Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Inspect the assembly browser and rename unclear components. Create or verify a complete BOM with part numbers and quantities. Plan an explosion direction that keeps parts readable and avoids crossing paths. Create the exploded view with consistent spacing. Add trail lines where they clarify movement. Place the view on a drawing sheet and add balloons linked to the BOM. Add one detail view for a small or hidden connection. Use the checklist to inspect alignment, readability, title block, and consistency. Requirements Engineering Requirements Every modeled component appears in the BOM Every BOM item is ballooned exactly once in the main view or detail Explosion order reflects a logical assembly sequence No part paths overlap in a confusing way Drawing includes title, scale, revision, and author Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the current approved assembly Keep the drawing to one sheet Do not use decorative backgrounds that reduce readability Deliverables What You Submit Updated assembly component names Exploded view drawing PDF BOM Ballooned assembly view One detail view Completed quality checklist Reflection Reflection Questions Which parts were hardest to separate visually? How did you choose the explosion direction? Could a technician infer assembly order? What makes the drawing portfolio-ready? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use larger spacing for large parts and smaller spacing for closely related fasteners, but keep the pattern consistent. Common Mistake An exploded view is not random separation. It should preserve relationships and communicate sequence. Stretch Goal Create a short animation that follows the same assembly order. Career Connection Technical illustrators and mechanical designers create exploded views for assembly, service, sales, and training. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Power-Limited Winch Design POE 1.4 Power-Limited Winch Design | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.4 Power-Limited Winch Design Design a winch that lifts the greatest useful load without exceeding a motor or power limit. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A drone recovery station has a small motor but must lift equipment safely. Your team must balance drum radius, speed, torque, and structural support. Objectives What You Will Practice Relate torque, radius, force, speed, and power Use calculations to guide design Test a mechanism under load Evaluate design tradeoffs Materials What You Need Low-voltage motor or hand-crank simulation Spools of different radii String Masses Timer Structural materials Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Record the available motor speed or hand-input condition. Create at least three drum-radius concepts. Predict which radius will lift fastest and which will lift the greatest load. Build a supported winch with one selected drum. Test a standard load and record lift time. Increase load in approved increments until the design reaches the limit. Calculate output work and average power for one successful lift. Revise the drum or support and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Lift through a fixed height No uncontrolled dropping or slipping Include a stable axle support and secure string attachment Use at least one calculation before selecting the final drum Final design must complete three repeatable lifts Constraints Constraints & Safety Use instructor-approved voltage and masses Keep hands clear of winding string Do not stall a motor for extended time Use a catch zone below the load Deliverables What You Submit Concept comparison Torque/radius calculations Test data Final winch photo or CAD Design tradeoff explanation Reflection Reflection Questions How did drum radius affect speed and lifting force? What limited the design first: motor, structure, traction, or string? Where was power lost? What safety factor would be appropriate for real cargo? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A smaller drum increases available line force but requires more rotations to lift the same distance. Common Mistake Calculating torque without using consistent units is a common source of error. Stretch Goal Add a ratchet or brake that prevents rollback during a power loss. Career Connection Actuation engineers design winches, reels, and deployment systems for aircraft recovery equipment and spacecraft mechanisms. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → POE Unit 1 Page

items.searchText: Precision Measurement Verification POE 0.2 Precision Measurement Verification | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.2 Precision Measurement Verification Measure a set of parts, compare repeated readings, and decide whether the measurements are trustworthy. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Replacement rover components arrived without complete inspection records. Your team must verify critical dimensions before the parts are released for assembly. Objectives What You Will Practice Use rulers and calipers correctly Evaluate repeatability and measurement variation Record measurements with appropriate precision Make an evidence-based accept/recheck decision Materials What You Need Three to five instructor-selected parts Metric ruler Digital or dial caliper Measurement data sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Identify the dimensions that are most important to fit or assembly. Measure each critical dimension three times without looking at previous results. Have a partner independently measure the same dimensions. Calculate the range for each set of measurements. Compare your readings with the partner readings and any reference dimension provided. Mark each dimension Accept, Recheck, or Reject and explain why. Write one improvement to the measurement procedure. Requirements Engineering Requirements Record units and instrument used for every dimension Use three repeated measurements per dimension Measurements must be readable and traceable to a labeled feature Decisions must cite numerical evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not force caliper jaws onto a part Use only approved parts Do not treat instrument display resolution as guaranteed accuracy Deliverables What You Submit Labeled part sketch Measurement table Range calculations Accept/recheck/reject decisions Procedure improvement note Reflection Reflection Questions What caused the largest measurement variation? Which instrument was most appropriate for each feature? How would temperature or surface damage affect results? What measurement would you verify first before assembly? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use the same contact points and instrument orientation each time you repeat a measurement. Common Mistake Changing where you measure a feature can create apparent variation that is actually a setup difference. Stretch Goal Design a simple go/no-go gauge concept for one critical dimension. Career Connection Quality engineers and metrology technicians verify incoming components before they enter aircraft or spacecraft assemblies. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → POE Unit 0 Page

items.searchText: Preflight Readiness Review POE 0.5 Preflight Readiness Review | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.5 Preflight Readiness Review Create and conduct the most reliable preflight inspection for a classroom rover or mechanism. Advanced 1-2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Two student teams are preparing identical systems for a mission demonstration. The winning team is not simply the fastest; it is the team whose checklist catches the most faults while remaining efficient. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate failure risks into inspection steps Sequence checks efficiently Use objective pass/fail criteria Validate a checklist through fault insertion Materials What You Need Classroom rover or mechanism Fault cards or instructor-inserted issues Checklist template Timer Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions List at least ten possible mission-preventing faults. Rank each fault by likelihood and consequence. Write a checklist with observable pass/fail criteria. Arrange checks from safe/no-power inspection through powered functional checks. Exchange systems with another team; the instructor inserts approved faults. Conduct the inspection while being timed. Record detected faults, missed faults, and unnecessary checks. Revise the checklist and repeat one validation round. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 12 checklist items Checklist must include identity, physical condition, power, movement, sensor/control, and final configuration No item may use vague wording such as “looks good” Score balances detection rate and completion time Constraints Constraints & Safety Only instructor-approved faults may be inserted Do not defeat guards or create electrical hazards Power must remain off during physical inspection unless instructed Deliverables What You Submit Risk-ranked fault list Preflight checklist Validation results Revised checklist Competition score summary Reflection Reflection Questions Which fault was easiest to miss? Which checklist item had the clearest pass/fail standard? What check could be automated? How did time pressure affect performance? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write checklist items as actions with a condition: “Verify battery connector is fully seated and locked.” Common Mistake A long checklist is not automatically better. Repeated or low-value checks can hide critical items. Stretch Goal Convert the final checklist into a QR-linked digital form. Career Connection Aerospace operations teams use configuration-controlled checklists for aircraft, launch vehicles, and ground support equipment. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Production Scheduling Under Demand Changes ADM 4.2 Production Scheduling Under Demand Changes | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. AeroSupply Operations Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Production Scheduling Under Demand Changes Create a production schedule that meets changing demand while respecting machine capacity and due dates. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications AeroSupply Operations Department: Production Planning Goal: Meet demand with limited machine capacity. Background Engineering Context AeroSupply receives urgent orders for three component types. Each product requires different processing time and setup. Your team must build a schedule that minimizes late orders and unnecessary changeovers. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate demand into capacity requirements Create and evaluate production schedules Consider setup time and bottlenecks Use metrics to justify a schedule Equipment What You Need Demand/order table Machine capacity data Processing and setup-time table Spreadsheet or scheduling board Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Calculate total required processing time for each product. Determine available capacity for each shift or day. Identify the bottleneck resource. Create Schedule A that prioritizes earliest due date. Create Schedule B that groups products to reduce setup time. Calculate late orders, total setup time, and machine utilization for both. Create a third hybrid schedule that improves the weak metric. Recommend the best schedule and explain the customer tradeoff. Requirements Engineering Requirements Schedule every order Do not exceed available machine capacity Report lateness, setup time, and utilization Meet all high-priority aerospace orders if feasible Constraints Constraints & Safety Use the provided processing times Machines cannot process two jobs simultaneously Setup time must be included Document any order that cannot be completed on time Deliverables What You Submit Capacity calculations Three schedules Metric comparison table Recommended schedule Customer-impact explanation Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why did reducing setups sometimes delay an order? Which resource limited output? How would overtime change the plan? What data would improve the schedule? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A schedule is only feasible if every processing and setup minute fits within available capacity. Common Mistake Sorting orders by due date without including setup time can create an impossible schedule. Stretch Goal Add a machine breakdown and revise the schedule within ten minutes. Career Connection Production planners balance customer due dates, equipment capacity, labor, and setup losses. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.1 Projectile Test-Range Analysis Collect launch data, model projectile motion, and evaluate how well predictions match the test. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small payload-deployment system must place a sensor inside a target zone. Your team will analyze a safe classroom launcher or simulation. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure launch conditions Apply horizontal and vertical kinematics Create graphs and uncertainty statements Compare model predictions with test results Materials What You Need Approved launcher or simulation Meter tape Angle tool if applicable Stopwatch or video timing Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define launch height, angle, and target coordinate system. Record at least five trials at one controlled setting. Calculate predicted flight time and horizontal range using the assigned model. Measure actual landing positions. Calculate average range, range spread, and percent difference from prediction. Graph the landing positions or range results. Identify at least three causes of model-test disagreement. Recommend a setting adjustment for the target zone. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least five valid trials Consistent launch setting All equations and units shown Include average and variation, not only one trial Recommendation must cite prediction and data Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only the approved range and launcher No aiming toward people or breakable objects Retrieve projectiles only after the range is clear Follow all eye-protection requirements Deliverables What You Submit Test setup diagram Calculations Trial data Graph Prediction comparison Targeting recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Which assumption in the model was least realistic? Was the error systematic or random? How would launch-height uncertainty affect the result? What additional measurement would improve the prediction? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use a coordinate system and clearly define where horizontal distance begins. Common Mistake Comparing a prediction to the single closest trial hides the actual variation in performance. Stretch Goal Use your data to create a 90% target interval for expected landing position. Career Connection Flight-test engineers compare analytical trajectories with instrumented tests for release systems, drones, and launch vehicles. Intermediate 2-3 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Fit testing has revealed one rocket component that is difficult to assemble, weak, or unreliable. Objectives What You Will Practice Translate test evidence into design changes Revise a parametric part Plan a fair comparison Document prototype improvement Materials What You Need Original component and CAD file Fusion 360 3D printer Calipers Test materials appropriate to the component Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Select one component and define the specific problem using evidence. Choose one measurable performance indicator such as insertion force, alignment error, mass, deflection, or assembly time. Record baseline measurements for the original component. Sketch two redesign options and select one. Revise the CAD while preserving required interfaces. Print the revised component with recorded settings. Run the same test on the original and revised versions. Decide whether the revision should be accepted, modified, or rejected. Requirements Engineering Requirements Define one measurable improvement target Preserve all required interface dimensions Change only features connected to the identified problem Use the same test method for both versions Document print settings and revision Constraints Constraints & Safety One component only unless approved Use classroom-approved materials and test loads Do not claim improvement without comparative evidence Deliverables What You Submit Problem statement and baseline data Two concept sketches Revised CAD and STL Original/revised photographs Comparison data Revision decision and justification Reflection Reflection Questions Did the redesign meet the target? What unintended effect appeared? Was the test sensitive enough to show a difference? What would be changed in Revision B? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Define the test and success target before redesigning. Otherwise, it is easy to declare any result an improvement. Common Mistake Do not change several unrelated features at once; you may not know which change caused the result. Stretch Goal Reduce mass or print time while preserving the performance improvement. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.

Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.1 Redesign for Limited Hand Strength Redesign an approved classroom product to reduce required grip force or improve control without removing its core function. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A user can understand a classroom product but has difficulty gripping, twisting, or pressing it because of limited hand strength. Objectives What You Will Practice Identify user needs through empathy and evidence Translate needs into measurable requirements Generate accessible concepts Evaluate a human-centered prototype Materials What You Need Approved classroom product User-needs interview sheet Sketching materials Cardboard, foam, clay, or other prototype materials Force gauge if available Procedure Student Instructions Select a product with a grip, cap, button, lever, or control. Create a respectful user profile based on limited hand strength; do not simulate a disability in an unsafe way. Observe the product and identify at least three barriers. Convert barriers into measurable requirements such as diameter, force, reach, or texture. Sketch three concepts and collect feedback from a peer acting as a reviewer. Build a low-fidelity prototype of the selected concept. Run a usability test using the same task for the original and redesign. Document feedback and make one revision. Requirements Engineering Requirements Address at least two identified user barriers Include at least three measurable requirements Preserve the product’s core function Avoid a design that creates a new safety hazard Collect and respond to user feedback Constraints Constraints & Safety Use respectful, person-centered language Do not ask a student to imitate pain or injury Prototype materials must be safe and reversible Do not permanently modify school property Deliverables What You Submit User profile and needs Barrier observations Three concept sketches Requirements list Prototype Original/redesign usability comparison Revision summary Reflection Reflection Questions Which user need was hardest to convert into a requirement? What feedback changed your design? Did improving accessibility help other users too? What would require additional real-user testing? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Ask what task is difficult and why. Avoid assuming the solution before understanding the user. Common Mistake Making a handle larger is not automatically accessible; reach, force, texture, feedback, and context all matter. Stretch Goal Redesign the product for one additional user need without reducing the first improvement. Career Connection Human factors and accessibility engineers design controls, tools, interiors, and equipment for a wide range of users. items.searchText: Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.1 Redesign the Rocket Launch Pad Redesign the launch pad to use less material while maintaining stability, rocket fit, and safe classroom handling. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Your original launch pad proved that a free-standing structure can support the classroom rocket. A launch systems team now wants a lighter, easier-to-build version that still protects and supports the vehicle. Objectives What You Will Practice Apply criteria and constraints to a redesign Generate and compare multiple concepts Collect stability test evidence Justify a final design using data Materials What You Need Original launch pad or drawings Provided 3D printed rocket Approved classroom build materials Ruler or tape measure Scale if available Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the original design and list three specific weaknesses. Measure and record the original mass, footprint, and rocket contact points. Create two new annotated concept sketches. Each concept must show how the rocket is supported. Use a decision matrix with at least four criteria to select a concept. Build the selected concept using fewer materials than the original. Test the pad on a level surface and on a 5-degree inclined surface. Place the rocket on the pad and perform three gentle disturbance tests from different directions. Record results, revise one feature, and repeat the test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Support the provided rocket without assistance Stand on its own for at least 60 seconds Remain upright during three disturbance tests Use at least 20% less material by mass or measured quantity Include at least one research-informed launch pad feature Constraints Constraints & Safety Use only approved classroom materials No adhesives or fasteners may contact the rocket body Must fit within a 30 cm by 30 cm footprint Must be completed within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Problem statement and criteria/constraints Two annotated concept sketches Decision matrix Before-and-after material comparison Test table with at least six trials Photo of final prototype One-paragraph design justification Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion had the greatest influence on your final design? What failed or moved during testing? What tradeoff did you make between mass and stability? What would you test next if the pad were used outdoors? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Move material away from low-stress areas and keep support members near the rocket contact points. Common Mistake Reducing material everywhere usually weakens the base. Remove material strategically instead of simply making every part smaller. Stretch Goal Reduce material use by 35% while keeping the same test performance. Career Connection Aerospace ground-support engineers design stands, fixtures, and launch equipment that protect vehicles before flight. items.title: Resilient Manufacturing System
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Resilient Manufacturing System ADM 4.4 Resilient Manufacturing System | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Orion Aerospace Systems Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.4 Resilient Manufacturing System Redesign a production process so critical orders continue after one machine or supplier failure. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orion Aerospace Systems Department: Business Continuity Goal: Continue priority production after a critical failure. Background Engineering Context A single machine currently performs a critical operation for an aerospace component. A recent outage stopped the entire line. Your team must create a resilience plan using alternate routing, inventory, or recovery strategies. Objectives What You Will Practice Map dependencies in a production system Analyze single points of failure Develop contingency and recovery strategies Evaluate resilience tradeoffs Equipment What You Need Current process map Machine and supplier capacity data Failure scenario cards Risk matrix Spreadsheet or planning board Procedure Student Instructions Create a current-state process map from raw material to shipment. Mark every machine, supplier, data system, and inventory dependency. Identify at least three single points of failure. Draw one failure scenario and calculate lost production if no action is taken. Develop three resilience options, such as alternate machine, safety stock, cross-training, or backup supplier. Estimate cost, recovery time, and production impact for each option. Use a weighted decision matrix to select a strategy. Create a response playbook with detection, containment, alternate operation, and recovery steps. Test the playbook using a second surprise failure scenario. Requirements Engineering Requirements Address at least three failure points Maintain priority production in the selected scenario Include detection and communication steps Quantify recovery time and production impact Constraints Constraints & Safety Use provided capacity and cost data Do not assume unlimited backup capacity Safety and quality requirements cannot be waived Document any unmet demand Deliverables What You Submit Dependency/process map Failure-impact calculations Three resilience concepts Decision matrix Response playbook Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which dependency was most critical? Why is maximum inventory not always the best solution? How did recovery time affect your choice? What information should be monitored in real time? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Resilience usually combines prevention, redundancy, flexible capacity, and a practiced response plan. Common Mistake A backup resource is not useful if it has never been qualified or cannot meet the required capacity. Stretch Goal Include a simultaneous cyber outage and supplier delay in the tabletop test. Career Connection Supply chain and business continuity engineers prepare factories for equipment, supplier, weather, and cyber disruptions. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 4 Page

Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 0 | Mission Brief 0.2 Reverse Engineer a Classroom Object Analyze a classroom object and create an engineering record that explains its parts, materials, assembly, and likely manufacturing methods. Beginner 45-60 minutes Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Engineers often study an existing product before they redesign it. Reverse engineering begins with careful observation, component identification, and reasoned predictions about how a product works. Objectives What You Will Practice Practice technical observation Identify product components and functions Connect materials to manufacturing processes Create an exploded concept sketch Materials What You Need One approved classroom object Engineering notebook Ruler Colored pencils or fine-tip pens Optional magnifier Procedure Student Instructions Select an object with at least four visible parts, such as a stapler, tape dispenser, scissors, hole punch, or marker. Create a clean isometric sketch of the complete object. Number every visible component and create a matching parts list. For each component, record its function and likely material. Predict how each part was manufactured: molding, stamping, extrusion, machining, forming, or another process. Create an exploded sketch showing the likely assembly order. Identify one design feature that improves safety, comfort, durability, or ease of assembly. Propose one redesign and explain the problem it solves. Requirements Engineering Requirements Identify at least four components Use labels and leader lines correctly Include a material and process prediction for every component Show a logical exploded assembly order Support predictions with visible evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not disassemble sealed, sharp, powered, or school-owned equipment without permission Complete all sketches by hand Do not use an internet image as the primary drawing Deliverables What You Submit Complete-object isometric sketch Numbered parts list Material and manufacturing table Exploded sketch Redesign annotation and explanation Reflection Reflection Questions Which component was hardest to understand? What visible clues helped identify the manufacturing process? Which material choice appeared most important? How would your redesign affect manufacturing cost? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Look for seams, draft angles, fasteners, surface textures, and repeated shapes. These are clues about manufacturing. Common Mistake Do not confuse a component function with its material. “Spring” is a component; “spring steel” is a material choice. Stretch Goal Compare your object with a competing version and identify three design differences. Career Connection Product design and manufacturing engineers routinely analyze competitor products to understand performance, cost, and assembly decisions. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 0 Next Lesson → IED Unit 0 Page

items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Reverse Engineer a Hand Tool IED Unit 0 | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 1 | Mission Brief 1.1 Reverse Engineer a Hand Tool Produce accurate multiview and isometric documentation for an approved hand tool. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A maintenance team needs replacement documentation for a hand tool whose original drawings are unavailable. Your team must create a clear measured sketch package. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure real objects accurately Create multiview and isometric sketches Apply dimensioning conventions Estimate functional tolerances Materials What You Need Approved hand tool Ruler and calipers Graph and isometric paper Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Select an approved tool such as an Allen wrench, screwdriver, small wrench, or pliers. Identify the primary functional features and measurement datums. Measure overall dimensions, thicknesses, diameters, and feature locations. Create front, top, and right-side orthographic views aligned correctly. Add dimensions without duplication. Create an isometric sketch using the same measurements. Identify two dimensions that require tighter tolerance and explain why. Have a peer use only your drawings to identify the tool and verify three dimensions. Requirements Engineering Requirements Include three aligned orthographic views Include one isometric view Show at least eight dimensions with units Avoid duplicate or missing critical dimensions Identify two tolerance recommendations Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not measure moving or sharp surfaces unsafely All drawings must be created by hand Use only the approved measuring tools Deliverables What You Submit Measurement table Three-view drawing Isometric drawing Tolerance notes Peer verification results Reflection Reflection Questions Which view communicated the most information? Which dimension was hardest to measure? Where could measurement error affect function? What would be needed to manufacture the tool? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Choose datums before measuring so feature locations are referenced consistently. Common Mistake Dimensioning every visible line creates clutter. Dimension the features needed to define the part. Stretch Goal Create a sectional or detail view of the most complex feature. Career Connection Drafters, CAD technicians, and mechanical engineers create drawings that allow products to be manufactured and inspected. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 1 Next Lesson → IED Unit 1 Page

Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.1 Reverse Engineer a Tape Measure Hook Measure and model a tape measure hook as a fully constrained, parametric CAD part. Intermediate 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A maintenance department needs a replacement tape hook, but the supplier no longer provides the part file. Objectives What You Will Practice Use calipers to collect part dimensions Create fully constrained sketches Build a parametric model Compare CAD geometry to a physical part Materials What You Need Tape measure hook or similar flat metal part Calipers Fusion 360 Engineering notebook Optional flatbed photo with scale Procedure Student Instructions Identify the part’s datums and create a measurement plan. Measure overall length, width, thickness, holes, slots, bends, and feature spacing. Create a parameter table before sketching. Build the base profile with geometric and dimensional constraints. Add holes, slots, fillets, and bends or approximations in a logical feature order. Verify that every sketch is fully constrained. Create a technical drawing with the dimensions needed for inspection. Compare at least five CAD measurements with the physical part and calculate error. Requirements Engineering Requirements Fully constrained sketches All critical dimensions driven by parameters Five comparison measurements within +/-0.5 mm Realistic fillets and feature order Complete drawing and STL export Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not disassemble a tape measure spring mechanism Model only the approved hook component Use metric units Complete within two class periods Deliverables What You Submit Measurement plan and table Fusion 360 file Parameter list Technical drawing PDF STL file CAD-to-part error table Reflection Reflection Questions Which measurement controlled the most geometry? Where was the largest error? How did constraints make revision easier? What manufacturing process likely created the original part? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Photographing the part next to a ruler can help verify overall proportions, but use calipers for final dimensions. Common Mistake Do not trace a photo and assume it is accurate; camera perspective can distort geometry. Stretch Goal Redesign the hook for easier grip while preserving all connection dimensions. Career Connection Reverse-engineering and sustaining engineers recreate legacy parts when drawings or suppliers are unavailable. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.2 Rover Acceleration Characterization Measure rover motion and determine whether acceleration is approximately constant during startup. Intermediate 1 class period Skill Builder Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A mission-planning team needs a simple model of rover startup motion to estimate stopping and maneuvering distance. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect position-time data Calculate velocity and acceleration Interpret motion graphs Judge whether a model is appropriate Materials What You Need Rover Straight measured track Video camera or motion sensor Spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Mark a straight test track and choose a consistent rover command. Collect position versus time using video frames or a motion sensor. Create a position-time graph. Calculate interval velocities and create a velocity-time graph. Estimate acceleration from the graph. Repeat the trial two more times. Compare acceleration values and decide whether a constant-acceleration model is reasonable. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least three trials Consistent battery and command settings Show calculation method for velocity and acceleration Use graphs with labeled axes and units Model conclusion must include evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a clear track Maintain immediate stop control Do not stand in front of the rover Secure loose cables and equipment Deliverables What You Submit Test method Position data Position-time and velocity-time graphs Acceleration estimate Model evaluation Reflection Reflection Questions Where was acceleration most constant? How did sampling interval affect the graph? What caused differences among trials? How would payload mass change startup motion? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use consistent time intervals and identify the center time for interval velocity values. Common Mistake Calculating one acceleration value from the entire run can hide changes during startup and steady motion. Stretch Goal Repeat with an added payload and compare acceleration statistically. Career Connection Vehicle dynamics and controls engineers characterize acceleration, braking, and traction for autonomous vehicles. items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Rover Anomaly Review Board POE 5.4 Rover Anomaly Review Board | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.4 Rover Anomaly Review Board Investigate a failed mission trial, identify the most likely cause, and approve a corrective action. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context During a rover mission rehearsal, the vehicle stopped early, missed the sample, or returned with incomplete data. Your team will act as an anomaly review board. Objectives What You Will Practice Separate facts from assumptions Build a fault tree or cause map Use evidence to rank causes Define corrective and preventive actions Materials What You Need Instructor-provided anomaly scenario and evidence packet Fault-tree template Test logs or code excerpts Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Create a timeline of confirmed events. List facts, unknowns, and assumptions in separate columns. Define the top failure event. Build a fault tree or cause-and-effect diagram with at least three branches. Use available evidence to eliminate or rank causes. Identify the most likely root cause and one contributing factor. Write a corrective action and a verification test. Present a return-to-test recommendation: approve, approve with limits, or hold. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use only evidence in the packet unless assumptions are labeled At least three plausible cause branches Corrective action must address the identified cause Verification test must have measurable pass/fail criteria Final recommendation includes residual risk Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not blame individuals; focus on system, process, design, and evidence Protect any provided student/team identifiers Do not modify original logs Deliverables What You Submit Event timeline Facts/unknowns/assumptions table Fault tree Root-cause statement Corrective-action plan Return-to-test decision Reflection Reflection Questions What evidence most strongly changed your conclusion? What cause remained possible but unproven? How could the process prevent recurrence? What additional data should future tests record? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Preserve multiple plausible causes until evidence supports eliminating them. Common Mistake Choosing the first obvious cause can lead to corrective action that does not prevent recurrence. Stretch Goal Create a revised checklist or code monitor that detects the anomaly earlier. Career Connection Aerospace anomaly review boards investigate test and mission failures before hardware returns to operation. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → POE Unit 5 Page

items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Rover Design Trade Study POE 5.2 Rover Design Trade Study | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.2 Rover Design Trade Study Compare three rover concepts using mission-weighted criteria and recommend one for detailed design. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context The project team has several promising rover concepts but limited time and budget. A structured trade study is required before committing to hardware. Objectives What You Will Practice Select decision criteria Assign defensible weights Score concepts consistently Perform sensitivity analysis Materials What You Need Three concept descriptions or team sketches Decision matrix template Mission requirements Calculator or spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the mission requirements and identify six to eight decision criteria. Assign weights totaling 100%. Define a 1-5 scoring scale for every criterion before scoring concepts. Score all three concepts and document evidence. Calculate weighted totals. Change the two largest weights by plus/minus 10 percentage points and recalculate. Identify whether the winner changes. Recommend a concept and state the largest unresolved risk. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least three concepts and six criteria Weights total 100% Scoring definitions written before final scoring All scores supported by evidence or assumptions Include one sensitivity analysis Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not change criteria solely to make a preferred concept win Label uncertain assumptions Use the same scoring standard for all concepts Deliverables What You Submit Criteria and weights Scoring definitions Completed trade matrix Sensitivity comparison Recommendation memo Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion drove the decision most strongly? Did sensitivity analysis change confidence in the winner? What missing test data would reduce uncertainty? Where might personal bias have affected scoring? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Write scoring anchors such as “5 = meets requirement with at least 20% margin.” Common Mistake Assigning numbers without defined scoring rules creates a false appearance of precision. Stretch Goal Add cost and schedule uncertainty using best-case and worst-case scores. Career Connection Systems engineering teams use formal trade studies to select architectures, sensors, propulsion, and mission concepts. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → POE Unit 5 Page

Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 5 | Mission Brief 5.1 Rover Mission Requirements Audit Turn a broad rover mission statement into clear, testable engineering requirements. Intermediate 1 class period Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A client has requested “a reliable rover that can transport a payload across rough terrain.” The statement is not specific enough to design or verify. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish needs from requirements Write measurable shall-statements Identify verification methods Detect conflicting or missing requirements Materials What You Need Mission statement Requirements template Engineering notebook Optional sample rover data Procedure Student Instructions Underline every user need or desired function in the mission statement. Convert each need into one or more measurable requirements. Add units, limits, conditions, and success criteria. Assign a verification method: inspection, analysis, demonstration, or test. Identify at least two missing requirements and one possible conflict. Prioritize requirements as Must, Should, or Could. Conduct a peer audit and revise unclear statements. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least ten measurable requirements Every requirement uses a defined condition and limit Each requirement has a verification method Avoid solution-specific wording unless required by the client Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not invent unrealistic performance limits Maintain traceability to the original mission need Clearly mark assumptions Deliverables What You Submit Need-to-requirement table Prioritized requirement list Verification matrix Conflict/missing-information note Revised final set Reflection Reflection Questions Which user need was hardest to make measurable? What requirement could unintentionally restrict design creativity? Which requirement has the highest mission risk? What question should be returned to the client? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A strong requirement states what the system must accomplish, not how the designer must accomplish it. Common Mistake Words such as reliable, fast, lightweight, and easy are not testable without a number or condition. Stretch Goal Add interface requirements for charging, payload attachment, or data transfer. Career Connection Systems engineers manage requirements and verification across complex aerospace projects. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 5 Next Lesson → POE Unit 5 Page

Advanced 2-3 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover design review requires objective evidence of reliability. Each team will complete repeated missions under the same conditions and receive one controlled fault scenario. Objectives What You Will Practice Define reliability metrics Run repeated controlled trials Calculate success rate Respond to a fault without unsafe behavior Materials What You Need Rover and mission course Standard payload Timer Fault scenario cards Data sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the scoring categories and identify how each will be measured. Complete a preflight inspection. Run three baseline missions and record time, path error, and task success. Receive one instructor-approved fault such as blocked sensor view, shifted target, or low-traction surface. Run two fault-condition missions. Calculate overall success rate and average completion time. Explain how the system detected or failed to detect the fault. Make one approved change and complete a final demonstration. Requirements Engineering Requirements Same code for official baseline trials Complete required mission task and return safely Record every trial, including failures Fault condition must not create unsafe motion Score includes reliability, not only fastest time Constraints Constraints & Safety Emergency stop required Instructor controls fault setup Do not alter another team’s equipment Keep all observers outside the course Deliverables What You Submit Preflight checklist Five-trial data set Reliability calculations Fault analysis Final demonstration result Reflection Reflection Questions What was the most frequent failure mode? Did the fastest trial represent normal performance? How should reliability be reported with only a few trials? What design change would reduce operator dependence? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use identical start configuration for every official trial to make the comparison fair. Common Mistake Deleting failed trials creates a misleading reliability result. Stretch Goal Complete ten consecutive missions and calculate a larger-sample success rate. Career Connection Flight-test and reliability engineers analyze repeated trials, anomalies, and fault responses before operational approval. Why did the highest winding level not necessarily give the best result? How did mass affect acceleration or consistency? What variable would you test next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Mark the axle so every trial begins with the same winding reference. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.1 Select a Material for a Drone Arm Compare candidate materials and recommend the best choice for a defined drone-arm scenario. Advanced 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small inspection drone needs a replacement arm. The material must be light, stiff enough, manufacturable, and affordable. Objectives What You Will Practice Use material properties in a trade study Distinguish strength, stiffness, density, and toughness Apply weighted decision criteria Defend an engineering recommendation Materials What You Need Candidate material data sheets Decision matrix template Calculator or spreadsheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the mission profile, arm dimensions, expected load, and available manufacturing processes. Compare aluminum, PLA, ABS, nylon, and carbon-fiber composite using density, stiffness, strength, toughness, cost, and manufacturability. Choose weighting factors that total 100%. Normalize or score each material consistently. Complete the weighted decision matrix. Perform one simple mass comparison using equal part volume. Identify one property not captured well by the numerical matrix. Write a recommendation with one risk and one verification test. Requirements Engineering Requirements Compare at least five candidate materials Use at least six criteria Explain all weighting choices Include one quantitative mass comparison Identify a verification test before flight use Constraints Constraints & Safety Use provided or credible property data Do not treat all composites as identical Recommendation applies only to the stated mission and geometry No physical load testing beyond approved classroom limits Deliverables What You Submit Material-property comparison table Weighted decision matrix Mass calculation Recommendation memo Risk and test plan Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion controlled the result? How would a crash-resistance requirement change the choice? Why might the lightest material not be best? What data would you verify with a supplier? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Strength and stiffness are different. A material may resist breaking but still bend too much. Common Mistake A decision matrix does not replace judgment. Poor data or arbitrary weights can produce a misleading winner. Stretch Goal Recalculate the matrix for a cold-weather mission or a low-cost training drone. Career Connection Materials and aerospace engineers select materials by balancing performance, environment, manufacturing, cost, and risk. items.searchText: Sensor Data Quality Investigation POE 4.3 Sensor Data Quality Investigation | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Work independently or with an approved partner. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.3 Sensor Data Quality Investigation Determine whether a sensor data set is accurate, precise, biased, or affected by noise. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A rover environmental sensor is producing inconsistent readings. Before replacing hardware, the test team must characterize the data and identify likely error sources. Objectives What You Will Practice Distinguish accuracy and precision Calculate mean, range, and standard deviation Detect bias and outliers Recommend a calibration or filtering method Materials What You Need Sensor or instructor-provided data set Reference standard Spreadsheet Graphing tools Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Collect or receive at least 20 readings under a constant condition. Record a trusted reference value. Calculate mean, range, standard deviation, and error of the mean from the reference. Create a time-series graph and a histogram or dot plot. Identify any outliers using an instructor-approved rule. Repeat measurements after one controlled change such as repositioning, shielding, or recalibration. Compare the two data sets. Recommend keep, calibrate, filter, reposition, or replace. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least 20 readings per primary condition Reference value clearly identified Include numerical measures of center and spread Do not remove outliers without documenting the rule Recommendation must be supported by evidence Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not expose sensors to unsafe conditions Do not fabricate readings Keep environmental variables controlled unless intentionally tested Deliverables What You Submit Raw data Calculations Two graphs Outlier decision Before/after comparison Sensor recommendation Reflection Reflection Questions Was the main problem bias or variation? What evidence supported removing or retaining an outlier? Which controlled change improved data quality most? What filter could reduce noise without hiding real changes? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Plot data in time order before summarizing it; drift may disappear in a simple average. Common Mistake Removing all unusual values because they look inconvenient can hide a real fault. Stretch Goal Implement and compare a moving-average filter with two different window sizes. Career Connection Instrumentation and test engineers validate sensors used for navigation, structures, propulsion, and environmental monitoring. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 4 Next Lesson → POE Unit 4 Page

Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Sensor-Calibrated Rover Stop Calibrate a distance sensor and program a rover to stop within a defined target zone. Intermediate 1 class period Practice & Review Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context An autonomous service rover must stop at a docking station without striking it or leaving too large a gap. Objectives What You Will Practice Collect sensor calibration data Use conditional logic Evaluate accuracy and repeatability Tune a control threshold Materials What You Need VEX rover or approved mobile platform Distance sensor Programming environment Tape measure Target wall Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Record sensor readings at known distances across the operating range. Create a calibration table and identify any offset or unstable region. Program the rover to approach slowly and stop at the initial threshold. Run five trials from the same start point. Measure final stopping distance for every trial. Adjust speed, threshold, or confirmation logic. Run five final trials and calculate average error and range. Requirements Engineering Requirements Stop inside the instructor-defined target zone Complete five consecutive final trials Use sensor data rather than a fixed travel time Include a controlled low-speed approach Constraints Constraints & Safety Use a clear test lane Install an emergency stop or immediate control method Do not run the rover toward people Keep sensor face unobstructed Deliverables What You Submit Calibration table Program with comments Initial and final trial data Average error and range Tuning reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why did stopping distance vary between trials? How did approach speed affect error? What sensor readings should be ignored? How could the rover detect a missing docking station? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Use several consecutive valid readings before declaring that the stop threshold has been reached. Common Mistake Using one sensor reading can make the rover react to noise or a brief reflection. Stretch Goal Add a second phase that aligns the rover after stopping. Career Connection Controls engineers calibrate sensors and tune approach logic for autonomous vehicles, docking systems, and robotic manipulators. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 3 | Mission Brief 3.1 Simplify the Rocket Assembly Redesign the assembly to reduce part count or assembly time while preserving required function and overall envelope. Advanced 2 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context The current rocket assembly works, but technicians report too many parts, repeated fasteners, and slow assembly. Objectives What You Will Practice Analyze assembly complexity Apply design for assembly principles Preserve interfaces and motion Compare original and revised assemblies Materials What You Need Existing rocket assembly CAD Fusion 360 Bill of materials Stopwatch or assembly-time estimate sheet Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Create a baseline BOM and count unique parts, total parts, fasteners, and assembly steps. Identify three assembly pain points. Generate two redesign concepts that combine parts, replace fasteners, improve alignment, or reduce orientation errors. Use a decision matrix to select a redesign. Modify the CAD assembly and update joints or constraints. Create an updated BOM and assembly sequence. Compare predicted assembly time and part count. Check for new manufacturing, repair, or tolerance problems. Requirements Engineering Requirements Reduce total part count or assembly steps by at least 20% Preserve rocket exterior envelope and required interfaces Maintain access to parts that may require replacement Use realistic manufacturing methods Update the assembly and BOM completely Constraints Constraints & Safety No change may interfere with the provided rocket requirements Use only available manufacturing processes Do not hide separate components by merely grouping them in CAD Deliverables What You Submit Baseline BOM and sequence Three identified pain points Two concept sketches Decision matrix Revised assembly file Updated BOM Before/after comparison Reflection Reflection Questions Which assembly step created the greatest difficulty? How did your redesign affect repairability? What tolerance issue could appear in the combined part? What physical test should verify the change? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Every time a technician must pick up, orient, or fasten a part is an opportunity for simplification. Common Mistake Combining parts can make manufacturing harder or prevent repair. Evaluate the full life cycle. Stretch Goal Create a mistake-proof feature that prevents one part from being installed backward. Career Connection Design-for-assembly engineers reduce part count, handling, fastening, and orientation errors to improve production. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed Back to Unit 3 Next Lesson → IED Unit 3 Page

items.title: Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization ADM 2.3 Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Falcon Manufacturing Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.3 Smart Conveyor Throughput Optimization Increase conveyor-line throughput while maintaining safe spacing and routing accuracy. Advanced 2 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Falcon Manufacturing Department: Production Engineering Goal: Increase verified line throughput by at least 20%. Background Engineering Context Falcon Manufacturing must raise output without purchasing a second line. The conveyors, robot, and routing cylinders are not synchronized, producing idle time in some zones and part bunching in others. Teams will optimize the coordinated process. Objectives What You Will Practice Measure system throughput and spacing Analyze interactions between robot and conveyor timing Use data to optimize a multi-device process Balance speed, accuracy, and reliability Equipment What You Need VEX CTE Workcell Conveyors Sensors Pneumatics 6-Axis Arm if used Thirty parts Stopwatch Spreadsheet Procedure Student Instructions Run a ten-part baseline trial and record total time, part spacing, and failures. Measure the time required by each major station. Identify the bottleneck station and explain your evidence. Propose at least three software changes. Test one change at a time with ten parts. Choose final conveyor speeds and release logic. Run a thirty-part final trial. Calculate throughput in parts per minute and percent improvement. Requirements Engineering Requirements Increase throughput by at least 20% Maintain zero collisions and correct routing Keep at least the approved minimum spacing between parts Complete thirty final parts without manual intervention Constraints Constraints & Safety Do not move hardware Conveyor speed may not exceed approved classroom limits Safety-stop code must remain active Final settings must be documented Deliverables What You Submit Baseline and final code Station-time study Throughput and spacing data Before/after graph Bottleneck explanation Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which station controlled maximum throughput? Why did increasing one conveyor not always improve the full line? How did reliability influence your final setting? What buffer would help the system? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Optimize the bottleneck first; speeding a non-bottleneck station may only create waiting or jams. Common Mistake Changing conveyor speed, robot speed, and waits simultaneously makes it impossible to identify the useful change. Stretch Goal Develop an adaptive release interval that changes based on downstream sensor status. Career Connection Industrial engineers use line-balancing and bottleneck analysis to improve complete production systems. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 2 Page
