Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 4 | Mission Brief 4.5 Smart Factory Integration Capstone Propose and demonstrate a secure, scheduled, and resilient smart-factory system for an aerospace product. Advanced 3-5 class periods Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing Department: Smart Factory Program Goal: Design and defend an integrated aerospace manufacturing system. Background Engineering Context Lockwood Aerospace Manufacturing is selecting a team to design its next small smart factory. The proposal must integrate automation, data, quality, scheduling, packaging, cybersecurity, and contingency planning into one coherent system. Objectives What You Will Practice Integrate technical and operational manufacturing systems Create production and information-flow models Use trade studies to justify decisions Present and defend a complete system proposal Equipment What You Need ADM workcell and/or digital twin Layout and process-mapping tools Demand and capacity data Cybersecurity and risk templates Presentation software Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Select one aerospace product or component from the provided options. Define product specifications, demand, due dates, and quality checks. Create a factory layout showing material flow, robot/conveyor stations, inspection, packaging, and shipping. Create an information-flow diagram showing sensors, production data, operator inputs, and protected systems. Develop a production schedule and calculate expected throughput. Program or simulate one critical automated sequence. Create a cybersecurity risk assessment with at least five controls. Create a resilience plan for one machine failure and one supplier delay. Build a decision matrix comparing your design with one alternate concept. Present the proposal and answer questions from a review panel. Requirements Engineering Requirements Meet the stated demand target or document the capacity gap Include automation, inspection, packaging, scheduling, cybersecurity, and resilience Provide at least one tested or simulated automation sequence Support major decisions with data or a trade study Include clear safety and reset procedures Constraints Constraints & Safety Use available classroom tools and realistic capacity assumptions No safety or quality requirement may be removed to improve throughput Protect sensitive production data in the system design Presentation time is limited to eight minutes Deliverables What You Submit Factory layout Material and information flow diagrams Production schedule and throughput calculation Automation code or simulation evidence Cybersecurity risk plan Resilience plan Decision matrix Eight-minute presentation Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which subsystem most limited factory performance? What tradeoff had the greatest effect on your design? How did cybersecurity influence physical layout or workflow? What would you validate before purchasing equipment? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip A strong smart-factory design connects physical flow, information flow, decision logic, and recovery planning. Common Mistake Adding more technology without defining interfaces and ownership can make a factory less reliable, not smarter. Stretch Goal Create a cost estimate and calculate the expected payback period for the proposed automation. Career Connection Smart manufacturing systems engineers integrate robotics, software, data, quality, cybersecurity, and operations. Back to Unit 2 View Code What You Submit Lesson Focus Sense, decide, sort Use an optical sensor reading to classify an object and move it to the correct output location. Lesson Overview Students explore how an automated system can identify and sort objects using sensor input. This example uses the optical sensor hue value to decide where the robotic arm should place the object. Notes This lesson introduces color-based sorting using an optical sensor. The robot picks up one object, moves it to the sensing location, and turns on the optical sensor light. The hue value is used to decide whether the object should go to one bin or another. The else branch provides a fail-safe response if the object does not match the expected color range. Final submitted code must include comments explaining pickup, sensing, decision logic, placement, and fail-safe behavior. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A launch provider is selecting a support frame design. Teams will compete using a scoring formula that rewards high load capacity and low structure mass. Objectives What You Will Practice Optimize structural geometry Use test data to revise a design Calculate an efficiency score Conduct a fair engineering competition Materials What You Need Standardized structural materials Adhesive Mass scale Load-test fixture Official dimension gauge Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Review the official span, height, and material limits. Sketch three possible structural layouts. Use a quick model or member-count estimate to select one. Build the structure and allow joints to cure. Measure mass and verify dimensions before the official test. Predict failure location and maximum load. Complete the official load test. Calculate the competition score using the provided formula. Document one redesign for a future round. Requirements Engineering Requirements Meet all dimensional limits Use only the issued quantity of material Structure must be free-standing in the fixture Official score uses successful load divided by structure mass No changes after official inspection Constraints Constraints & Safety Follow destructive-test safety boundary Do not stand over the structure Use only approved loading increments Wear eye protection Deliverables What You Submit Three concepts Inspection record Mass and load results Efficiency score Failure analysis Redesign sketch Reflection Reflection Questions Which design choice contributed most to the score? The package must protect the part while minimizing material and waste. Objectives What You Will Practice Balance protection and material use Apply life-cycle thinking Design packaging around a product Use test evidence to revise a solution Materials What You Need Provided rocket component or surrogate Corrugated cardboard, paperboard, paper, or approved recycled material Scale Ruler Drop-test area Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Measure the component and identify surfaces that must be protected. Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Protect the component by controlling movement and distributing impact, not just by adding more material. Common Mistake A package made from recyclable material is not sustainable if it uses far more material than necessary. Stretch Goal Design a reusable package that completes ten shipping cycles. Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions IED Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Thirty-Minute CAD Sprint Model a randomly assigned object accurately within 30 minutes, then evaluate which modeling choices improved speed and quality. Intermediate 30 minutes plus review Competition Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context Rapid CAD work is useful when engineers need a concept model for a meeting or prototype decision. Objectives What You Will Practice Plan an efficient feature sequence Use constraints and parameters quickly Prioritize critical geometry Review CAD quality under time pressure Materials What You Need Fusion 360 One approved object or dimension card Calipers or ruler Timer Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Draw or receive an object such as a LEGO-style brick, die, battery spacer, USB shell, or simple bracket. Spend three minutes identifying the base feature, repeated features, symmetry, and likely parameters. Record a short modeling plan before opening a sketch. Model for 25 minutes. Use the final two minutes to rename features, check constraints, and inspect dimensions. Export one screenshot showing the browser and completed model. Compare the model with the object or dimension card. Record one shortcut that helped and one rushed decision that caused rework. Requirements Engineering Requirements Use at least one named parameter Keep all major sketches fully constrained Include every critical feature Use patterns or symmetry where appropriate Finish within 30 minutes Constraints Constraints & Safety No imported models No help from another student during the timed period Accuracy is more important than decorative details Object must be instructor-approved Deliverables What You Submit Modeling plan Fusion file Final screenshot Accuracy checklist Short time-management reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Which feature should have been created first? A strong feature order saves more time than sketching immediately. Common Mistake Fast modeling is not the same as careless modeling. Unconstrained sketches create hidden problems later. items.searchText: Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake ADM 2.4 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Orion Robotics Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions ADM Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.4 Two-Station Manufacturing Handshake Create a safe request-ready-transfer-confirm handshake between two connected workstations. Advanced 2-3 class periods Engineering Challenge Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Production Specifications Orion Robotics Department: Systems Integration Goal: Exchange parts safely between two automated stations. Background Engineering Context Orion Robotics is connecting two manufacturing cells. Station A must never release a part until Station B is ready, and Station B must confirm receipt before Station A begins the next cycle. A failed signal could damage equipment or lose a product. Objectives What You Will Practice Design machine-to-machine communication logic Represent a process with states and flowcharts Program confirmation and timeout behavior Validate communication under normal and fault conditions Equipment What You Need Two connected VEX CTE workcells or a simulated two-station setup Object sensors Conveyors Signal tower Python projects Engineering notebook Procedure Student Instructions Define four signals: request, ready, transfer complete, and receipt confirmed. Create a sequence diagram showing which station sends each signal. Program Station B to announce ready only when its receiving zone is clear. Program Station A to wait for ready before releasing a part. Program Station B to confirm receipt after its sensor detects the part. Add a timeout that stops both stations if confirmation does not arrive. Run five normal transfers. Simulate a blocked receiving zone and a missing confirmation; verify safe response. Requirements Engineering Requirements Complete five consecutive normal transfers Never release into an occupied receiving zone Stop safely after a communication timeout Provide visible fault indication on the signal tower Constraints Constraints & Safety No assumptions based only on elapsed time Each transfer requires positive confirmation Stations must start from a documented reset state Fault testing must use approved simulations only Deliverables What You Submit Handshake state/sequence diagram Station A and B code Normal and fault test log Reset procedure Reflection Reflection Reflection Questions Why are both ready and receipt signals needed? What could happen if one station resets unexpectedly? How did the timeout improve safety? How would a PLC implement this handshake? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Name signals by meaning and state, such as receive_zone_clear, rather than vague names like flag1. Common Mistake A single ready signal is not enough if the sending station never verifies that the product arrived. Stretch Goal Coordinate three stations and include a line-wide stop and reset procedure. Career Connection Controls engineers design handshaking logic between robots, PLCs, conveyors, and inspection machines. Before You Submit Notebook evidence included Requirements checked Testing documented Reflection completed ← Previous Lesson Back to Unit 2 Next Lesson → Advanced Manufacturing Unit 2 Page

Engineering Context What You Will Practice What You Need Student Instructions Engineering Requirements Constraints & Safety What You Submit Reflection Questions POE Unit 2 | Mission Brief 2.2 Wing-Spar Material Trade Study Compare candidate materials for a model wing spar and recommend the best option for the mission. Intermediate 1-2 class periods Aerospace Mission Back to Challenge Hub Download Challenge Brief (PDF) Engineering Design Brief Work independently or with an approved partner. Read the complete brief before gathering materials or beginning construction. Background Engineering Context A small unmanned aircraft needs a wing spar that is stiff, light, affordable, and manufacturable with available tools. No single material is best in every category. Objectives What You Will Practice Compare material properties Create weighted decision criteria Conduct simple bending tests Defend a materials recommendation Materials What You Need Samples of wood, plastic, aluminum, composite substitute, or approved materials Mass scale Ruler Test fixture Small loads Decision matrix Procedure Student Instructions Define mission priorities for mass, stiffness, cost, availability, and manufacturability. Measure sample dimensions and mass. Perform a consistent bending test on each material using the same span and load. Record deflection and any permanent damage. Normalize or rank each material for the five criteria. Create a weighted decision matrix. Recommend one material and identify the biggest risk in that choice. Requirements Engineering Requirements At least four candidate materials Same span, support spacing, and test load for every sample Decision matrix must include at least five criteria Recommendation must cite both test data and mission priorities Constraints Constraints & Safety Stay below instructor-approved load limits Wear eye protection during bending tests Do not test brittle materials near faces Handle sharp metal edges carefully Deliverables What You Submit Material property table Bending-test data Weighted decision matrix Mission recommendation Risk statement Reflection Reflection Questions Which criterion most strongly affected the result? Did the stiffest material have the best overall score? How would production quantity change the decision? What missing property would you test next? Download PDF Print This Page Engineering Tip Compare materials using equivalent geometry whenever possible; geometry can dominate stiffness. Common Mistake A decision matrix is not objective if weights are chosen after seeing the test results. Stretch Goal Repeat the trade study for a different mission that prioritizes cost or impact resistance. Career Connection Materials and structures engineers select alloys, polymers, composites, and sandwich structures based on mission-specific tradeoffs. Back to Unit 2 View Code What You Submit Lesson Focus Stop, signal, respond Use event-based programming to stop motion and show a clear visual safety response. Lesson Overview Students learn how safety controls can be built into an automated workcell. This example uses a signal tower button to stop robot motion, display a message, and change tower lights when control has stopped. Notes This lesson focuses on safe workcell behavior and emergency stop logic. The signal tower button is used as an input that triggers a stop response. The control-stopped event changes the signal tower colors to show that the arm has stopped. The repeated movement loop creates motion that can be interrupted by the safety control. Final submitted code must include comments explaining the stop function, event handlers, signal tower behavior, and repeated motion. items.searchText: Engineering, physics, and advanced manufacturing resources for aerospace-minded students. About | LockwoodSTEM LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Jonathan Lockwood Make engineering feel real, useful, and possible. Learn by building and documenting. What students can find here IED POE ADM Aerospace as the design lens A classroom built for making What this site reinforces Document evidence Revise with purpose Work safely Communicate clearly Ready to use the site? Explore the LockwoodSTEM Challenge Library About LockwoodSTEM Engineering, physics, and advanced manufacturing resources for aerospace-minded students. LockwoodSTEM is a student-facing hub for course lessons, FabLab resources, engineering design workflows, and classroom systems used in the Academy of Advanced Aerospace Engineering at Cornerstone Charter Academy. Explore Courses Visit the FabLab JL Instructor & Academy Chair Jonathan Lockwood Engineering, physics, robotics, and FabLab learning built around hands-on problem solving and real documentation. Mission Make engineering feel real, useful, and possible. This site is designed to help students move from ideas to evidence. Lessons connect design thinking, technical communication, CAD, programming, prototyping, testing, and reflection so students can build confidence as problem solvers. Learning approach Learn by building and documenting. Students are expected to sketch, model, build, test, revise, and explain their decisions. The goal is not just completing a project; the goal is developing the habits engineers use to communicate and improve their work. Course pathways What students can find here LockwoodSTEM organizes course materials, unit pages, lesson pages, resources, and FabLab supports in one place. IED Introduction to Engineering Design focuses on design process, sketching, measurement, CAD, prototyping, technical drawings, and portfolio-ready documentation. POE Principles of Engineering connects mechanisms, systems, structures, energy, circuits, data, and engineering analysis through applied design challenges. ADM Advanced Manufacturing introduces automation, robotic workcells, sensors, digital twins, cybersecurity, supply chain thinking, and Industry 4.0 workflows. Academy of Advanced Aerospace Engineering Aerospace as the design lens The academy uses aerospace-themed problems to help students practice engineering habits in a focused context. Students apply classroom concepts to rockets, rovers, mechanisms, manufacturing systems, technical documentation, and design challenges. Problem definition and criteria/constraints Research-informed brainstorming and concept selection CAD, prototyping, fabrication, and testing Technical communication and presentation evidence CCA FabLab A classroom built for making The FabLab supports hands-on learning with student workstations, digital fabrication tools, robotics equipment, engineering notebooks, and certification-based safety systems. 3D printing and prototyping workflows Laser cutting, shop safety, and tool certification Robotics, automation, and programming practice Documentation, inspection, and revision habits Student habits What this site reinforces Document evidence Notebook entries, sketches, screenshots, code, photos, test data, and reflections show how the work developed. Revise with purpose Students are encouraged to use feedback and testing results to make their designs stronger. Work safely FabLab access depends on safe habits, tool certification, PPE, and responsible use of equipment. Communicate clearly Strong engineering work includes clear decisions, constraints, technical details, and final explanations. Start here Ready to use the site? Students should begin with the course page, open the current unit, and follow the lesson pathway in order. items.title: Advanced Automation in Manufacturing
items.description: LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools.
items.searchText: Advanced Automation in Manufacturing ADM Unit 2 | Advanced Automation in Manufacturing LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Build smarter automated systems Lesson Sequence Essential Questions Learning Targets Major Deliverables Unit 2 support materials Recommended Certifications Resources Key Vocabulary ADM Unit 2 Advanced Automation in Manufacturing Students explore industrial workcells, workcell safety, sensors, machine vision, pneumatics, handshaking, predictive maintenance, productivity, optimization, and coordinated movement. 🚀 Engineering Challenge Hub View Lessons Unit Challenge Back to ADM Unit Goal Build smarter automated systems This unit focuses on how manufacturing systems sense conditions, communicate between devices, move materials, improve productivity, and coordinate multiple actions safely. Unit pathway Lesson Sequence Open each lesson in order and document your work as you move through the unit. Lesson Type Title Focus Open Industrial Workcells, Sorting & Pneumatics Students learn how automated workcells are designed, operated, programmed, and improved using safety procedures, logic, material transportation, and pneumatic motion. Activity 2.1.1 Activity Industrial Workcell Explore how machines, robots, sensors, conveyors, and people work together in an automated manufacturing system. Open Lesson Activity 2.1.2 Activity Workcell Safety Learn how safety zones, emergency stops, procedures, and safe operating habits protect people and equipment. Open Lesson Activity 2.1.3 Activity Sorting by Color Use sensor input or programmed logic to identify and sort objects based on color or another visible property. Open Lesson Activity 2.1.4 Activity Conditionals and Loops Use programming logic to make decisions, repeat actions, and control automated processes. Open Lesson Activity 2.1.5 Activity Material Transportation Investigate how materials move through a workcell using conveyors, robots, carriers, or other handling systems. Open Lesson Activity 2.1.6 Activity Pneumatics Learn how compressed air creates controlled motion through cylinders, valves, and actuators. Open Lesson Project 2.1.7 Project Sorting Challenge Design, program, test, and document an automated sorting process that separates or organizes objects using defined criteria. Open Lesson Machine Vision, Sensors & System Communication Students explore how automated systems detect, classify, inspect, and communicate before completing the next step in a process. Activity 2.2.1 Activity Machine Vision Explore how cameras and vision systems can identify, inspect, measure, or sort objects in manufacturing. Open Lesson Activity 2.2.2 Activity Bring Your Own Sensors Investigate different sensor types and how each could be used to detect conditions in a manufacturing workcell. Open Lesson Activity 2.2.3 Activity Sensor Applications Apply sensor input to solve a manufacturing problem involving position, presence, color, distance, orientation, or status. Open Lesson Project 2.2.4 Project Handshaking Create or analyze a system where devices communicate before moving to the next step of an automated process. Open Lesson Predictive Maintenance, Productivity & Optimization Students examine how manufacturing systems are monitored, maintained, measured, and improved using data and evidence. Activity 2.3.1 Activity Predictive Maintenance Explore how data, sensors, inspection, and maintenance records can identify problems before equipment fails. Open Lesson Activity 2.3.2 Activity Maximizing Productivity Analyze how workflow, timing, automation, layout, and process decisions affect productivity in a manufacturing system. Open Lesson Project 2.3.3 Project Optimization Impact Study Evaluate how one change to a process affects productivity, quality, reliability, cost, or efficiency. Open Lesson Coordinated Movement Challenge Problem Students combine workcell safety, sensors, communication, timing, material movement, pneumatics, and optimization in a final unit challenge. Problem 2.4.1 Problem Coordinated Movement Design, program, test, and document an automated process that requires multiple parts of a manufacturing system to coordinate movement safely and reliably. Open Lesson Essential Questions How do industrial workcells combine machines, sensors, robots, and people into one system? How can sensors, logic, and communication improve automated manufacturing? How do engineers monitor, maintain, and optimize automated systems? How can multiple devices coordinate movement safely and reliably? Learning Targets I can identify major components of an automated workcell. I can explain how sensors, conditionals, loops, and handshaking control automation. I can describe how pneumatics and material transportation support manufacturing flow. I can use data and testing evidence to improve a manufacturing process. Major Deliverables Engineering notebook entries Workcell layout or system diagram Code or program documentation Sensor/input-output evidence Testing, debugging, and optimization notes Coordinated Movement Challenge reflection Student resources Unit 2 support materials Recommended Certifications Engineering Safety Engineering Documentation Robotics / programming expectations Hand & Cutting Tools, if building fixtures Soldering or electronics safety, if using sen Advanced Manufacturing Unit 2 Unit

items.description: IED Unit 4: Aerospace Mechanisms, Materials & Electromechanical Systems lesson hub.
items.searchText: Aerospace Mechanisms, Materials & Electromechanical Systems IED Unit 4 | Aerospace Mechanisms, Materials & Electromechanical Systems | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 4: Aerospace Mechanisms, Materials & Electromechanical Systems lesson hub. Build and defend a functional aerospace mechanism or electromechanical system prototype. What Unit 4 Builds Unit 4 Individual Lessons Unit 4 Resources Introduction to Engineering Design Data, Decision Matrix, Planning, and Design Review IED Unit 4 Aerospace Mechanisms, Materials & Electromechanical Systems Unit mission: Investigate materials, mechanisms, motion, friction, data, statistics, circuits, motors, and electromechanical integration through an aerospace prototype challenge. Lesson Map Resources Back to IED Hub Unit Focus Build and defend a functional aerospace mechanism or electromechanical system prototype. Test Integrate Revise Every lesson builds evidence for the final technical demonstration and design documentation. Unit Overview What Unit 4 Builds Students connect physical science, materials, mechanisms, circuits, and data analysis to an engineering prototype. Materials + Testing Students compare material properties, test samples, interpret measurement error, and make evidence-based selections. Mechanisms + Motion Students explore linkages, hinges, cams, gears, pulleys, friction, forces, motion graphs, and system behavior. Electromechanical Prototype Students integrate simple circuits or motors, develop test protocols, analyze data, revise, and demonstrate a working system. Lesson Map Unit 4 Individual Lessons Each lesson has its own presentation and immersive lesson page. Lesson Title Focus Presentation 4.1 Unit 4 Challenge Launch: Aerospace Mechanisms, Materials & Electromechanical Systems How can materials, mechanisms, circuits, and data work together in an aerospace system? PPTX 4.2 Aerospace Materials and Material Properties How do material properties influence aerospace design decisions? PPTX 4.3 Material Testing Lab How can engineers test materials before choosing them for a prototype? PPTX 4.4 Statistics and Measurement Error How can statistics help engineers trust and interpret test results? PPTX 4.5 Mechanisms and Types of Motion How do mechanisms change or control motion in aerospace systems? PPTX 4.6 Mechanism Exploration: Linkages, Hinges, Cams, Gears, and Pulleys How can physical mechanism exploration reveal design possibilities and limitations? PPTX 4.7 Friction, Force, and Mechanism Performance How does friction affect whether a mechanism works reliably? PPTX 4.8 Motion Graphs and System Behavior How can graphs help engineers understand system behavior over time? PPTX 4.9 Electrical Safety and Simple Circuits How can simple circuits safely support an engineering prototype? PPTX 4.10 Motors and Electromechanical Motion How can electrical energy create useful mechanical motion? PPTX 4.11 Concept Generation and Decision Matrix How can engineers choose a mechanism concept using evidence and criteria? PPTX 4.12 System Architecture and Subsystem Planning How do subsystems work together in an aerospace prototype? PPTX 4.13 CAD Planning and Assembly Layout How can CAD planning prepare a mechanism for physical construction? PPTX 4.14 CAD Modeling Workday: Components, Motion, and Fit How do engineers model and check parts before building? PPTX 4.15 Prototype Build Day 1: Structure and Mechanism How do engineers build the structure and core mechanism of a prototype? PPTX 4.16 Prototype Build Day 2: Electrical or Electromechanical Integration How can electrical or electromechanical features be integrated safely into a prototype? PPTX 4.17 Testing Protocol Development How do engineers design fair tests to evaluate whether a prototype works? PPTX 4.18 Prototype Testing and Data Collection How can engineers collect useful data from a prototype test? PPTX 4.19 Data Analysis, Graphing, and Design Conclusions How can data help engineers decide whether a prototype was successful? PPTX 4.20 Iteration and Prototype Revision How do engineers decide what to change after testing a prototype? PPTX 4.21 Final Technical Documentation: Mechanism, Circuit, Data, and Revision How do engineers document a functional system so others can understand, test, build, or improve it? PPTX 4.22 Unit 4 Technical Demonstration and Reflection How can engineers use a technical demonstration to communicate how a system works and how it improved? Design structures that balance strength, stiffness, mass, materials, and load performance. What Unit 2 Builds Aerospace Payload Support Structure Design goal Required evidence Performance data Unit 2 Individual Lessons Unit 2 Resources Principles of Engineering Engineering Resources Unit 2 Challenges POE Unit 2 Aerospace Structures & Materials Unit mission: Analyze how structures carry loads, how materials behave, and how evidence supports a payload support design. Lesson Map Resources Back to POE Hub Unit Focus Design structures that balance strength, stiffness, mass, materials, and load performance. Analyze Test Defend Every lesson builds toward a payload support structure supported by calculations, material evidence, and load-test data. Unit Overview What Unit 2 Builds Students investigate loads, free body diagrams, vectors, moments, equilibrium, trusses, centroids, stiffness, materials, density, testing, and structural design evidence. Structural Analysis Students identify force effects and use diagrams, vectors, moments, and equilibrium to explain structural behavior. Materials + Testing Students compare material families, density, structural efficiency, and test behavior using controlled evidence. Design Challenge Students plan, build, load-test, iterate, and defend an aerospace payload support structure. Unit Project Aerospace Payload Support Structure Design and test a lightweight structure that supports a payload under defined criteria and constraints. Design goal Support the required payload safely while using material and geometry efficiently. Required evidence Problem statement, criteria and constraints, sketches, calculations, decision matrix, prototype photos, load data, and final design review. Performance data Teams collect repeated measurements such as supported load, mass, deflection, failure point, structural efficiency, and revision evidence. items.searchText: Parametric CAD and Part Design IED Unit 2 | Parametric CAD and Part Design | LockwoodSTEM IED Unit 2: Parametric CAD and Part Design lesson hub. Model, print, test, and revise using evidence from CAD and physical tolerances. What Unit 2 Builds Unit 2 Individual Lessons Unit 2 Resources Introduction to Engineering Design FabLab Certifications IED Unit 2 Parametric CAD and Part Design Unit mission: Build accurate CAD parts, prepare models for fabrication, and use a 3D printed tolerance tester to recommend future assembly clearances. Lesson Map Resources Back to IED Hub Unit Focus Model, print, test, and revise using evidence from CAD and physical tolerances. Model Print Test Every lesson builds toward a printable tolerance tester and a clearance recommendation for future rocket assemblies. Unit Overview What Unit 2 Builds Students move from sketch-based documentation into controlled, editable, fabrication-ready CAD models. CAD Control Sketch constraints, dimensions, parameters, and features make models precise and editable. Aerospace Parts Nose cones, fins, mounting features, and printed testers connect CAD tools to aerospace design decisions. Fabrication Evidence Slicer previews, print settings, measurements, and fit tests connect digital models to physical parts. Lesson Map Unit 2 Individual Lessons Each lesson has its own presentation and immersive lesson page. Lesson Title Focus Presentation 2.1 From Engineering Documentation to CAD How does CAD build on sketching and documentation? PPTX 2.2 Fusion 360 Interface and File Setup How do engineers set up a CAD file for organized work? PPTX 2.3 Sketch Planes and 2D Sketching How does a 2D sketch become the foundation of a CAD model? PPTX 2.4 Sketch Constraints How do constraints control design intent? PPTX 2.5 Dimensioned CAD Sketches How do dimensions make CAD models precise and adjustable? PPTX 2.6 Extrude Basics How does extrusion turn a sketch into a solid part? PPTX 2.7 Cut Features and Holes How do cuts and holes create functional features? PPTX 2.8 Fillets, Chamfers, and Design Intent How do edge features improve function, safety, and printability? PPTX 2.9 Revolve Features: Nose Cone and Nozzle How can rotation create aerospace-shaped parts? PPTX 2.10 Patterns and Symmetry: Rocket Fins How can patterns create repeated features accurately? PPTX 2.11 Parametric Rocket Part Modeling How can parameters make a model easier to revise? PPTX 2.12 CAD Model Check and Revision How do engineers check a model before fabrication? PPTX 2.13 Preparing CAD Files for 3D Printing How is a CAD model prepared for 3D printing? PPTX 2.14 Slicer Basics and Print Settings How do slicer settings affect a printed part? PPTX 2.15 FabLab 3D Printer Certification How do safety and workflow expectations prepare you for printing? PPTX 2.16 Final 3D Printed Tolerance Tester Workday How can a printed tester help determine future assembly clearances? PPTX 2.17 3D Printing Post-Processing How do engineers inspect and finish a printed part? PPTX 2.18 Final Tolerance Tester Review and Recommendation What clearance should be recommended for the next rocket assembly project? items.searchText: Securing the Supply Chain ADM Unit 4 | Securing the Supply Chain LockwoodSTEM student engineering courses, lessons, challenges, resources, and FabLab tools. Protect the system Lesson Sequence Essential Questions Learning Targets Major Deliverables Unit 4 support materials Recommended Certifications Resources Key Vocabulary ADM Unit 4 Securing the Supply Chain Students explore cybersecurity, data integrity, secure software, demand planning, procurement, production scheduling, packaging, accessibility, and resilient manufacturing. 🚀 Engineering Challenge Hub View Lessons Unit Challenge Back to ADM Unit Goal Protect the system This unit focuses on how manufacturers protect products, data, people, timelines, quality, and delivery systems from disruption. Unit pathway Lesson Sequence Open each lesson in order and document your work as you move through the unit. Lesson Type Title Focus Open Cybersecurity, Data Integrity & Secure Software Students explore how cybersecurity affects connected machines, sensors, software, data, people, and production environments. Activity 4.1.1 Activity CIA Triad Learn how confidentiality, integrity, and availability apply to connected manufacturing systems and production data. Open Lesson Activity 4.1.2 Activity Human in the Lab Explore how human decisions, access, mistakes, and procedures affect the safety and security of a manufacturing system. Open Lesson Activity 4.1.3 Activity Malware Investigate how malicious software can disrupt machines, corrupt data, delay production, or create unsafe conditions. Open Lesson Activity 4.1.4 Activity Problems With Data Analyze how missing, incorrect, corrupted, or poorly formatted data can affect manufacturing decisions and product quality. Open Lesson Activity 4.1.5 Activity Secure Software Explore how software design, updates, access control, and secure coding habits help protect automated systems. Open Lesson Project 4.1.6 Project Malfunctioning Lab Analyze a lab scenario where a system is malfunctioning due to data, software, cybersecurity, or human-factor issues. Open Lesson Demand, Procurement, Scheduling & Packaging Students explore how manufacturing teams plan for demand, choose suppliers, schedule production, and package products for shipping and use. Activity 4.2.1 Activity Determining Demand Investigate how manufacturers estimate demand and use that information to plan materials, production, staffing, and delivery. Open Lesson Activity 4.2.2 Activity Procurement Explore how companies select, purchase, and manage materials, parts, tools, and suppliers needed for production. Open Lesson Activity 4.2.3 Activity Production Scheduling Analyze how manufacturing teams organize time, machines, people, and materials to meet production goals. Open Lesson Activity 4.2.4 Activity Packaging Study how packaging protects products, supports shipping, communicates information, and affects cost and sustainability. Open Lesson Activity 4.2.5 Activity Accessibility in Packaging Evaluate how packaging design affects usability, accessibility, safety, and customer experience. Open Lesson Project 4.2.6 Project Packing Optimization Improve a packing or packaging solution by balancing space, protection, cost, usability, accessibility, and shipping efficiency. Open Lesson Resilient Manufacturing Challenge Problem Students combine cybersecurity, supply chain planning, packaging, accessibility, scheduling, and risk analysis in a final unit challenge. Problem 4.3.1 Problem Resilient Manufacturing Analyze or design a manufacturing process that can prevent, detect, respond to, and recover from disruptions while protecting production, data, products, and people. Open Lesson Essential Questions Why is cybersecurity important in connected manufacturing? How can data, software, and human decisions disrupt production? How do demand, procurement, scheduling, and packaging affect supply chain performance? How can manufacturers design systems that prevent, respond to, and recover from disruptions? Learning Targets I can explain the CIA triad in a manufacturing context. I can identify data, software, cybersecurity, and human-factor risks. I can analyze how demand, procurement, scheduling, and packaging decisions affect production. I can recommend improvements that increase manufacturing resilience.
